title: The Crossing
body: Humans come ashore on Dia-thìr, bringing their Church with them, and are given leave to stay. They are the first strangers met since the Sundering.

title: The ships met off the north-west
body: That winter the mist that had lain on the eastern sea since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it lifts from the northern water. Two fishing boats of Achadh àrsaidh, working the water off the north-west cape where the Sea-Watcher is seen, meet three ships coming down out of the thin grey from the north, and hail them; neither side understands the other. The fishers turn south and the ships follow them down the coast toward Cuan shean. The fishers call the place Coinneachadh nan Long, the meeting of the ships, and the boats of Achadh àrsaidh still slow there.

title: The word brought home to Achadh àrsaidh
body: The second of the two Achadh àrsaidh boats that met the strangers' ships off the north-west cape turns home and brings the word to its households, while Lachlann Odhar's boat leads the strangers' ships south toward Cuan shean. Achadh àrsaidh is the first place on the island to hear of the strangers, and it hears of them from its own fishers.

title: Lachlann Odhar leads the ships down the coast
body: Lachlann Odhar steers south from the north-west cape the length of a winter day, past the empty headlands of the north-west, with the strangers' ships shortening sail to keep behind him. He runs his boat up the shingle at Cuan shean after dark and wakes the custodians.

title: The ships stand off Cuan shean in the westerly weather
body: A run of westerly gales keeps Na Trì Longan standing off and on beyond the bar of Cuan shean for many days. The town watches them from the dunes, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid forbids any boat to put off to them or any fire to be lit on the strand.

title: Three ships off Cuan shean
body: Three ships down from the north anchor off Cuan shean, the first hulls of their size seen from Dia-thìr since the fleet of the Sundering. Their master, a captain the rolls name Edmund Harrow, comes ashore unarmed with eleven men and asks by signs for water.

title: The rider from Cuan shean reaches Cathair dhearg
body: A rope-maker's son of Cuan shean rides the valley road to the capital in a day with Oighrig nic Leòid's letter on the ships. The clerk of the council reads it standing. The council's answer, two days later, bids Cuan shean feed the strangers, keep them apart and decide nothing.

title: Oighrig nic Leòid gives water on the shingle
body: Edmund Harrow wades ashore at Cuan shean with an empty cask, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid gives him and his eleven men water from the town well under the old law of the shore. She has seven casks filled and refuses anything more on her own word.

title: Three of Harrow's men buried above the tide-line
body: Three of the strangers, sick from the long voyage, die on the strand below the dunes at Cuan shean. Their own people bury them above the tide-line with a reading from a book and kneeling on the sand, while the town's children watch from the dunes.

title: Harrow's men mend nets on the dunes
body: Recovered from their sickness, the strangers penned below the dunes at Cuan shean begin mending the fishers' nets spread on the strand, unasked. The fishers learn from them a flat knot that does not slip, and call it the strangers' knot.

title: Buttons traded for fish on the strand
body: The first trade between the island and the strangers begins on the strand at Cuan shean, yellow-metal coat buttons for fish. The custodians forbid it twice and it goes on behind the dunes; at last Oighrig nic Leòid lets it be, and the fishwives wear the buttons on cords.

title: Forty days on the dunes
body: The custodians of Cuan shean will not decide alone, and send inland to the capital for counsel. For forty days the strangers are fed on the beach and kept below the dunes.

title: Manannan's priests keep the tide-prayer through the forty days
body: Through the forty days the strangers are fed below the dunes, the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut at every tide without missing one. The harbour scribe enters their number each week, nine, with the weather and the thinness of Ceò Mhanannain.

title: The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich rides south
body: Word of the ships reaches Baile fhiadhaich, up the western coast, in two days. Its custodian rides south to see them, and writes to the council that the strangers' ropes are better than ours and their manners worse.

title: Oighrig nic Leòid's letter to the council from her sickbed
body: From her bed at Cuan shean Oighrig nic Leòid writes to the council that she gave the strangers water under the law of the shore and nothing more on her own word, and that a leave given in the roll cannot be ungiven. She asks that it be read before the vote. The clerk notes it received.

title: The strangers sheltered in the net-lofts
body: With the autumn gales the custodians of Cuan shean let the strangers off the open strand into the net-lofts along the harbour. The ships lie in the harbour with their yards sent down and a few hands aboard. The roll enters the lofts as a shelter for the winter and no leave.

title: Oighrig nic Leòid falls ill
body: At Samhain the custodian of Cuan shean takes a cough that goes into her chest, and by an Dùbhlachd she cannot leave her bed. Custodians riding up to the council at Cathair dhearg stop at her bedside on the way.

title: The Council of Custodians grants leave
body: The Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg, which has sat in the crown's place since the crown fell empty at the close of the Age of Sundering, confirms the strangers' leave to stay under the high custodian Tormod mac Ailein. The council roll gives the vote as with one voice; a later hand in the margin notes that three custodians were absent.

title: The leave read on the strand at Cuan shean
body: A custodian of Cuan shean reads the council's leave to the strangers from an upturned boat on the strand, with a stranger who has learned some words in the net-lofts putting it into his own tongue. The strangers cheer three times and begin to send their ships' yards back up.

title: The quarter of sea they came from
body: Old sailors at Cuan shean say that the strangers came in from the same quarter of sea the fleet of the Sundering sailed into. The council forbids the saying in its hall. It is written down all the same, and never answered.

title: The struck line in the council roll
body: Bidden to strike from the council's roll the old sailors' saying about the quarter of the sea, the clerk at Cathair dhearg strikes it and writes beneath the striking what he was told to strike, so that the next clerk should know. The saying stands in the roll so, struck and unanswered.

title: Lachlann Odhar's words at the harbour wall
body: Going home at last to Achadh àrsaidh in an Gearran, Lachlann Odhar stands on the harbour wall at Cuan shean and says aloud that the ships came out of the quarter Cabhlach an Scaraidh sailed into. Nobody on the harbour answers him, and he puts out for the north.

title: The land beyond
body: The strangers name their homeland in their own tongue, but no scribe of the Dia-thìrich writes the word down. From the first season the scribes call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and its people simply the humans.

title: The humans pray in a sail-loft at Cuan shean
body: On the day the strangers keep for their god a sailmaker of Cuan shean lends them his loft against the rain. They kneel on the sailcloth, the captain with the rest, while a priest reads from a book; they light no fire and burn nothing. Two priests of Manannan watch from the stair and go down to the water to say their own prayer. It is the first entry of the humans at prayer under a roof.

title: Wren and the priests come up to Cathair dhearg
body: Two priests of the humans and a boy ride up from Cuan shean on ponies of the town, a long day's road, and come over the bridge at dusk soaked through. The council lodges them in a house below the temple and gives them a long room on the east side of the hall. The younger priest, Samuel Wren, coughs in the damp of the lake country.

title: Crìosd and an Eaglais written in the council roll
body: In the same season as an Tìr Thall the clerk of Comhairle a' Chùraim enters the name of the strangers' one god as the island hears it, Crìosd, and calls their faith an Eaglais, after the word their priests use of the whole company of their believers. They are the first words of the humans' tongue that the island takes and keeps.

title: The keeping of the word-list given to Gormshuil nic Fhearchair
body: The humans' priests ask Cuan shean for someone to trade words with them at a table, and Cuan shean sends to the capital. Tormod mac Ailein calls Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, who sits on the council for Clann Fhearchair and writes the best hand in the hall, and the council gives her the keeping of the island's side of the list. Her niece Muireall is to make the fair copy.

title: The first attempts at speech
body: For a whole season clerics of the humans' Church and custodians of Dia-thìr labour to make a store of words in common. Neither side's account of what was agreed survives whole.

title: Wren sets his months against the moons
body: Wren draws the twelve months of the humans' sun-year as a wheel, and Gormshuil nic Fhearchair gives him the island's moons from Samhnas round to the stags' moon. He writes each moon's name beside the month it most nearly matches. For Eadrach, the between-moon, he finds no place, and writes it outside the wheel with the humans' mark of a question.

title: Wren names the fuel of his own country
body: Over a brazier of peat in the long room Wren shows by signs that his people burn peat too, and also a black stone dug from under the ground, which they burn in every house. Gormshuil nic Fhearchair writes his word for it and, in the Dia-thìris column, the black stone the humans dig in their own country and burn on their hearths.

title: Wren's word-lists
body: The human cleric Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair keep word-lists side by side through the season of speech-making. Wren's list survives in the Administration's letter-books. Gormshuil's is lost; only its first leaf, with forty words for the colours of broken coal, is known from a copy.

title: Muireall copies the first leaf
body: In the gap-moon Gormshuil nic Fhearchair gives her loose sheets to her niece Muireall to copy fair into a book for Clann Fhearchair, and orders the colours set first, before cup and bread, alone on the first leaf with room left at the foot. Muireall copies the forty words in her young, careful hand and stops at the right-hand column, where the humans' side has one word to give.

title: The basket of broken coal on the table
body: In the wolf-moon Gormshuil nic Fhearchair takes a double handful from the capital's measure for the shrines and tips it on the table before Samuel Wren in the winter sun. She names forty colours at the breaks. Wren writes some of them, then stops, turns a piece in the light and gives one word for the whole heap. She waits for him to ask for hers; he holds up a candle.

title: One word for the coal
body: The humans have a single word for the coloured coal, and it is their word for the black fuel they burn at home. Gormshuil's copyist notes that no Dia-thìris word in either list answers to it, and that the humans did not ask for one.

title: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair begins the humans' letters
body: Since Wren cannot learn her colours, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair asks him by signs to teach her his letters. He writes them across a sheet of his white paper, large and small, and her name beneath as he hears it, and she copies it stroke by stroke. By the end of the spring she can spell out a line of his word-list, and finds his one word under her colours.

title: Trade begins
body: At first the trade is fair on both sides: the goods of Dia-thìr for tools and knowledge the lonely island lacks. For a few years it seems it may last.

title: The first bargains entered in the council roll
body: At the moon of the bright fire the strangers' iron, glass, lamp-oil and paper come up to the capital's market, and wool, hides, salt fish and dyed cloth go down to Cuan shean. Comhairle a' Chùraim enters the first bargains in its roll, fleece for knife and cloth for glass, with both prices in the island's reckoning. The measure is good on both sides.

title: The copy of the list sent to the loft at Muileann chaol
body: Having watched the humans burn their spoiled paper, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair has Muireall make a second fair copy of the whole list, the colours first and the note at the foot of the first leaf. She seals it in an oak chest with the seal of Clann Fhearchair and sends it east with the carriers to the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais, where nothing is burned.

title: The trading post at Ros dhomhain
body: The humans set up a trading post at Ros dhomhain, the capital's harbour, and give iron tools, window glass, lamp-oil and paper for wool, salt fish, hides and dyed cloth. The first tally-book of the post, kept by the trader Thomas Pike, balances evenly through its first year.

title: The custodians' clerk keeps a slate beside Pike's book
body: The custodians of the capital shore set a clerk on a stool by the door of the humans' post at Ros dhomhain. He keeps his own tally of the day's goods on a slate in the old strokes, and each evening he and Thomas Pike read their two counts aloud and find them level.

title: Goods carted from Cuan shean to the post
body: In the first weeks of the post every bale and cask goes between the strangers' ships at Cuan shean and the counter at Ros dhomhain by cart over the moor road, two days each way. The carters of Cuan shean charge by the creel, and Harrow goes to the pilots of Caol leathan for a way by water.

title: The pilots' double toll entered as fair
body: The pilots of Caol leathan go over the smallest of Harrow's hulls and name twice the toll of a Dia-thìreach boat for bringing her up the Abhainn gheal. Harrow is angry. Pike enters the price in the post's tally-book and writes beside it that it is fair, since the pilots know the shallows.

title: The first hull on Loch chrom
body: Pilots of Caol leathan bring the first of the strangers' ships up the Abhainn gheal into Loch chrom, towing her with boats through the shallows below Baile ghlas, and she anchors off Ros dhomhain. Thereafter the humans' goods come to the capital shore by water, and the pilots charge a stranger's hull twice the toll of a Dia-thìreach boat.

title: Cathair naomh sends its wool
body: Cathair naomh, the city above Seann Toll on the northern coast, sends its first wool south to the humans' post by coasting boat. Its custodians take their payment in paper and ink, and with them begin the town's roll afresh.

title: The gift of paper to Cathair naomh
body: Paying the custodians of Cathair naomh for their wool in paper and ink, Pike adds a quire of his own writing-paper uncounted. It is the one line of the post's first tally-book that he does not balance, and he marks it as a gift.

title: Harrow sails north-about with three hulls
body: At the end of an Lùnastal Edmund Harrow sails from Cuan shean for an Tìr Thall with all three hulls, north-about, carrying hides and dyed cloth. He leaves Thomas Pike at Ros dhomhain with four men, the loft, the tally-book and the goods not yet traded.

title: Iron in the smithies
body: The smiths of Cathair dhearg take the humans' bar-iron gladly and learn to temper it in a winter. Within a few seasons the old bronze hoes are melted down for bells.

title: The ships' smith at the forge in Cathair dhearg
body: A smith off Harrow's ships, sent up by Pike, comes to the smiths' lane below Drochaid Cathair dhearg and works through the autumn at the forge of Gilleasbuig Gobha. Having no words in common, the two smiths agree on the colours of hot iron.

title: Gilleasbuig Gobha's first tempered blade
body: In the last days of an Dùbhlachd Gilleasbuig Gobha tempers his first blade alone at his forge in Cathair dhearg, a knife of the humans' bar-iron drawn to the straw next the brown. It cuts hide that the old bronze knives only bruise. He gives it to his wife Sìne.

title: Iron hoes on the capital's fields
body: Through am Faoilleach and am Màrt the smiths of Cathair dhearg forge iron hoes, and the farmers above the lake pay for them with their old bronze hoes, brought down in sacks. Some of the bronze hoes bear the marks of the fields they worked.

title: The bells of Cathair dhearg cast from the hoes
body: At the asking of the custodians, Gilleasbuig Gobha and two smiths of the lane melt down the bronze hoes in a mould-pit behind his forge and cast four bells. They hang in the market gate, at the bridge and at the temple of Cathair dhearg, and are first rung together at Lùnastal.

title: Dyes for Baile Mòr mhòr
body: The weavers of Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast trade their cloth for the humans' dyes, a red and a blue brighter than any the island could make. Within a few years the old madder fields about the town go back to grass.

title: Harrow's second voyage
body: Harrow sails for home with hides and dyed cloth and comes back with four ships in place of three. He brings carpenters, a surgeon, and a letter from a trading house in an Tìr Thall asking what else the island has.

title: The trading house's letter read at the post
body: Toward the end of an Dàmhair Thomas Pike reads at his counter the letter Harrow has brought from the trading house over the sea, aloud in both tongues. It asks what else the island has: timber, tin, copper, lead, and what the rocks hold. Gilleasbuig Gobha hears it read.

title: The shipwrights of Inis mhòr
body: The shipwrights of Inis mhòr come to look at the humans' hulls and measure them with knotted cords. Their guild had built nothing greater than a coaster since the fleet of the Sundering, and the old craft of building for deep water was half forgotten.

title: The surgeon Jonas Tull
body: The humans' surgeon, Jonas Tull, sets the broken leg of a fisherman of Cuan shean who had been given up as lame. The town's custodian enters it in the roll as the first debt owed to a stranger.

title: Oighrig nic Leòid witnesses the setting of the leg
body: Old and ill, Oighrig nic Leòid, custodian of Cuan shean, is carried to the fisherman's house to watch Jonas Tull break and set the crooked leg again. Told he has done it eleven times and nine have walked, she says that nine of eleven is more than the island has, and writes the debt in the roll.

title: Salt from Seann Warr
body: The salt-pans of Seann Warr begin to sell to Pike's post by the barrel. They are the first goods of Dia-thìr that the humans come back asking for twice.

title: Pike's first two years balanced
body: In the first days of an Giblean Thomas Pike closes the tally-book of the post at Ros dhomhain on its second year. Over two nights he and the custodians' clerk go through every line of both years, book against slate, and the two counts stand level.

title: Wool at Caol leathan
body: The walled harbour of Caol leathan sends its first wool-ship to the humans' post. Its merchants will be paid only in iron by weight, and the tally-book of the post names them the hardest bargainers on the island.

title: Pike writes home of the island's coal
body: Answering the trading house, Thomas Pike writes of the island's timber, salt, wool, hides and smiths, and that it has copper, tin and some silver. Having held a piece from a custodian's hearth to the window, he writes that the island has coal of a middling sort, and much of it.

title: Gilleasbuig Gobha forges a hinge for Pike's chest
body: Gilleasbuig Gobha makes a new hinge of the strangers' bar-iron for the iron-bound chest under Pike's counter, where letters for over the sea are kept. He tempers it to the blue and will take nothing for the work. Pike's letter on the coal goes over the sea in that chest.

title: Carpenters and a cooper come ashore at Baile dhìreach
body: A boat of the humans' post rows down from Cuan shean deep with sawn plank and grounds on the shingle north of the quay at Baile dhìreach. Seven men of Harrow's ships come ashore, the carpenter William Rook and the cooper Samuel Hale among them, seeking a sheltered beach for a slip where the small craft of the post may be mended and built.

title: The rule of the shingle read to the strangers
body: The shingle above the wrack-line at Baile dhìreach is held in keeping for the whole town and may not be sold. Seonag nic Aoidh of the salt-house reads the town's rule to the strangers on the shore: the well drawn in turn, no fire on the shingle in the herring season, no hammer on the rest-nights. Rook says his men will keep it.

title: The first mixed settlement
body: A small coastal town takes in both Dia-thìrich and humans under one rule. It is not tried again.

title: The compact written in both tongues
body: Through the moons of harvest six sit at the mending-table in the net-loft of Baile dhìreach, three of the town and three of the strangers, and write the town's rule twice. A clerk of Inis thais writes the Dia-thìris book and William Rook the humans'. The net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh and the cooper Samuel Hale are fetched to find the words for the moorings.

title: The chair set to turn at the humans' new year
body: The six of Baile dhìreach find that the town's year turns at Samhain and is counted by moons, while the humans' year turns in the dead of winter on a fixed day. They write in both books that Iain mac Chaluim holds the chair until the humans' year turns, and William Rook for the year after, and so in turn.

title: Baile dhìreach under one council
body: The small port of Baile dhìreach on the south-west coast takes Dia-thìrich and humans under one council of six, three of each. Its founding compact is written twice, once in each tongue, the only such compact of the age.

title: The first council of Baile dhìreach
body: The council is chaired in alternate years by the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim and the human carpenter William Rook. The harbour dues go half to the custodians at Cathair dhearg and half to the humans' post.

title: Samuel Hale tightens the herring barrels
body: The human cooper Samuel Hale takes down the leaking herring barrels of Baile dhìreach stave by stave and makes every one of them tight by the end of summer, beginning with the idle row of the salter Ruairidh. He takes a bowl from the pot for his pay, and asks for Dia-thìris words, which he writes under his own.

title: The first boat off the humans' slip
body: On the first evening of Lùnastal the humans' slip at Baile dhìreach launches a small coaster of the strangers' pattern, deeper in the keel than the boats of the south-west. She is built for the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim, paid for in fish and labour and rigged with the town's rope; his wife pours sea water on her bow and asks Manannan to keep her.

title: A stranger's prayer at the lamps of the drowned
body: At the dark of the year Baile dhìreach sets lamps along its quay for its drowned, as the harbours of the west do. The humans of the shingle stand in the line, and the cooper Samuel Hale says a prayer to Crìosd in his own tongue for shipmates lost in the northern sea on the voyage out. Eilidh nic Ruairidh sets a lamp for them.

title: The first human house on the shingle
body: The carpenters of Baile dhìreach lay a slip of split logs, raise an open shed, and build a house of sawn plank on a sill of beach stones, with a window of glass. Since nothing may be built on the shingle, the town rules that the house is a tent, and calls it so. The humans' book of the town enters it as the first house.

title: Two letters on the harbour of Baile dhìreach
body: The humans' post at Ros dhomhain writes to ask why the dues of a harbour its own men have half rebuilt go wholly to the custodians at Cathair dhearg. The custodians of Inis thais write to ask by what rule strangers keep a yard on a shingle held in keeping. Iain mac Chaluim says the town must write its rule down.

title: The first dues shared
body: At its first sitting the council of six of Baile dhìreach settles a quarrel over a mooring ring and sends the harbour dues out in two halves: one in a sack by a boy up the road to the custodians at Cathair dhearg, the other round by boat to the humans' post at Ros dhomhain.

title: Ruairidh refuses the cooper
body: On the night of Samhain, while the town keeps its fire on the headland above the quay and the humans watch from the last cairn, the cooper Samuel Hale comes to the door of the salter Ruairidh to ask for his daughter Eilidh nic Ruairidh. Ruairidh sends him away, saying that a council is one thing and a hearth another.

title: The bidding carried to Inis thais
body: In the black moon the council of Baile dhìreach sends its compact along the shore to the temple city of Inis thais in both tongues, with a clause bidding any town of the coast sit with it on the same terms. The pilot Murchadh mac Iain carries it by boat and brings back word that the custodian will write.

title: Inis thais declines the compact
body: The city of Inis thais, whose harbour lies a few miles from Baile dhìreach, is bidden to join the joint council and declines. Its custodian writes that one town may be a trial, but two would be a rule.

title: Iain mac Chaluim hands the chair to William Rook
body: On the morning the humans' year turns, in the net-loft of Baile dhìreach, the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim gives up the chair of the council of six and the carpenter William Rook takes it, as the compact bids. Both books enter it in a line, the one by the day and the year, the other by the moon. The letter from Inis thais is read the same morning.

title: Rook's ruling on the dragged mooring
body: A boat of the post drags her anchor at Baile dhìreach and fouls the salter Ruairidh's mooring, and her master will not pay. William Rook, in the chair, orders his own countryman to pay the town's rate for rope and ring, in iron by weight, that day, and asks Ruairidh whether the rate is fair.

title: The storm of the wolf-moon at Baile dhìreach
body: A three-day storm off the west drives the sea over the quay of Baile dhìreach and up the shingle towards the boats. On the second night the town and the humans haul the boats over the crest together with ropes, blocks and a capstan-bar from the slip. The salt-house chimney and half the roof of the humans' house are lost.

title: Ruairidh relents
body: After half a moon of the carpenter in the chair, in which nothing in Baile dhìreach has fallen but a chimney, the salter Ruairidh helps the humans roof their house again and sends word by his daughter Eilidh nic Ruairidh that the cooper Samuel Hale may come up to the house for his bowl himself.

title: A supply ship lost on the western reefs
body: A human supply ship strikes the reefs off the western coast in fog, and nine of her crew drown. Her master was sailing by a chart drawn from memory, the humans' letter-books complain, on a coast lit only by the old driftwood fires.

title: The nine drowned buried on the western shore
body: The nine drowned of the human supply-brig are buried in the dunes above the tide-line at Baile fhiadhaich, on ground the custodian gives. A townswoman wets each grave with sea-water as the coast does for its own drowned. The mason Torcall Clachair cuts nine headstones with a line for the sea, and the ship's mate scratches the names beneath.

title: The chart from memory brought to the post
body: The mate of the lost brig carries her drowned master's chart, drawn from memory, to the post at Ros dhomhain. It sets the point where she struck a mile too far out to sea and shows no reefs below it. The ships' masters at the post argue over it at Thomas Pike's counter.

title: The beacons asked for
body: Human seamen, strange to the coasts of Dia-thìr, ask for standing beacons. The builders of the Dia-thìrich agree, not yet seeing what the beacons will bring.

title: The masters of building answer the strangers
body: Comhairle a' Chùraim passes the strangers' asking to the seven master builders of Cathair dhearg. They agree that towers may be raised on the headlands where each place's custodian gives leave, with a Dia-thìreach builder to choose the ground. Torcall Clachair alone asks about coal, and the old ruling that no coal feeds a sea-fire is kept.

title: The beacon headlands walked
body: The human navigator James Fenn and the Dia-thìreach mason Torcall Clachair walk the coast together to choose the places of the new beacons, and mark the five headlands of the old fires. Fenn's chart survives; Torcall's cairns for the most part do not.

title: Pike writes of the natives
body: Thomas Pike enters in the post's letter-book that the islanders have agreed to the lights without difficulty and without asking what they would cost. It is the first page of his letter-book to call the Dia-thìrich the natives. The custodians' roll sets down the same asking as a request that the old sea-fires be built higher and kept all night.

title: No fire on Binnean a' Chlachair
body: James Fenn asks for a night fire on the summit of Binnean a' Chlachair, the highest ground of the island. Torcall Clachair and the herders of Muileann gheal refuse, keeping the custom of the hills. Torcall lays one stone on the herders' cairn, and Fenn takes his sights by day to a linen square, four days slower. The two winter at Muileann gheal.

title: Torcall's first cairn on the Tobar dhearg headland
body: On the southern cape at Tobar dhearg, beside the old dry-stone fire-tower where the village households burn driftwood and seal fat in turn, Torcall Clachair builds a cairn to mark ground for a new tower. James Fenn writes a name from his own shore on the cape in his chart. Torcall answers that the cape has a name.

title: The second cairn on the eastern cape
body: At Baile ìseal, whose fire is lit to bring the boats home in a storm, Torcall Clachair and James Fenn sit up with the watch and see a raiders' light on the nearest islet. The watchman says a greater light would bring home more men of both kinds. He helps Torcall lift the capstone of the second cairn.

title: The households of Àth dhearg asked hearth by hearth
body: The custodian of Àth dhearg will not give away the fire-shelf above the rock-cut stair, saying it belongs to the households who cut it. Torcall Clachair and James Fenn go round the hearths for eleven days. Most say yes and two say no. The third cairn is raised at the end of the shelf, and the custodian climbs up with bread.

title: Three yards of ash at Muileann bheag
body: Seeking the depth for a tower's footing, James Fenn digs beside the old shore-fire on the northern point at Muileann bheag with Torcall Clachair and a boy of the village. They go down through bands of black ash and red earth and find no rock at three yards. Torcall sets the fourth cairn inland on sound rock.

title: Baile chrom's condition for the fifth cairn
body: The households of Baile chrom, whose headland fire has always warned boats off the water of Uilebheist na Mara, say the old fire cannot both warn and call. They give leave for a tower on condition that the old fire be kept alight beside it on driftwood. James Fenn agrees, and Torcall Clachair builds the fifth cairn.

title: The fire on the north-west headland raised for Fenn
body: At Lùnastal Torcall Clachair keeps a high fire of driftwood and seal fat on the headland at Baile chrom for three nights, burning no coal. On the third night James Fenn, rowed west by fishers of Achadh àrsaidh past Coinneachadh nan Long, sees it sink below the sea's rim at near thirty miles. The sea end of his line is fixed there.

title: The cairns of the line laid across the island
body: Through the autumn James Fenn sights station after station east from the Baile chrom headland, and Torcall Clachair raises a narrow cairn capped with a white stone on each chosen top. Hired boys carry a chain of iron links between them. The string of cairns crosses the moors south of Cnoc bheag and the hills of the interior.

title: Fenn's line
body: On the same survey James Fenn runs a line of sights across the whole island, from the open sea off the north-west, where ships coming down from the north first raise the land, to the water off the eastern cape. He makes it a hundred and fifty-five miles, some thirty of them sea at the western end. It is the first measure of Dia-thìr from side to side, and every chart the Company draws afterwards is scaled to it.

title: The council asked for a ruling on the marriage
body: Iain mac Chaluim writes for the council of Baile dhìreach to the custodians at Cathair dhearg, asking whether the marriage of a Dia-thìreach net-maker to a human cooper may be entered in the custodians' roll, and whether its children stand as a Dia-thìreach mother's. The rider returns with no answer. The council resolves to enter the marriage itself.

title: A marriage in two tongues
body: At Baile dhìreach the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh weds the human cooper Samuel Hale. The council enters the marriage in both its books; the custodians at Cathair dhearg, asked for a ruling, send none.

title: Torcall witnesses in the Dia-thìreach book
body: At the wedding on the quay of Baile dhìreach no custodian comes to witness. James Fenn signs for the bridegroom in the humans' book, and Iain mac Chaluim calls the mason Torcall Clachair from the crowd to sign the Dia-thìreach book. William Rook and Iain mac Chaluim close the two books side by side.

title: The island's names written on Fenn's chart
body: On the night of the wedding at Baile dhìreach James Fenn writes the Dia-thìris names of the five headlands under his own on his chart, as Torcall Clachair tells them: Tobar dhearg, Baile ìseal, Àth dhearg, Muileann bheag and Baile chrom. At the mountain in the middle of his line he writes Binnean a' Chlachair.

title: Harrow asks for the terms in writing
body: Edmund Harrow comes up the lake road to Cathair dhearg with Thomas Pike to speak for him and asks Tormod mac Ailein that the terms on which the humans stay be written and signed by both sides. He says that a man is coming from an Tìr Thall to speak for its government, and that he himself has asked for him. The council's leave, he says, stands only in the council's roll.

title: Tull draws Ceann a' Chùraim's tooth
body: Passing through Cathair dhearg on his way to the post at Ros dhomhain, the surgeon Jonas Tull draws a rotten tooth from the jaw of Tormod mac Ailein, which the capital's physician had left to wait a month. Tormod keeps the tooth in a box. It is the second debt owed to a stranger that the custodians know of, and it is owed by Ceann a' Chùraim.

title: Pell lands at Cuan shean
body: Josiah Pell comes ashore at Cuan shean from the first ship of the year down from the north, dry-shod on a plank, with a leather case he lets no one carry. He asks for a horse. Oighrig nic Leòid, who gave Harrow water, lends him her own and writes to the council the same day that he did not ask for water.

title: Pell rides to the council hall
body: Josiah Pell rides the twenty-six miles from Cuan shean to Cathair dhearg in a day and, passing by the humans' post, asks at dusk for the council hall and Ceann a' Chùraim. Tormod mac Ailein comes down to him in his house-shoes. With no one to carry words between them, Pell greets him with the island's word of leave-taking, learned on the ship.

title: The terms asked for in two tongues
body: In the talks at Cathair dhearg and Ros dhomhain, with Samuel Wren putting each sentence into the other tongue, Tormod mac Ailein asks that the terms be written twice, as the compact of Baile dhìreach was. Pell answers that one text must govern before the lawyers of an Tìr Thall, and that a copy in Dia-thìris will follow when there is leisure. Wren gives it as an dèidh làimh.

title: The first written treaty
body: The terms on which the humans stay are first set down in writing, in the humans' tongue only. No one among the Dia-thìrich speaks against it at the time.

title: The treaty signed at Cathair dhearg
body: The treaty is signed in the council hall at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein for the custodians, and for the Administration by Josiah Pell, newly come as the humans' first Commissioner. Tormod could not read the tongue it was written in. Who read it to him is not told.

title: Gormshuil called back from Muileann chaol
body: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, gone east with the season's copies for the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol, is sent for by rider when the talks with Pell run fast. She starts back the day the rider finds her, but the rain is on the hills and the fords are up, and she is still on the road when the terms are signed.

title: Gormshuil given a copy of the terms
body: Two days after the signing Gormshuil nic Fhearchair comes in from the hills, reads the entry in the roll standing, and asks Pell through Samuel Wren for the terms in the strangers' tongue, since the copy in Dia-thìris is to wait for leisure. Pell's secretary makes one within the week. She begins to read it a word at a time, and does not bring it before the council.

title: The masons of the capital build for Pell
body: The masons of the masons' lane at Cathair dhearg take up Pell's house on the rise, paid in bar-iron by the humans' day, which begins at midnight where the island's begins at dusk. They float grey stone over the lake on rafts and build the house square to Pell's drawn plan, facing the harbour, with its back to the capital. The council does not ask it turned.

title: The clerk leaves the day blank
body: Entering Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg in the council's roll, the custodians' clerk writes the year by the count of An Diosal and the moon of Bealltach. The strangers have dated their sheets by their own day and month, and no one in the hall can turn the one into the other, so he leaves the day empty. It is the first such page in the roll.

title: The rise above Ros dhomhain given
body: Pell asks the council for the bare rise behind the harbour of Ros dhomhain, where the town's goats graze, to build a house for Riaghaltas nan Coigreach. The goat-keepers are paid in iron pots and are glad of it, and the council gives the ground without a vote, holding it a matter of goats.

title: The Residency above Ros dhomhain
body: Josiah Pell builds a house of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain and calls it the Residency. Captain Harrow, needed ashore no longer, goes back to the sea trade.

title: Harrow takes his leave of Tormod
body: Edmund Harrow comes up to Cathair dhearg with Thomas Pike to say that Pell will govern now and a ship's master is needed ashore no longer. He tells Tormod mac Ailein that he and Pike are to have a licence to trade, and that the charter will be sent to the council and found in order. He sails north-about from Ros dhomhain two tides later.

title: The Company chartered
body: Harrow and Pike found a trading house under licence of the Administration, known on Dia-thìr simply as the Company. Its charter gives it first refusal of "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield."

title: The charter lodged with the council
body: A copy of Cairt na Companaidh comes to the council at Cathair dhearg in the strangers' tongue, four sheets under a red seal. The clerk enters its coming in the roll and lays it in the chest under the east window of the hall, beside the unanswered letter from Baile dhìreach, and there it lies a month unread.

title: Gormshuil reads the charter to Tormod
body: At midsummer Gormshuil nic Fhearchair takes the charter from the council's chest and reads it by night to Tormod mac Ailein at his hearth. In the clause of all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield she finds Wren's one word for the coal, and she shows him that the charter's licence hangs from the line on goods he had asked to hear twice. He asks her to keep it between them.

title: The shore at Cathair dhomhain sold
body: Thomas Pike buys a strip of shingle and rough grass above the lake at Cathair dhomhain from a fishing family that has drawn its nets there since An Aois Naomh, for a keg of nails, two lamps and a sheet of window-glass. The custodian of the lake shore enters the sale. It is the first ground on Dia-thìr the strangers hold by sale and not by the council's leave.

title: The warehouse at Cathair dhomhain
body: The Company builds a stone warehouse at Cathair dhomhain, along the lake shore from the capital, to keep its tools from the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. It is the first building on Dia-thìr the Company owns outright.

title: The warehouse door hung
body: The oak door of A' Chompanaidh's warehouse at Cathair dhomhain comes down the shore road from Cathair dhearg and is hung at dusk on strap hinges forged by Gilleasbuig Gobha in the smiths' lane below the bridge. Thomas Pike locks it with a long iron key. Tormod mac Ailein, who has walked out from the capital, watches it hung; the lake-shore roll calls it a good door.

title: The strangers' fever
body: A fever comes ashore at Cuan shean with a crowded ship and runs down the west coast. Ninety-one Dia-thìrich die, and eleven humans. The custodians shut the town to ships for a season, and Pell protests in writing.

title: The hill's coal carried to Cuan shean
body: Eleven carriers of the hills bring the measured coal for the western hearths down from the store at Taigh na Fèithe to Cuan shean, five days on the road with ponies and a custodian's clerk. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom goes among them for the first time. Oighrig nic Leòid counts the baskets in by lamplight at the custodians' store.

title: The carriers kept at Cuan shean
body: When the fever breaks out among the net-sheds, the clerk of the hill carriers and Oighrig nic Leòid forbid the eleven to take the road home, lest they carry the sickness into the hills. The carriers stay in the town through an t-Samhain, carrying water to the fever houses and the dead to their burying.

title: Oighrig answers Pell's protest
body: Pell's letter protesting the shutting of Cuan shean is read to Oighrig nic Leòid in the custodians' store by the humans' trader of the quay. It claims the harbour open under Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg and holds the town answerable for spoiled cargo. She asks whether it says anything of the dead, and sends back the number, forty-one, and word that the ships may wait.

title: The fever at Baile àrsaidh
body: The strangers' fever comes to Baile àrsaidh, a day's walk up the coast, and kills its custodian and both her sons. No humans dwell in the town at all, and the custodians of the west take note of it.

title: The fever turned back at Cnoc àrsaidh
body: At Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west the townsfolk block the road with carts and turn back every traveller for a season, and the fever does not reach them. The Administration fines the town for hindering trade.

title: Prospectors in the central hills
body: The Company sends two prospectors, Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer, into the hills east of the capital. They come back with sacks of broken coal, and word that the black seam runs "further than can be walked in a day."

title: The fever dead buried beyond the dunes
body: The custodians of Cuan shean will not lay the fever dead in the old ground by the harbour, and bury them in the sand beyond the dunes, out of sight of the town. The human dead lie in the same ground in a row of their own, read over by their priest. The burying slackens at the dark of the year and ends before Là Fhèill Brìde.

title: The hills keep their roads open
body: After the fever at Baile àrsaidh, where no human lived, the custodians of the hills meet at Taigh na Fèithe and talk of shutting the hill roads. They decide against it, since the roads carry the meal, the salt and the lamp-oil. Their roll gives the reason in the words of Seonag Liath of the old cutting: nine years of salt eaten with the strangers.

title: Cnoc àrsaidh pays its fine in wool
body: Cnoc àrsaidh, fined by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach for turning back travellers with its carts, pays the fine in sacks of wool. The hill carters carry the story east and tell it at the mill of Muileann chrom as a jest against the strangers, who have no use for so much wool.

title: The prospectors find no guide
body: Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer come up the road to Muileann chrom with a letter of A' Chompanaidh asking lodging and a guide into the hills. The miller houses and feeds them, but no man of the hill will lead strangers onto it with a hammer. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill offers himself for a silver coin of an Tìr Thall, against his father's wish.

title: The seam walked with the prospectors
body: For eleven days Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill leads Stone and Mercer through the hills north and east of Muileann chrom, by the stream-cuts where the seam shows. They break coal at every gully, a sack to each, and Mercer counts the paces between. Raghnall names the colours of the broken coal; the prospectors have one word for all of it. He carries a sack down on his own back.

title: The custodians write for the coal
body: The custodians of the vein send a letter in Dia-thìris to Thomas Pike at Ros dhomhain, asking that all the coal broken on the hill above Muileann chrom without leave be brought back to be laid in the rock with the proper words. They write twice more in the spring before any answer comes.

title: The sacks returned to the rock
body: The custodians of the vein demand the broken coal back, to lay it in the rock again with the proper words. The Company returns half. The custodians' roll enters the other half as "carried west."

title: The first mining contracts
body: Trade sours into bargain. Dia-thìrich hands mine the vein on a scale that no reverent custom had ever used.

title: The first pit at Muileann chrom
body: Under the first contract a Dia-thìreach crew of thirty opens a working at Muileann chrom, paid by the ton in iron tools and lamp-oil. The custodians' own cuttings had never been measured by weight at all.

title: Six sacks come back to Muileann chrom
body: At the summer's end a human carter brings six of the thirteen sacks back up the road to the mill of Muileann chrom with a paper no one there can read. Asked for the rest, he points west, towards Ros dhomhain and the ships, and turns his cart round.

title: The first contract read at the mill
body: Abel Stone brings the first contract of A' Chompanaidh to Muileann chrom with two carts of steel-pointed picks, bar-iron and lamp-oil. It is read at the mill in both tongues. The interpreter from Ros dhomhain can find no Dia-thìris for the ton and calls it "a great load, weighed". Some of the older hewers walk out before the end.

title: Raghnall chosen to lead the thirty
body: Abel Stone names Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, who walked the seam with him, to lead the first crew of the hill. The crew is thirty: young men of the hewers' and shepherds' households, two from the mill and three older hewers of the old cutting. Raghnall's father, a hewer of that cutting, will not join it.

title: The returned half laid in the rock
body: At the old cutting above Muileann chrom the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe and Seonag Liath sort the returned coal by colour and by gully, and the hewers lay it back into the clefts with clay while the custodians say the words for a thing taken out of season. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill carries all six sacks up to the face. He gives the clerk the word "west" for the rest.

title: The first ton weighed at Muileann chrom
body: On the day the first pit is opened below the old cutting, A' Chompanaidh sets up an iron beam on a timber tripod at the pit-mouth. At dusk the clerk adds his figures and Stone calls out one ton, the first coal of the hills ever weighed. The crew cheers, and the figure is written in the pit-book against Raghnall's name.

title: The first crew paid in iron and oil
body: On the first market-day after the opening of the pit, the crew of thirty at Muileann chrom are paid for their tons in picks and lamp-oil at the rate written on the contract, to the last measure of oil. The pit-book of A' Chompanaidh balances to the line.

title: A coal quay at Ceann fhada
body: The Company builds a stone quay at Ceann fhada, a fishing hamlet below the hills, for loading coal into coasting barges. The fishermen are paid for their foreshore in iron nails, by weight.

title: The nails weighed again at Ceann fhada
body: The river-fishers and pilots of Ceann fhada, paid by weight in iron nails for the foreshore under the new coal quay, carry their nails to the fish-shed and weigh each man's share again on the old beam they weigh salmon on. Every share is true to the ounce. A pilot enters in the roll of Ceann fhada that the weight was true and the men ashamed.

title: The first coal barge goes down from Ceann fhada
body: Carts from the pit at Muileann chrom tip the first coal into a flat barge moored against the new quay at Ceann fhada. Two pilots of the hamlet, paid by A' Chompanaidh, take her down the Abhainn uaine at the sweeps, since no one else knows the river.

title: Wren's grammar
body: Samuel Wren finishes a grammar of Dia-thìris for the Mission, the house of the humans' Church on Dia-thìr. It is careful and true in most things, and it gives the word for the vein's custodians as "keepers of the coal."

title: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair reads Wren's grammar to the custodians
body: At the Samhain sitting of the council at Cathair dhearg, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair reads Samuel Wren's grammar aloud to the custodians of the hills and puts it into Dia-thìris. She tells them that in the humans' tongue a keeper is one who has a thing and holds it until paid. Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr enters in her roll that the strangers' book calls the custodians keepers.

title: The hawk-priests read Wren
body: The hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag ask the Mission for a copy of Wren's grammar, to read what the humans write of them. The Mission sends one. Of all the copies that survive it bears the most notes in the margins.

title: A hawk-priest's note beside the three words
body: In the copy of Wren's grammar kept by the hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag, a priest writes in the margin beside the humans' name for the custodians, in Dia-thìris, that Wren writes as a man counts sacks, and signs it with a hawk's head.

title: The custodians of the hills called on the contracts
body: At the dark of the year the council at Cathair dhearg calls the custodians of the hills to say what their villages make of the contracts coming up from Muileann chrom. It hears four days of talk of iron, lamp-oil and the ton, and makes no ruling.

title: The Mission chapel
body: The Mission raises a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain, the first church on the island. Its bell is the first iron bell on the island, and the custodians ask that it not be rung before the fishing fleet is out.

title: The bell rung once before the fleet was out
body: On the morning of its hanging the iron bell of the chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain is rung for the first service while the fishers are loading their boats in silence, as the rule of that quay requires. The crews unload and go home. Three boats of more than twenty go out on the lake that day.

title: The chapel bell kept until the fleet is out
body: At the chapel door the custodian of Ros dhomhain tells the minister, with Samuel Wren putting it into the humans' tongue, that a bell over the water before the boats are out is the bell for the drowned. The minister agrees at once, and the bell is rung thereafter only when the last boat is clear of the harbour mouth.

title: The contract carried up to Doire mhòr
body: A boy of Muileann chrom carries a contract of A' Chompanaidh up to Doire mhòr, naming the south slope of its hill under the oaks for a working. Beathag Dhubh has it read to her twice in the mill-house at Muileann chrom by the young man of Ros dhomhain who puts A' Chompanaidh's words into Dia-thìris.

title: The first refusal
body: One mining settlement will not sign a contract. For the present it is passed by, not punished.

title: Beathag calls Doire mhòr's households to the hearth
body: On the evening the day for the marks goes by, Beathag Dhubh calls the seven households of Doire mhòr to her fire and has the contract told to them. They talk of iron, oats and sheep. The oldest woman of the hill says that the hill is not theirs, and the households give the answer to the custodian to give.

title: Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr
body: The settlement that refused was Doire mhòr, in the hills above Muileann chrom, and its custodian was Beathag Dhubh. Her answer to the Company's agent is known only in his words: that the hill was not hers to sell nor his to buy.

title: The agent's report sent down from Muileann chrom
body: The agent of A' Chompanaidh who climbed to Doire mhòr writes that night at the pit-office by the mill that the custodian heard him out in the rain, did not ask him in, and answered that the hill was not hers to sell nor his to buy. He sends it to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir with the week's figures and advises that the working be opened elsewhere.

title: The road around Doire mhòr
body: The Company opens its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, and runs its cart-road round the fields of Doire mhòr and not through them.

title: The road pegged across Doire mhòr's fields and moved
body: Surveyors of A' Chompanaidh peg the line of the new cart-road from Cnoc fhiadhaich straight across the three best fields of Doire mhòr. Beathag Dhubh sends word to the custodian of Muileann chrom that the fields are in no contract. Five days later the surveyors pull their pegs and lay the line round the foot of the field walls, a mile the longer.

title: Fenn's lens carried to Tobar dhearg
body: The great glass for the new tower on the southern cape, ground over the sea, is carried from Ros dhomhain to Tobar dhearg on a cart packed in straw. James Fenn sets it in the lamp-room of the tower Torcall Clachair has raised over the old fire-tower.

title: Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg lit
body: The first of the new beacons is finished on the southern headland at Tobar dhearg: a round tower of grey stone raised over the old fire-tower, paid for by the Company, with a Dia-thìreach keeper. Torcall Clachair builds it; James Fenn sets its lens.

title: The cart-road round Doire mhòr finished
body: Hill men paid in iron finish the cart-road of A' Chompanaidh from Cnoc fhiadhaich round the fields of Doire mhòr to the quay at Ceann fhada, with a timber bridge at the lower ford of the Doire mhòr stream. The first loaded carts come round the bend in the autumn.

title: The carters water their horses at Doire mhòr
body: The carters on the new road ask Beathag Dhubh's leave to water their horses at the stream where the road crosses it below Doire mhòr, and she gives it. In wet weather they eat their bread under the oaks before the last pull down to the river.

title: The first keeper of Tobar dhearg
body: The first keeper of the southern beacon is Anna nic Dhòmhnaill of Tobar dhearg village, a fisherman's widow, who climbs the tower twice a night for the rest of her life. The village holds the keepership as a trust and keeps it in its own families through the age.

title: Anna nic Dhòmhnaill's tally of lit nights cut on the stair wall
body: Anna nic Dhòmhnaill, keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, who cannot write, begins her count on the wall of the tower stair below the lamp-room: one stroke cut with a knife for every night the light is lit, and a stroke across every thirty.

title: Raiders in the north-western waters
body: A Company brig is boarded off the north-west coast and stripped of her cargo of tools. The raiders are never known. The Administration blames the custodians of the coast, and the custodians answer that those waters have always kept their own law.

title: The answer of the coast read in the hills
body: The council at Cathair dhearg copies the answer of the custodians of the north-western coast to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir over the stripped brig, that those waters have always kept their own law, and sends it round the districts. It is read out at the mill at Muileann chrom.

title: Beathag writes the road into the roll of Doire mhòr
body: Under the sixteenth year Beathag Dhubh enters in the roll of Doire mhòr the answer of the coast word for word, and then the road round the village's fields, a mile the longer and well built, with two words after it: for now.

title: The hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag show Wren their margins
body: Samuel Wren comes to Cnoc bheag at the hawk-priests' asking and is shown their copy of his grammar, written in along every margin in the stag-letters. Beside his words keepers of the coal they have set the island's word three times, which means those who have the care of the vein. Wren copies all their notes by the priest's fire.

title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
body: Samuel Wren copies the writing on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag and sends it over the sea to the scholars of an Tìr Thall. No answer comes. The custodians tell him the stone is older than the Dia-thìrich and that none living can read it.

title: The custodian of Cnoc bheag answers Wren at the stakes
body: At Carragh Cnoc bheag the custodian of the town tells Samuel Wren what her house has told every asker: the stone is older than the Dia-thìrich, the old schools' letters matched nothing on it, and the four words below were cut later by one who could read no more of it. Wren copies the line three times in the rain.

title: The first coin
body: The humans' coin is brought in beside the old barter, for ease, it is said. Within ten years nothing that needs a tool from over the sea can be had for anything else.

title: Wren blesses the striking-press at Ros dhomhain
body: At Josiah Pell's asking Samuel Wren says a prayer over the new striking-press in its shed on the quay at Ros dhomhain, in the humans' tongue and then in Dia-thìris for the fishers watching at the door. The first mark is lifted from the die with tongs and dropped ringing in the tray.

title: The mark and its hundred pence
body: The coins are struck at Ros dhomhain from silver and copper shipped from an Tìr Thall: the mark and its hundred pence. The first striking bears a ship on one face, and nothing of Dia-thìr on either.

title: Muireall's rubbing of the first mark sent to the loft
body: Samuel Wren brings one of the first marks to Gormshuil nic Fhearchair in the long room of the council hall. Her niece Muireall takes a rubbing of both faces, writes beneath it that the island is on neither face, and the rubbing goes east that autumn with the season's copies to the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol.

title: Cathair mhòr refuses the mark
body: The market of Cathair mhòr, greatest below the hills east of the capital, refuses the humans' coin for a whole year. The custodians of the town give way when the Company's tool-sellers will not cross their bridge.

title: Two books at the capital market
body: At the market of Cathair dhearg the tool-sellers take only marks, while cloth and fish still go by barter. The custodians' clerks begin to keep two sets of books, and complain of it in both.

title: The market-clerk's sentence in both books
body: Tadhg, the custodians' market-clerk at Cathair dhearg, keeps the dues of barter in one book and the dues in marks in another, and can make no single figure of them for the council. At the foot of each he writes that the one book cannot be added to the other, in the stag-letters and again in the humans' tongue.

title: The masters of Dùn thais invite Wren
body: The masters of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Dùn thais write to Samuel Wren at Ros dhomhain, in the stag-letters, asking him to come for the dark of the year and dispute with them. He goes east with the carriers at the end of an t-Samhain, five days on the road through Cathair mhòr and the hills.

title: Wren's winter at Dùn thais
body: The masters of the druid school at Dùn thais receive Samuel Wren for a winter of disputation. He asks them why the vein should be holy; they ask him why his fuel should be burned. Neither telling of that winter names a winner.

title: Wren's letter home on the druids
body: From Dùn thais, in the last days of the year, Samuel Wren writes to the house of his order over the sea by the packet of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir. He sets down a tale the eldest master told at the hearth of a holy man's voyage west in a boat of hides, very like the voyage of Naomh Breandan as an Eaglais tells it, told from the other shore.

title: Drochaid Cathair dhearg rebuilt
body: Company masons rebuild in dressed stone the old bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg, wide enough for coal-carts to pass two abreast.

title: Queen Sìleas's stone set back in the bridge
body: When the masons of A' Chompanaidh take down the parapets of Drochaid Cathair dhearg, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair asks the master mason to keep the block cut with Queen Sìleas's name. He has it dressed on its back and sides, its face left as it was, and sets it again in the new downstream parapet near the middle of the bridge.

title: The Commissioner's carriage
body: Company wheelwrights build a closed carriage for Josiah Pell, and he drives in it over the new bridge from the Residency to the council at Cathair dhearg. It is the first carriage on the island. The custodians still walk to the council, and say so.

title: Tormod mac Ailein walks behind the carriage
body: Josiah Pell's carriage stops beside Tormod mac Ailein and Gormshuil nic Fhearchair on the new bridge, and Pell offers Ceann a' Chùraim a seat as far as the council hall. Tormod thanks him and answers aloud that they will walk, and the two custodians come up the hill on foot long after the carriage.

title: Gormshuil reads the harbour articles to the council
body: Before the signing of Puingean a' Chalaidh, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair reads the eight sheets aloud to the council at Cathair dhearg, each clause first in the humans' tongue and then in Dia-thìris. Ailean Ruadh of Baile ghlas asks to hear the clause on the anchorages twice.

title: The Harbour Articles
body: A second compact, the Harbour Articles, fixes the dues and anchorages of Ros dhomhain in the Company's favour. Like the first treaty it is written in the humans' tongue only, and this time two custodians refuse to sign.

title: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair refuses Puingean a' Chalaidh
body: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair passes the sheet of Puingean a' Chalaidh on unsigned, and tells Josiah Pell in his own tongue that she will not put her name under what she has read. Ailean Ruadh of Baile ghlas refuses with her. The council's roll names the two, the first custodians to refuse a writing of the strangers.

title: The fishermen of Baile ghlas
body: The fishermen of Baile ghlas, whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain time out of mind, are charged anchorage under the Harbour Articles. They take their catch to their own small harbour and sell it there to anyone but the Company.

title: The northern concession
body: The council grants the Administration upland pasture in the north-west about Muileann àrsaidh, for human families who will not work in the pits. The grant is for grazing; the families build houses of stone.

title: The council's letter on the grazing
body: At Tormod mac Ailein's sickbed Gormshuil nic Fhearchair reads him the letter from Muileann àrsaidh. At his word she writes to the families on the grazing, in both tongues, that the council granted summer grazing and shielings, and sends it north the next morning.

title: Death of Tormod mac Ailein
body: Tormod mac Ailein, the high custodian who signed the first treaty, dies at Cathair dhearg. The council chooses Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh after him, who had never met a human before the Crossing and has dealt with little else since.

title: Tormod mac Ailein buried at Cathair dhearg
body: Six custodians carry Tormod mac Ailein to the ground behind the council hall, with the bells of the capital ringing, and the mourners lay their stones on the grave going round sunwise. Josiah Pell walks up from the bridge-foot bareheaded to stand at the edge of the ground. Samuel Wren stands at the gate.

title: Tormod mac Ailein waked three nights
body: Tormod mac Ailein is waked three nights in his house below the temple at Cathair dhearg, by the old custom. On the second night the council, meeting below, chooses Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh in a single evening, and the roll enters the choice as unanimous.

title: Harrow lost at sea
body: Edmund Harrow's ship does not come back from the crossing. The Company passes wholly into Thomas Pike's hands, and the humans' letter-books mourn Harrow as the man who found Dia-thìr.

title: Harrow's name read in the chapel at Ros dhomhain
body: A' Chompanaidh's men at Ros dhomhain give up Harrow's ship a month past her day. The chapel bell is rung slowly, the flag over the warehouse is lowered to half its pole, and Thomas Pike reads Harrow's name and the names of his crew at the humans' prayers, with Samuel Wren's help.

title: Pike's letter to the council
body: The humans' clerks write to the council at Cathair dhearg, in their own tongue and under seal, that A' Chompanaidh has passed wholly to Thomas Pike. Coinneach Glas reads the letter to the sitting and it is entered in the roll.

title: The counters' fee held over
body: At its autumn sitting the council, its share of the vein-dues now paid in marks by A' Chompanaidh and fewer than before, finds it cannot meet every fee. The fee of the counters who keep the boards of the measured handful is held over to the next sitting.

title: Half of Dùn dhearg comes to the board
body: At Samhain only the old households of Dùn dhearg bring their sacks to the counters' board in the old granary. The young households have bought their coal by the sack at the market of Cathair mhòr off A' Chompanaidh's carts. Pàdraig Cam counts the season without a fee.

title: The Small-Burning Law lapses
body: Centuries of measured burning end within one generation. The Law is never repealed; once its keeping no longer pays, it is no longer kept.

title: The last count at Doire mhin
body: The custodians of Doire mhin keep the old count of the Small-Burning Law, the measure of coal that might be burned in a year, one season longer than any others. They enter it in their roll with the note that no one asked for it.

title: The counter of Dùn dhearg dies
body: Pàdraig Cam, counter of Dùn dhearg for forty years, dies in an Gearran. His son is at the pits of Muileann chrom and does not take the board, which hangs in the old granary with the pegs of the last Samhain in their holes. Fionnghal nic Artair begins her letter to the council.

title: A defence of the Law at Dùn dhearg
body: Fionnghal nic Artair, a custodian of Dùn dhearg, writes to the council in defence of the Small-Burning Law, the only such defence that survives. She holds that the Law was never for the coal's sake but for the people, who would become whatever the burning made them.

title: The council files the letter from Dùn dhearg
body: Fionnghal nic Artair reads her letter standing to the council at Cathair dhearg. Coinneach Glas thanks her and bids it kept with the rolls, and the roll enters it as read and filed. The same sitting grants Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir leave to widen the road to Muileann chrom for the coal-carts.

title: Fionnghal nic Artair rides to Cathair dhearg
body: In an t-Ògmhios Fionnghal nic Artair rides west from Dùn dhearg with her letter in defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig sewn in calfskin. She lodges at Doire mhin, where the custodian Anndra mac Eòin shows her the last count of the valley, and reads him the letter by his lamp.

title: A fair copy of the defence for the loft
body: At Gormshuil nic Fhearchair's asking Fionnghal nic Artair makes a fair copy of her letter in her own hand. Muireall nic Fhearchair sends it to the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol, where the custodians' papers are kept dry.

title: Murchadh Seabhag preaches at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Murchadh Seabhag preaches that Mòd, the Hungry Hawk of Acaill, starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them. The sermon is copied and carried to the camps, and it is the first writing of the Dia-thìrich that the Company's agents are told to seize.

title: The hawk sermon carried south in the bird-bags
body: A scribe of the hawk-shrine at Seann Skell writes Murchadh Seabhag's sermon down from his mouth. Fowlers taking birds to the autumn markets carry copies south, and from the markets carters and pedlars bring them into the camps of Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, where readers are given their supper to read them aloud.

title: The hearths of Achadh naomh
body: The households of Achadh naomh, in the hills north of the workings, who keep Na Seann Spioradan, will not light their hearths with coal bought of the Company. They burn peat as their grandparents did, and their elders teach that coal burned for wages is burned without the ancestors' leave.

title: A' Chompanaidh's agents seize the hawk sermon in the camps
body: A' Chompanaidh's agents at Muileann chrom go from hut to hut through the crews' camp with a basket and take every copy of Murchadh Seabhag's sermon they find, eleven in one morning. One woman burns her copy on her hearth before them, and her name is written down.

title: Fionnghal nic Artair at the hearths of Achadh naomh
body: Bidden by the elders of Achadh naomh, Fionnghal nic Artair rides north through the hills in an Giblean and reads her letter at the hearth of Sìleas nic Uilleim to the whole village. Asked what burns on her own hearth, she answers bought coal. She is sent home with a creel of peats.

title: The custodians at the pump-house of Muileann chrom
body: Three custodians sent by Coinneach Glas, Fionnghal nic Artair among them, go down to Muileann chrom to ask that the tally of the hill be kept. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill takes them to the pump at the deep gallery, where the furnaces are fed by the cartload.

title: Burning by the cartload
body: The Company's furnaces at Muileann chrom burn coal by the cartload to drive the new pumps, and no heed is paid to the custodians' tally of what the hill may give in a year. Coinneach Glas's council asks that the tally be kept, and is sent a copy of the Company's accounts.

title: A' Chompanaidh's accounts filed beside the defence
body: The copy of A' Chompanaidh's half-year accounts, sent in answer to the council's asking, is read aloud in its totals by Coinneach Glas and laid in the press of the council hall on the shelf that holds the letter of the custodian of Dùn dhearg.

title: Henry Maddox Commissioner
body: Josiah Pell sails home to an Tìr Thall and does not return. After him comes Henry Maddox, bidden to double the yield, with a letter from the Company promising him a share of it.

title: Maddox greets the council
body: Henry Maddox comes before the council at Cathair dhearg in An t-Àrd-mhaor's carriage, greets each custodian in Dia-thìris learned on the ship, and tells them his orders are to double the yield of the pits. He does not speak of A' Chompanaidh's letter promising him a share of it.

title: The oaks of Cathair fhada
body: Maddox buys the oak woods about Cathair fhada for pit-props. The town had cut them sparingly for generations; they are gone within the working lives of the men who fell them.

title: The last oak of Cathair fhada's own cutting
body: Before A' Chompanaidh's fellers come, the woodreeve of Cathair fhada and his men fell with axes the one oak the spring lot had fallen on, as the town had cut since An Aois Naomh, and plant six acorns in the ring of its roots. The fellers begin with long saws on the morning after.

title: The woodreeve of Cathair fhada before the council
body: Eòghann mac Phàdraig, woodreeve of Cathair fhada, asks the council to undo the sale of the town's oak woods to Maddox. The council holds that the custodians of Cathair fhada, in debt to A' Chompanaidh's store for seed, had the right to sell, and the clerk enters it.

title: The custodian of Dùn dhearg goes back to peat
body: Home from Cathair fhada in am Màrt, Fionnghal nic Artair has the coal raked out of her grate and lights it again with the peats of Achadh naomh. She sends to find a man of Dùn dhearg who still knows how to cut peat, and pays him what he asks.

title: The heading at Cnoc fhiadhaich driven without props
body: Under Henry Maddox's order to double the yield, the new gallery at Cnoc fhiadhaich is driven north along the seam on the pay of the ton, and the oak props from Cathair fhada stop at the head of the carters' drift. The agent of A' Chompanaidh writes that the heading will be timbered when the yield allows.

title: The first deaths of haste
body: A tunnel worked faster than any Dia-thìreach crew would have worked it falls in and kills eleven. It is entered as an accident.

title: The eleven buried at Muileann chrom
body: The eleven dead of the fall at Cnoc fhiadhaich are buried in the ground above the mill at Muileann chrom on the fourth day after the fall. Marsaili nic Sheumais, keeper of the old cutting for Taigh na Fèithe, reads their names at the graves and writes each into the roll with father, mother and hearth, and the place as under the wild hill.

title: Old Dòmhnall says the words at the pit-mouth
body: When the eleven are brought out of the fallen heading at Cnoc fhiadhaich, Dòmhnall, an old hewer of the custodians' cutting and father of Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, says the words of the face at the mouth of the drift, and the old hewers take them up. They had not been said at that pit-mouth since it was opened.

title: The fallen heading cleared and timbered
body: The fall at Cnoc fhiadhaich is cleared by midsummer and the heading timbered pair by pair as it is cleared, with oak brought up from Cathair fhada in an t-Ògmhios. The crews are paid nothing for the days of digging, and the yield of the year is short.

title: The eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich
body: The fall was at Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a gallery driven forward without the timbering the Dia-thìrich crews had asked for. The custodians' roll names all eleven dead. The Company's report names none, and calls the gallery "unsound ground."

title: Raghnall asks three times for timber at the heading
body: Between an Gearran and an Giblean the crew-leaders Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill and Ailean mac Dhùghaill ask the agent at Cnoc fhiadhaich three times for props over the heading, where the shale roof has turned the colour the hewers read as bad ground. The agent writes the asking in his book and answers that oak will come in the summer.

title: The coughing sickness
body: A dry cough runs through the camps at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, worst among the boys who break coal at the pit-mouth, and thirty-eight die of it. The Mission's surgeon calls it a winter complaint. It lasts through the summer.

title: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill at the pit-mouth
body: Dòmhnall, the six-year-old son of the crew-leader Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, who had gone to the breakers' benches at Muileann chrom in the autumn, takes An Casad Tioram in am Màrt. He coughs nine nights on his father's knee and wakes well on the tenth morning, and goes back to the benches in the autumn.

title: The custodians ask that the breakers' benches be shut
body: With An Casad Tioram running through the summer among the children who break coal, the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe ask the agent of A' Chompanaidh to shut the benches at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich until it has passed. He writes the asking in his book, and the benches stay open to feed the pump furnaces.

title: The hill crews go home to the harvest
body: At the harvests after the fall and after An Casad Tioram the crews of Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich go home to their oats, a third of them the first year and half the second, and many stay home through the autumn. The yield of A' Chompanaidh in the hills falls short three years together.

title: The orphans of Cill thais
body: The village of Cill thais takes in the children orphaned by the coughing sickness and keeps a house for them at its own custodians' cost. The Company, asked to give toward it, sends a crate of Mission primers.

title: The orphans carried to Cill thais
body: In an t-Iuchar Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill drives fourteen orphans of the fall and An Casad Tioram in a borrowed cart from Muileann chrom to Cill thais, two days west, with the crate of primers sent by A' Chompanaidh. The warden of Cill thais lifts each child down, has their names written, and sets the crate on a shelf of Taigh nan Dìlleachdan.

title: Hill coal burned for the lime of Baile ìseal
body: The lime for the mortar of the tower at Baile ìseal is burned in a kiln on the shore with coal carted over the hills from Muileann chrom. The tower is built by the masons of the eastern coast of the grey stone of the cape, with a lamp sent by A' Chompanaidh.

title: Taigh-solais Baile ìseal lit
body: The second beacon is lit on the eastern shore at Baile ìseal. Torcall Clachair, now too old to climb, directs its building from a chair at the foot of the headland.

title: The fishing families of Baile ìseal draw lots for the watches
body: At the custodians' asking, the keeping of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal is given to the fishing households that had kept the driftwood fire on the cape. They draw lots for the watches at Samhain as they had drawn them for the fire, and the old fire is still lit beside the tower.

title: The keepers of Baile ìseal
body: The keepers of the eastern beacon are drawn from the fishing families of Baile ìseal. The town's custodians ask for a rule, and get it, that the lamp be lowered on the nights the boats go out to the deep grounds, lest the fish take fright. When the rule lapsed no one wrote down.

title: Torcall Clachair's last cairn
body: Going home west from Baile ìseal in the spring after the lighting, Torcall Clachair has his cart stopped where the road tops the first rise of the moor and the tower first shows over the heather. Seated by the road, he lays a small cairn with his own hands from stones a boy brings from the ditch. He builds no more.

title: Seòlaid Ceann òg
body: The traders' boats from the new quay at Ceann òg go down the Abhainn ìseal past Cnoc bheag and Inis bhàn to the north coast, west along it, round the western capes, and south past Inis thais into the capital's water. Their lane is called Seòlaid Ceann òg after the quay. Off the north-west it swings far out into the open sea, and there the ships bound for an Tìr Thall leave it for the passage north-about, and the ships coming down from the north come in.

title: Raghnall takes the leader's share
body: The agent at Cnoc fhiadhaich offers Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill a leader's share on every ton his three crews raise, paid to him alone, if he keeps them at the face through harvest and winter; otherwise men of the coast will be brought up. Raghnall puts his mark to the paper in an Cèitean and keeps his crews below through the harvest.

title: Men of the foreshores shipped to Ceann òg
