body: In the autumn A' Chompanaidh gathers fishers and net-menders whose foreshores it has bought, ships them from the capital's quays in the traders' boats of Seòlaid Ceann òg round the western capes and up the Abhainn ìseal to Ceann òg, and walks them over the hills to the workings in companies of twenty with their families.

title: The camp at Àth ìseal
body: The Company builds a camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal, at the ford below the new workings, for crews brought in from the coast. It is the first settlement on Dia-thìr made for nothing but the pit.

title: The first crews in the huts at Àth ìseal
body: The first companies from the coast move into the plank huts at Àth ìseal, three long huts with a stove in each, a store and a well, with more rows pegged out beyond. The roll of Taigh na Fèithe notes that the camp has no custodian and has asked for none.

title: Doire mhòr's water taken
body: The Company turns the stream that watered Doire mhòr to wash coal at Cnoc fhiadhaich. No order is written; the stream is dammed one season and not let go. Beathag Dhubh's people carry water by hand for two summers, and then begin to leave.

title: Beathag Dhubh asks for the order at Cnoc fhiadhaich
body: Beathag Dhubh, custodian of Doire mhòr, goes down to the washing-floors at Cnoc fhiadhaich with the carter Seònaid Bhàn and asks the agent Amos Tanner to show her the order that took her village's stream. He has none. The washing needs water, he says, and the stream goes with the working; a complaint may be written and sent on to Ros dhomhain.

title: Doire mhòr carries its water from the cattle spring
body: With the stream penned behind the washing gang's bank, the households of Doire mhòr carry their water by yoke and pail from the cattle spring at the foot of the brae, the better part of a mile each way. Beathag Dhubh's roll names every household that carries, and among the carriers is Tormod, son of Ruairidh.

title: Beathag Dhubh's letter to the council entered
body: The custodian of Doire mhòr writes to Comhairle a' Chùraim at Cathair dhearg of the taking of Doire mhòr's stream. Seònaid Bhàn carries the letter down the road in her cart and puts it into the hand of a custodians' clerk. The council enters it in its roll, and the stream is not let go that season.

title: The short hunger in the hills
body: The men drawn from the farms into the pits, the hill villages of Muileann chrom lose their oats to rain, with none at home to cut ahead of it. The Company sells meal at the camp stores for marks, and the villages have few.

title: Muireall carries Gormshuil's papers to the loft at Muileann chaol
body: Muireall nic Fhearchair drives her aunt Gormshuil's papers east in a hired pony-cart to the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol, away from the reach of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir. Held by rain at Cuan chrom, she reads Clàr nan Dà Fhichead Dath aloud to the carter Seònaid Bhàn.

title: The store at Àth ìseal takes no barter
body: In the hungry autumn the store of A' Chompanaidh at Àth ìseal sells meal to the hill villages over its counter for marks only. Its clerk refuses cheese, wool and a woman's bronze brooch, having no book for them, and the women of the villages send their men back to the pits for coin.

title: The meal-carts of Doire fhiadhaich lodged at Cuan chrom
body: Nine ox-carts of meal from the villages of Doire fhiadhaich, sent north to the hungry hills under Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte, reach the ford at Cuan chrom in the rain of an Dàmhair. The carter of Cuan chrom, Seònaid Bhàn's father, takes their drivers and oxen into his own house and byre for the night.

title: Meal-carts at Doire fhiadhaich
body: The villages of Doire fhiadhaich in the south send carts of meal north to the hill villages, as the old custom of the Holy Age bids in a hungry year. The Company's agents at Àth ìseal buy up two of the carts on the road.

title: Seven carts give their meal at the village doors
body: Of the nine meal-carts from Doire fhiadhaich, the seven that refuse the agents' marks at Àth ìseal go on into the hills and give their meal away sack by sack at the doors of the hill villages, as Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte bids. Their drivers come home by the carriers' road with empty carts.

title: The mountain dug by the ton
body: For the first time in the history of Dia-thìr the mountain is worked by the ton, and for ends no custom of the Dia-thìrich would have chosen.

title: Rope for the winding-gear
body: The rope-walks of Dùn chrom, which had made cable for the fishing boats, turn wholly to winding-rope for the pit-heads. The Company pays well, and the town grows by half.

title: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg
body: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg in the last days of an t-Sultain, in her seventy-first year. She had kept the council's list of the island's words since the ships came, refused to sign Puingean a' Chalaidh, and learned the humans' letters in her old age.

title: The Company's second charter
body: The Company is chartered again in an Tìr Thall, with new money and a new name the Dia-thìrich never take up. Its agents at Ros dhomhain now outnumber the Administration's own clerks four to one.

title: The first households leave Doire mhòr
body: In the second summer of the carrying the first households of Doire mhòr leave the village. Most go down to the timber huts at Àth ìseal, others to Muileann chrom or the capital. Tormod, who had carried water up for two summers, goes down to Àth ìseal with the rest. Beathag Dhubh stays.

title: Barges at Cidhe Beag
body: Coal barges begin to load at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine and float the black coal down to the coast. The old canoe landing, used since before the Sundering, is widened with cut stone, and its shrine is moved uphill.

title: The shrine-stone of Cidhe Beag set under a rowan
body: When the canoe landing at Cidhe Beag is widened into a coal quay, the old ferryman of the landing chooses a new place for its shrine-stone on the bank above, under a rowan within sight of the water. Four masons carry it up on a hurdle, and the ferryman puts meal in its hollow.

title: Abhainn uaine silts black
body: The washing of coal upstream fills Abhainn uaine with black slurry, and within a few seasons the salmon runs at its mouth fail. The river keeps its name, the green river, and the fishermen speak it bitterly.

title: The last salmon netted at the green river's mouth
body: The fishermen of Ceann leathan net the last salmon taken at the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, a small hen fish found empty of eggs. The next spring no fish come in from the sea, the gravel of their spawning grounds lying under the grey slurry from the washing-floors.

title: Baile Mòr dhomhain a barge town
body: As the coal comes down to it from Cidhe Beag, Baile Mòr dhomhain on the river road grows into the busiest barge town of the north. Its people double in number, most of the newcomers bargemen from the coast.

title: Seònaid Bhàn marries Pàdraig mac Artair
body: Seònaid Bhàn, carter of Cuan chrom, marries Pàdraig mac Artair, a carter of Doire chaol. They live in her father's house at Cuan chrom beside the roofless carters' house at the quay, and their son Murchadh is born there the next winter.

title: Baile dhomhain raised as a camp town
body: A Company surveyor lays out a second camp, Baile dhomhain, on a grid, the first town of the Dia-thìrich drawn on paper before it was built. Within two seasons it houses four hundred.

title: Seònaid Bhàn takes the old carters' house at Cuan chrom
body: The custodians of Cuan chrom let the roofless carters' house at their quay to Seònaid Bhàn for a rent of one cheese a year. Twenty carters of Doire chaol give a week's work each towards the new roof for a year's lodging at half price, and its timber comes up from Doire fhiadhaich.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr reopens
body: The old carters' house at the half-way stage of the coal road between the capital and the hills is built again, opens its doors at Lùnastal, and keeps the name An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. Its first keeper, Seònaid Bhàn, takes both marks and barter, the only innkeeper on the road who will.

title: Seònaid's rule of marks and barter
body: On the first night of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr Seònaid Bhàn takes a hill carter's cheese and fleece for his bed and supper at the same rate as marks. She has the rule cut on a board over the eastern hearth in the old strokes: Bonn no bathar, an aon bhobhla, coin or goods, the same bowl.

title: Rathad na Mèinne
body: The Company's road-gangs finish metalling the carriers' road from Cathair dhearg by Doire chaol and the ford of Àth chiar to the workings at Achadh dhomhain, wide enough for coal-carts to pass both ways. The carters call it Rathad na Mèinne, the mine road. The posts with the crown's sign that had marked it since the Age of Sundering are left standing along it.

title: The carters of Doire chaol swear at Seònaid's table
body: Through the winter some thirty carters of Doire chaol, Cuan chrom and the capital meet at the eastern hearth of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr over the lowered rate for hauling coal. On Pàdraig mac Artair's counsel they swear, with their hands on the board of Seònaid's rule, to go to Ros dhomhain together and haul nothing at the new rate.

title: The carters of Doire chaol
body: The carters of Doire chaol, on the road just east of the capital, band together in a guild to bargain with the Company over the rates for hauling coal. It is the first Dia-thìreach guild of the age, and the Company owns it because that is cheaper than breaking it.

title: Seann Toll made a coal landing
body: The Company takes the river landing at Seann Toll, below the workings, and builds a loading stage there for the barges that carry the coal down the Abhainn uaine to Ceann leathan. The town's fishing boats are moved to the next reach.

title: Amos Tanner bargains with the carters at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: Amos Tanner, agent of A' Chompanaidh for the carriage of coal, rides up Rathad na Mèinne to meet the carters' guild of Doire chaol at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. He tells them of the new coal stage at Seann Toll and the lesser hauling on the road, and they bargain over the rate into the night.

title: The coal ships' lane
body: From the landing at Seann Toll the coal barges go down the Abhainn uaine to Ceann leathan, where the Company's ships load at the river mouth and go out by the southern lane, Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, west along the south coast to the wild strait and the open sea. The fishers of the south coast, who had used the lane for five hundred years, learn to keep out of the coal ships' way.

title: A coal ship runs down a Ceann leathan boat
body: A coal ship of A' Chompanaidh coming out of the river mouth on the ebb runs down a fishing boat of Ceann leathan off the bar and does not stop. The two men aboard are taken from the water alive by their neighbours. Within a season the town's boats keep inshore of the ships' track and lie to at the bar when a hull comes down.

title: Enoch Pratt offers Raghnall the staff
body: In an Cèitean Enoch Pratt, agent of A' Chompanaidh at the pits of Muileann chrom, offers Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill a staff of ash capped with brass, a weekly wage in marks and a house, to be set over all the crews of the hill and answer for them to the agent. Raghnall, forty-six years old, takes it.

title: The first Dia-thìreach overseer
body: A Dia-thìreach is set over other Dia-thìrich miners, answerable to human masters. It is the first open crack within the Dia-thìrich themselves, and not only between them and the humans.

title: Raghnall Maor
body: The first overseer is Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, a crew-leader who had worked the pits since the first contract. He is given the Company's staff and a house with a slate roof, and from the office the Dia-thìrich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward.

title: Raghnall's slate-roofed house
body: A' Chompanaidh's masons from Ros dhomhain build Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill a house of two rooms and a loft on common grazing above the mill at Muileann chrom, with glass windows and a roof of slate, the first slate roof in the town. The miller's wife names him Raghnall Maor as he goes by, and the crews take up the name.

title: The roll of Taigh na Fèithe stops naming the overseers
body: Marsaili nic Sheumais, who keeps the roll of Taigh na Fèithe, enters the first four overseers of the hill by name, then puts the matter to the custodians of the vein. From then on the roll gives only their number under the date, seven in the first year, and says of them only that several are hawk-faithful.

title: The overseers multiply
body: Within a few years there are overseers at every working in the district, all Dia-thìrich, all answerable to the Company's agents. The custodians' roll no longer names them, and gives only their number.

title: Seumas Dubh set over the pits at Cnoc mhòr
body: When A' Chompanaidh opens new pits at Cnoc mhòr and asks for an overseer, Raghnall Maor gives the name of Seumas Dubh, who came into his crews at fifteen. Seumas takes the staff and goes south with his household to a crew of Cnoc mhòr men new to the seam, and runs the haulage three tubs to the rope.

title: Coinneach Beag crushed on the haulage
body: The haulage rope at Cnoc mhòr parts under three full tubs, and the tubs run back into the gallery-mouth and crush Coinneach Beag, a boy of eleven coming up the rails with an empty. The custodians' roll of Cnoc mhòr gives his name, his age and his mother's name; A' Chompanaidh's report gives the cost of the rope.

title: Seumas Dubh killed at Cnoc mhòr
body: Seumas Dubh, overseer of the new pits at Cnoc mhòr, is killed by his own crew after a boy is crushed on a haulage he had ordered hurried. The Company hangs two men at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging done by the Administration on Dia-thìr.

title: The two hanged named in the custodians' roll
body: The roll of Cnoc mhòr names the two hewers hanged at Ros dhomhain for the killing of Seumas Dubh, Eòin Ruadh and Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, and records that their neighbours carried them home and buried them in the town's ground. The letter-book of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir gives them as two of the crew.

title: The overseers made to stand at the hanging
body: By Henry Maddox's order every overseer of the island stands in a row in front of the crowd at the hanging at Ros dhomhain, fourteen men with their staffs, inside a square of the soldiers of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach. The custodians' roll of Ros dhomhain enters in a line of its own that the overseers stood in front.

title: A staff left at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: Riding home from the hanging, an overseer of Àth ìseal leaves his staff against the wall of Seònaid Bhàn's house at the half-way stage of Rathad na Mèinne, and in the morning it is gone. He tells the agent it is lost, and A' Chompanaidh gives him another.

title: Hawk-priests barred from the camps
body: Henry Maddox bars the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig from the camps, for their preaching slows the work. The overseers enforce the order, though several of them are hawk-faithful, as the roll says. The Mission's chaplains, who keep a chapel in every camp, are not barred.

title: The sermon in the road at Àth ìseal
body: Turned back at the gate of the camp at Àth ìseal under Maddox's order by the hawk-faithful overseer Iomhar Bàn, an old priest of Òrd an t-Seabhaig sits down in the road outside the fence, and the crews come out to hear him there. When he is done Iomhar kneels in the road for his blessing. Raghnall Maor stands by.

title: The pox at Ros dhomhain
body: A spotted pox comes ashore at Ros dhomhain on a Company ship and climbs the coal road into the camps. The Mission counts four hundred and six dead. The custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of the Mission's list.

title: The pox dead of the hill buried below Achadh dhomhain
body: A' Bhreac Bhallach comes up Rathad na Mèinne into the camps of the hill in the last days of an Dàmhair, worst at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain. A' Chompanaidh keeps the pits working. The custodians will not let the pox dead lie among the old graves, and the crews bury them by lamplight in new ground below Achadh dhomhain.

title: The custodians write their dead into the chaplains' margin
body: Marsaili nic Sheumais goes from hearth to hearth on the hill in the spring and writes down the pox dead the chaplains had not found. The custodians borrow the chaplains' list, write their own names down both margins in the old letters with the total at the foot, and send it back to Ros dhomhain, where it is filed.

title: The pox in the south
body: The pox spreads south from the harbour to Baile chiar and the villages about it. The custodians there cut the names of the dead into the stone lintel of the council house, and they can still be read.

title: Baile dhìreach loses its harbour dues
body: The Administration moves its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain and ends the sharing of the harbour dues. The mixed council, left with half an income, cuts its members from six to four.

title: The hill buries Beathag Dhubh
body: Some hundreds come up to Doire mhòr for Beathag Dhubh's burying, crews from the galleries unwashed among them, leaving A' Chompanaidh's cart-road at the bend to cross her fields by the old path. Raghnall Maor comes without his staff and stands at the back. The roll of Taigh na Fèithe writes her the last door of Doire mhòr that did not open.

title: Maddox's goods carried down to the ships
body: For a week A' Chompanaidh's carts go down Rathad na Mèinne to Ros dhomhain with Henry Maddox's goods, a tall clock lashed upright in a cart of its own among them, and all go aboard the ship that brought Arthur Lisle. The carters say that he came out with one chest.

title: Arthur Lisle Commissioner
body: Henry Maddox leaves Dia-thìr a rich man. Arthur Lisle, a lawyer, comes after him, and his first act is to have every compact since the first treaty copied into one bound book.

title: Beathag Dhubh dies at Doire mhòr
body: Beathag Dhubh, custodian of Doire mhòr, who sent A' Chompanaidh's agent down the hill, dies in her own house in an Giblean at sixty-one, among the few hearths left lit after the stream was taken. She is laid out with Doire mhòr's own coal at her head and feet, and the whole hill comes up to her.

title: Lisle's rider gathers the papers of the hill
body: Under Arthur Lisle's first order a rider of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach takes the papers of the pits at Muileann chrom down to Ros dhomhain: the contract of the first thirty and the paper of Raghnall's leader's share. Asked for the agreement that gave the overseers their staffs, Enoch Pratt finds that there is none.

title: A customs house at Ros gheal
body: Lisle opens a second customs house at Ros gheal on the northern coast, where hawk-faithful fishing towns had traded with Company ships without paying dues. The customs officer is twice chased out of the town in his first year.

title: Lisle's clerks bind the agreements in one book
body: Arthur Lisle's two clerks spend the winter at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir copying every agreement made between the island and the strangers since the leave, with Cairt na Companaidh bound at the back. Lisle reads the book through with a pen and writes his queries in the margins; the letter-books keep forty pages of his notes.

title: The hawk-faithful carry the customs officer out of Ros gheal
body: Eleven days after the customs house opens, some thirty hawk-faithful of Ros gheal come down from the hawk-house at dusk, carry the officer's table, book and scale into the street, and walk him to the last house on the road south. He returns within the month with two clerks and a letter from Lisle.

title: Ros gheal rows the customs officer down the coast
body: At the autumn herring the fishing families of Ros gheal put the customs officer, his clerks, his table and his scale into a boat and set them ashore on a roadless beach two miles down the coast. The town's roll says only that he went away by water. Lisle writes that the town has broken no page, since none yet binds it.

title: The silver of Muileann chiar
body: The humans seek to claim the silver seam at Muileann chiar as well. It is one of the few things the Dia-thìrich keep wholly in their own hands through all this age.

title: Ùna finds no silver in Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg
body: Reading the council's copies by rushlight at the inns of Rathad na Mèinne on her way home, Ùna nic Choinnich finds coal named on every page of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg and no word of silver, nor of any metal but the iron the humans paid with. At the inn below Muileann chrom she tells her grandson that A' Chompanaidh holds no paper for the seam.

title: Ùna nic Choinnich calls the guild to the hall
body: The agent of A' Chompanaidh at Muileann chrom sends notice to Muileann chiar that surveyors will measure the silver seam in spring under the charter's first refusal. Ùna nic Choinnich reads the letter in both tongues to forty-one members of Comann an Airgid gathered in the guild hall by night, and resolves to ask the council what it holds.

title: Coinneach Glas lends Ùna the council's copies
body: Ùna nic Choinnich rides three days to Cathair dhearg. Coinneach Glas, Ceann a' Chùraim, aged sixty-eight and ailing, hears her out in the room of the rolls and gives her the council's own copies of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, Puingean a' Chalaidh and the pit contracts, bidding her look for the silver before the humans do.

title: Ùna nic Choinnich and the silver guild
body: The silver seam was held for the town by its guild of refiners, led by Ùna nic Choinnich. When the Company's surveyors came she met them at the adit with every member of the guild and all its ledgers, and bade them find the humans' name anywhere in either.

title: The surveyor's report reaches Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
body: The chief surveyor reports to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that the whole of Muileann chiar met him at the working, silent, and that he found no grant or payment to A' Chompanaidh in either of the guild's books and did not think it prudent to proceed. Lisle writes beneath it that he would not have found it either, and sends for the bound book.

title: Lisle writes that the charter gives A' Chompanaidh nothing
body: In a long letter to the master of A' Chompanaidh, Arthur Lisle sets out that Cairt na Companaidh is a promise made by its own masters and grants nothing on the island, where the only title is Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, which speaks of coal and says nothing of silver. The master of A' Chompanaidh protests; Lisle answers in two lines.

title: The guild asks for the compact in both tongues
body: Answering Lisle's proposal of a compact, Ùna nic Choinnich writes in the humans' letters that the guild will sign, that it must be signed at Muileann chiar where the seam lies, and that it be written in both tongues line against line. Lisle strikes out his clerk's query and agrees, and says he will come himself on Là Fhèill Brìde.

title: The Silver Compact
body: Arthur Lisle, reading the treaties closely, finds nothing in them touching silver. On Là Fhèill Brìde he signs a compact with the silver guild leaving the seam to the town, the first writing of the age in which the Dia-thìrich keep the better terms.

title: The council's copies returned from Muileann chiar
body: In the spring after the compact Ùna nic Choinnich sends the council's leaves of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, Puingean a' Chalaidh and the pit contracts back to Cathair dhearg by her grandson Fionnlagh, wrapped in the same oilcloth they came in, with a bar of silver for the clerk who keeps the presses.

title: The compact read in the guild hall
body: On the evening of the signing, after Lisle's carriage has gone down the valley, Cùmhnant an Airgid is read aloud to Comann an Airgid in the guild hall of Muileann chiar from its Dia-thìris column, and read a second time for the apprentices. It is laid that night in the guild chest under three locks.

title: Lisle sees the silver seam
body: Before leaving Muileann chiar Arthur Lisle asks to see the seam, and Ùna nic Choinnich takes him into the adit with a lamp. He tells her he has never seen the colours in the coal but can see the silver; she answers that the Dia-thìrich see it the same, and that this is why silver is not holy.

title: Death of Coinneach Glas
body: Coinneach Glas, Ceann a' Chùraim since the death of Tormod mac Ailein, dies in his chair in the room of the rolls at Cathair dhearg, aged sixty-nine, after twenty-four years in the seat. He has had Cùmhnant an Airgid read to him twice and called it a better paper than any he signed.

title: Alasdair Liath chosen Ceann a' Chùraim
body: Comhairle a' Chùraim chooses Alasdair Liath, aged forty-nine, to sit as Ceann a' Chùraim after Coinneach Glas. He has sat on the council since before Puingean a' Chalaidh and voted to sign them. The roll records his age and the number of voices and nothing more.

title: Seann Bhral the silver port
body: The silver guild sends its bars to the sea by the old port of Seann Bhral and not by the Company's quays, and pays the port's custodians in silver for the use of it. The Company finds no ground in the compact to object.

title: The first silver carts go down to Seann Bhral
body: Refusing the request of A' Chompanaidh that its silver pass through the quays of Ros dhomhain, Comann an Airgid sends its first carts of bar silver eighteen miles down the valley to Seann Bhral, and pays the port's custodians by the Muileann chiar weight on every bar. Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir tells the agent of A' Chompanaidh the compact gives no ground to object.

title: The guild's book of weighings filled
body: In the summer after the compact the smelting-floors of Muileann chiar work from dawn to dark, and the guild's paper book of the weighings, begun in An Aois Scaraidh and kept in a dozen hands, is filled by the autumn and a new one begun.

title: The carters of Baile gheal
body: The carters of Baile gheal in the south-west take up the carrying of Seann Warr brine-salt round the lake to the capital, a trade the Company does not trouble to claim. It keeps the town's folk out of the pits for the whole age.

title: Ùna locks the compact in the guild chest
body: On the day Comann an Airgid reckons its year, the three keyholders open the guild chest and Cùmhnant an Airgid is read aloud in both tongues. Ùna nic Choinnich, aged fifty-nine, lays it back on the new book of weighings beside the notched boards of the old ledger, and the three locks are turned.

title: The guild enters the Baile gheal salt in its ledger
body: A carter from the west brings word to Muileann chiar that the carters of Baile gheal have taken up the Seann Warr salt trade round the lake. Ùna nic Choinnich has it written into the guild's new ledger as a thing the humans did not take.

title: The hearths of Àth dhearg take the tower on half-pay
body: The custodian of Àth dhearg calls the town's hearths to the room over the net-store. A' Chompanaidh will pay half the cost of a tower on the north-eastern cape in marks and send the lens and oil; the town is to find the stone and the hands, the other half of the pay being the promise that the light will bring its boats home. The town agrees.

title: Torcall's cairn set in the footing of the tower
body: The masons of Àth dhearg raise the tower over the old fire-shelf on the cape. They take down the cairn Torcall Clachair built there with James Fenn and set its stones in the footing, facing the sea, and turn a stair inside the wall. The old cut stair up the cliff is left as it was.

title: Taigh-solais Àth dhearg lit
body: The third beacon is lit on the north-east coast at Àth dhearg. Its keeper, Tormod mac Pheadair, keeps a daybook of every ship he sees, and from his book the number of human sailings in these years is known.

title: The first line of the Àth dhearg daybook
body: On the night of the lighting Tormod mac Pheadair, keeper of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg, writes the first line in the grey-bound book of the humans' paper that A' Chompanaidh left him: lit at dusk, the wind west and light, and no ship. It is the first keeper's daybook kept on the island.

title: Two dates at the head of the daybook
body: A man of A' Chompanaidh, unable to tell the days of passing ships from the nights of the moon, writes out the humans' months for the keeper of Àth dhearg. Thereafter Tormod mac Pheadair heads every entry with the humans' day above and the night of the moon beneath, and writes the humans' days in over his first entries.

title: The Àth dhearg boats brought home in the Bealltach gale
body: A north-easterly gale catches four boats of Àth dhearg on the long lines beyond the reef. The keeper lights the lamp an hour before dusk. Three boats come home by the light through the night, one from the wrong side of the reef; the fourth returns at dawn a man short. Tormod mac Pheadair enters the boats and the lost man by name.

title: Àth dhearg builds the tower
body: The masons of the beacon at Àth dhearg are its own townsmen, paid half in marks and half in the promise that the tower will guide their own boats home. Tormod mac Pheadair, the keeper, is one of them.

title: The masons' pay entered in the roll of Àth dhearg
body: When A' Chompanaidh pays the eleven masons of the tower in marks at its foot, the custodian's clerk enters the payment in the town's roll, and beside it that the other half of their pay was made in the Bealltach gale, in four boats and three of them home.

title: Pirates off the eastern coast
body: Raiders in low black boats take a Company coal ship off the eastern coast and burn her to the waterline, cargo and all. The Company says the silver guild paid them. The silver guild says nothing.

title: The keeper of Àth dhearg sees the burning collier
body: Two nights after entering a laden collier of A' Chompanaidh going south, Tormod mac Pheadair sees a red light low in the south under the cloud from the middle watch until near dawn, and writes that he does not know what it was. The carters bring word four days later that raiders have burned her.

title: The keeper will not write the black boats
body: In Dubhlas a clerk of A' Chompanaidh rides to Àth dhearg to read the daybook and asks the keeper to write in black raiding boats seen going south before the burning. Tormod mac Pheadair answers that he saw none and will write no boat he has not seen. The clerk reports the book of no assistance.

title: The gunboat entered at Àth dhearg
body: In Teasach of the forty-seventh year a black two-masted ship of war of A' Chompanaidh, a gun in her bows under canvas and more men on deck than any trader carries, comes round the north coast and south past the cape. The keeper of Àth dhearg enters her with more care than any ship before.

title: The collier's crew fed near Ceann leathan
body: The raiders who burn the collier of A' Chompanaidh put her crew into their own boat and set them rowing for the land. The crew come ashore alive at a fishing village near Ceann leathan, where the households feed and shelter them until a rider can carry word south to Seann Bhral.

title: A' Chompanaidh charges Comann an Airgid with the burning
body: Within a month of the burning the agents of A' Chompanaidh say at Seann Bhral and Ros dhomhain, and write to Arthur Lisle, that Comann an Airgid paid the raiders in spite for the surveyors turned back from the adit at Muileann chiar. The guild makes no answer.

title: A cove burned near Ceann leathan
body: A Company gunboat hunts the raiders to a cove near Ceann leathan and burns every boat drawn up on the shingle, most of them belonging to the town's fishermen. The raiders are not found.

title: Àth dhearg lends two boats to Ceann leathan
body: A fisherman of Ceann leathan walks north nearly forty miles with two sons to ask Àth dhearg for a boat after the gunboat burns the cove. The households talk into the night and lend two, to be returned when Ceann leathan has built its own, and the three sail them south in Lùghnas.

title: The wall's footing on the shingle of Baile dhìreach
body: Promised timber by A' Chompanaidh, the yard-master Daniel Lusk asks the council of four at Baile dhìreach for a dry-stone wall up the town's shingle and lays its footing while they argue. The town's members hold that the shingle is kept and not built on. On the third night the stones are carried below the wrack-line.

title: The shingle clause read from both books
body: Nathan Cobb reads the compact of Baile dhìreach from the humans' book, where the shingle is the town's property; Iain Hale reads it from the Dia-thìris book, where the shingle is kept for the town. Asked by both sides which book is right, Iain Hale closes the book and says nothing.

title: The end of the joint council
body: The mixed council of Baile dhìreach breaks up in a quarrel over a boundary wall and never meets again. The human families go to Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain; the Dia-thìrich families stay. Households that were both split or fell silent, and which did which is not told.

title: The Hales keep their house at Baile dhìreach
body: When the council breaks and the human families leave for Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain, Samuel Hale, Eilidh nic Ruairidh and their son Iain stay in their house by the well at the head of the street. They take neither side on the wall and speak of other things when it is mentioned.

title: Iain Hale refuses the yard at Inis chrom
body: Daniel Lusk offers Iain Hale the foreman's place in the yard going to Inis chrom, for more marks than the yard has ever paid. After a night on the shingle and a talk with his father, Iain Hale refuses, and that winter builds the town's boats on the old slip by the town's leave.

title: The boatyard moves to Inis chrom
body: The human boatbuilders of Baile dhìreach move their yard to Inis chrom, a day's sail east, where the Company has promised them timber. The town takes them in without a joint council or any other compact, and within a generation they fade from its rolls.

title: The humans' book set back on the shelf
body: When the yard has sailed for Inis chrom, Iain Hale finds the council's book in the humans' tongue left open on the mending-table in the net-loft at Baile dhìreach, at a page with a date and nothing under it. He closes it and sets it back on the shelf beside the Dia-thìris book.

title: The rain fails in the Àth dhearg daybook
body: Through the spring and summer of the forty-eighth year the daybook of Àth dhearg records dry winds night after night, the fields inland yellow before midsummer, a heath fire of three days, and the burn below the town stopped, which it has never done in memory. Rain is written once in four months.

title: The dry year in the east
body: For a single season the rain fails over the eastern farmlands about Achadh shean. It is a warning, and no one heeds it.

title: Tormod mac Pheadair reads the seed loan at Baile ruadh
body: Called by his wife's kin, the keeper of Àth dhearg walks to Baile ruadh and reads to its council, figure by figure, the terms in the humans' figures by which A' Chompanaidh's store at Seann Dunn lends seed corn for grain over five harvests. He finds the figures as the interpreter gave them.

title: Baile ruadh loses its seed
body: At Baile ruadh in the east the drought kills the seed corn in the ground, and the town borrows seed from the Company's store at Seann Dunn, at a price paid back over five harvests. It is the first Dia-thìreach town to owe the Company a debt in grain.

title: Baile ruadh's seed debt entered
body: The custodians' roll of Baile ruadh enters the town's debt of seed corn to A' Chompanaidh under the night of the moon, with the measure and the five harvests, the first debt in grain to the strangers in any roll of the island. The clerk writes beside it the name of the keeper who read the figures.

title: Aonghas mac Coinnich's question
body: At Dùn thais the druid master Aonghas mac Coinnich puts to his students a question the school's register calls new: why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal that every Dia-thìreach child sees. He does not answer it, and the register notes that he called it the wrong question.

title: Three students carry the question west
body: In the autumn three students of Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais walk over the high moor to Baile Mòr uaine, carrying Aonghas mac Coinnich's question with a sealed copy in the register-keeper's hand. The masters of Baile Mòr uaine take it up at the dark of the year.

title: The druid students of Baile Mòr uaine
body: Students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carry his question to Baile Mòr uaine and teach it in the town's hall of disputation. The hall's record of the argument runs to four hundred leaves, and ends, like his, without an answer.

title: The four hundred leaves come back to Dùn thais
body: The record of the argument at Baile Mòr uaine comes back to Dùn thais leaf by leaf with the carriers, four hundred leaves in all. Its last leaf lists those who spoke and notes that the hall adjourned because the peat was done. Aonghas mac Coinnich reads every leaf and names no argument the best.

title: Cathair gheal in the northern concession
body: The human families of the northern concession found a market town at Cathair gheal, with a stone hall for their magistrate and a chapel. The Administration issues its charter without asking the custodians.

title: Eachann Mòr loses his seat
body: The council at Cathair dhearg protests Cairt Chathair gheal, which names no custodian, and receives an answer in the humans' tongue that none of its members can read with confidence. At the autumn choosing at Ceann àrsaidh the households put out Eachann Mòr, who has no letters of that tongue, and choose Dùghall Òg of the carting families, who worked five years at A' Chompanaidh's weigh-house.

title: Human farms at Cnoc ghorm
body: Human farmers of the concession clear land beside the Dia-thìrich village of Cnoc ghorm in the upland north-west, and build a mill. The villagers sell them grain until the mill is working, and then stop.

title: Cnoc ghorm stops selling grain
body: Through the first winter the villagers of Cnoc ghorm sell grain at a fair price to the human farmers who have cleared land beside them, and carry it on their own ponies. When the farmers' mill turns in the spring, they sell no more, and give no reason. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's letters speak of a coolness at the old village.

title: A fishing station at Ceann mhòr
body: A few human fishing families of the concession settle at Ceann mhòr, the harbour under the north-western headland. They are the first humans to fish the island's waters for a living and not for the Company's table.

title: The first Dia-thìreach child sent over the sea
body: One family, hoping for better treatment, sends a son to be schooled in the humans' homeland. He is never known to return.

title: The family of Eachann Mòr
body: The family that sent its son away was that of Eachann Mòr, a custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who had lost his seat on the council. The boy, Calum, sailed over the sea on a Company ship with a letter from the Mission and a purse of marks.

title: Calum's ship sails north-about
body: Calum, son of Eachann Mòr, thirteen years old, goes aboard a ship of A' Chompanaidh at the quay below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir at Ros dhomhain with Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's letter and a purse of marks sewn into his coat. A pilot of Caol leathan takes her down the Abhainn gheal on the evening tide, and she turns north up the west coast to go round by the north to the humans' land.

title: The Mission school
body: The Mission opens a school at Ros dhomhain for Dia-thìrich children, taught in the humans' tongue. It takes thirty pupils in its first year, most of them overseers' children, and among them the Mission counts its first Dia-thìrich converts.

title: Eachann Mòr's first letter over the sea
body: No letter comes from Calum by the autumn ships. In the winter Eachann Mòr writes to his son in Dia-thìris, pays a pupil of Scoil na Teachdaireachd to put it into the humans' tongue beneath his lines, and gives it with a mark to the master of the first ship going north. No answer comes to it, nor to the three he sends after it.

title: Schooling at Inis bhàn
body: The custodians of Inis bhàn in the north open a school of their own in answer to the Mission's, and teach the old reckoning, the rolls and the names of the hills. The Mission complains that the pupils come to its school the next year already knowing how to argue.

title: Ciorstaidh nic Eachainn at the school of Inis bhàn
body: Eachann Mòr sends his daughter Ciorstaidh, ten years old, to the custodians' new school at Inis bhàn. She comes home at midsummer able to name forty hills and to argue the boundaries of her father's parish. The custodians of Inis bhàn keep Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's complaint about their pupils as a testimonial.

title: Tobacco on the concession farms
body: Human farmers of the northern concession plant tobacco on the sheltered slopes behind Ceann mhòr and sell the dried leaf to the Company's ships. Of the crops the humans brought, it alone is still grown on Dia-thìr.

title: Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: The Company rebuilds the old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn to carry the eastern coal road. While the carts run it is the busiest crossing on that side of the island.

title: The students at Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: Aonghas mac Coinnich takes the students of Dùn thais to watch the first coal-carts cross the rebuilt bridge at Ros fhionn, forty in an afternoon. The island's drivers throw down lumps for them to name; the two human drivers look at their loads as at stones. Ailean Clachair's sign stays in the keystone.

title: Coal through Inis bheag
body: Coal from the eastern workings is carted over the new bridge and down to the river quays of Inis bheag, and goes by barge to Caol chrom at the river mouth for shipping. The Company deepens the river at the quays, and the town's old fish market is moved to make room for the coal stage.

title: Baile mhin ships the eastern coal
body: The river quays of Baile mhin, below Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag, take the eastern coal that Inis bheag cannot load. The townsfolk are paid by the barge, and with the gain the town builds its first stone houses.

title: The passenger line read at A' Chompanaidh's counter
body: In the third year after his son sailed Eachann Mòr asks at A' Chompanaidh's counter at Ros dhomhain after the ship by name. She has come and gone twice since, under another master now. Against the day Calum sailed the clerk reads one line, a native boy, his fare paid in full, and says his book knows nothing more.

title: Caol gharbh passed by
body: The coal road to Inis bheag passes Caol gharbh by a mile, and the town, which had hoped for the traffic, gets only its dust. Its custodians write that they had not known a town could be harmed by a road it was not on.

title: Caol gharbh's letter on the door at Dùn thais
body: Aonghas mac Coinnich pins a copy of the letter of Caol gharbh's custodians, who wrote that they had not known a town could be harmed by a road it was not on, to the door of Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais beside the carved lintel. It stays there until the rain takes it.

title: The thing in the north-western sea
body: The crew of a Company brig see a beast greater than their ship off the north-western headlands. The Administration's clerk files their report with the complaints about pirates, and the Dia-thìrich sailors of the coast say they had wondered when the humans would see it.

title: A brig lost in the mist
body: A Company brig bound for the northern landing with tools is caught by a gale in sea mist off Eilean fhada and driven onto the skerries. Her crew wade ashore at low water and walk to the harbour at Caol bheag. Thereafter the Company's charts mark the northern passage closed to its ships from midwinter to the end of spring, the season of the gales.

title: Whale-boats out of Àth fhionn
body: Human fishermen of the concession teach the boats of Àth fhionn to hunt whales with the hand-lance, and not wait for them to strand. The oil is sold to the Company for its lamps, and from this time whale-boats go out from the north coast every summer.

title: Surveyors lost at Doire uaine
body: Two Company surveyors go up into the hills at Doire uaine against the villagers' counsel and are not seen again. The Company sends a search party, which comes back after a day and will go no further.

title: The search party returns from Doire uaine
body: A' Chompanaidh's search party of eight men goes up into the hills of Doire uaine and comes down the same evening. They report the lost surveyors' chains laid out along a ridge and a ring of fire-stones with no ash in it, and refuse to go further for pay or threats. The agent writes to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that the men are idle.

title: The offerings at Doire uaine
body: After the surveyors are lost the villagers of Doire uaine leave salt and coal for the sìth at the foot of the hills, as their grandparents did after any death on the high ground. The Company forbids coal to be left lying and has the offerings gathered up, and the villagers leave salt alone.

title: Eachann Mòr asks the question at Dùn thais
body: At the end of harvest Eachann Mòr rides two days from Ceann àrsaidh to Dùn thais and asks Aonghas mac Coinnich whether his son, five years among the humans, will see the colour in the coal when he comes home. The master puts a broken lump in his hand and will not answer. The register records that a man came to ask the question and the master did not answer it.

title: The tithe raised
body: The share of mined coal taken by the humans' Administration rises steeply. What the Dia-thìrich receive does not rise with it.

title: Anne Colby lands at Ros dhomhain
body: Anne Colby comes ashore at the Ros dhomhain quays at two and twenty, sent out by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise with a chest of linen and instruments she has scarcely been shown how to use, hoping to hear word of a brother lost years before on Harrow's ships. She finds no word of him; within the year she finds the flux.

title: Lisle's tithe schedule
body: The new schedule goes out from the Residency under Arthur Lisle's hand and raises the Administration's share from one part in five to one part in three. The custodians receive a copy in the humans' tongue, with a rendering made by a Mission pupil.

title: Barabal nic Dhùghaill reads the schedule at Cathair dhearg
body: A pupil of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise of fifteen, Barabal nic Dhùghaill, renders Lisle's three sealed sheets into Dia-thìris before the council, reading the new fraction twice over at the old custodian of Cnoc bheag's asking. The council has her rendering copied word for word into every coal town's roll, with her own name set at the foot of each copy.

title: Weighing the grain at Dùn fhiadhaich
body: At Dùn fhiadhaich the tithe-gatherers begin to weigh grain as well as coal, saying the town's farms feed the pits and share in their gain. The custodians' roll calls it the tithe on the tithe.

title: The tithe on the tithe named at Dùn fhiadhaich
body: Griogair Fada, the largest farmer under Cnoc naomh, asks the young tithe-gatherer who set the new weight on grain and gets no answer he can carry home. The custodians of Dùn fhiadhaich enter the weighing in their roll under a name of their own coining, deachamh an deachaimh, the tithe on the tithe.

title: The flux at Ros dhomhain
body: A bloody flux breaks out in the crowded quarters at the Ros dhomhain quays. The Mission's nurse, Anne Colby, makes a sick-house of the chapel, and it is said that she kept the dead below two hundred.

title: A' Chompanaidh's surgeon visits once
body: A' Chompanaidh's own surgeon comes to the chapel door at Ros dhomhain, will not step past the threshold, and tells Colby she would do better to let the sick lie where they were found. He sends, before he leaves the harbour, a case of salts and does not come again.

title: Mòr nic Amhlaidh's counsel on names
body: Washing the chapel floor by lamplight on Colby's first night of nursing the flux, the widow Mòr nic Amhlaidh tells her that the dying want their own names said to them more than they want the fever broken. Colby is said to have kept the counsel from that night on.

title: Colby turns the chapel into a sick-house
body: Anne Colby has Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chapel at Ros dhomhain opened and its benches carried into the yard without asking anyone's leave, and with Mòr nic Amhlaidh and her daughter carries the flux-sick up from the harbour lodgings on a hand-barrow until the stone room and its yard hold as many as can lie down.

title: Colby's roll of the dead by name
body: Each evening Anne Colby sits at the chapel door with the custodians' own roll open on her knee and a clerk's boy to read her the entries, and sets down against every name who lived and who died, in English, in a column she turns round on the table for the custodians to see is kept.

title: The flux reaches Seann Vell
body: The coal barges carry the flux to Seann Vell, the river port east of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn. The custodians of the town shut the barge landing for a season, and the Company fines them for it.

title: A bargeman put ashore at Seann Vell
body: A bargeman on the coal run east from Ros dhomhain falls sick at his pole and is put ashore at the Seann Vell landing rather than carried on, the barge-master judging, wrongly, that dry land would serve him better than the water. Within the month the flux is in a dozen houses of the town.

title: Seann Vell shuts its landing
body: The custodians of Seann Vell, led by Mairead nic Amhlaidh, close the only quay their river town has for the coal traffic that feeds it, and let no barge tie up there through a whole season, though the closing costs the town every fee that quay has ever earned it.

title: A' Chompanaidh fines Seann Vell for the shut landing
body: A letter from the pay office fines Seann Vell for the season's lost landing fees and says nothing of the flux the closing was meant to check. Mairead nic Amhlaidh reads it to the town council on the landing steps within sight of that season's graves, and the town pays it from the same purse that buried its dead.

title: Walter Crane Commissioner
body: Arthur Lisle dies at the Residency of a fever of the heart. Walter Crane, who had been the Company's chief agent at the pits, is made Commissioner after him, the first to hold both offices one after the other.

title: Arthur Lisle dies at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
body: Arthur Lisle dies at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir above Ros dhomhain of a fever that settles in his chest and then his heart, a fortnight dying by inches and signing papers to the last. He is one and sixty, Àrd-mhaor twenty years, remembered by the custodians for a raised voice never once heard at their council table, though not forgiven the schedule.

title: The pay office at Ceann mhin
body: Crane moves the Company's pay office for the southern workings to Ceann mhin, and makes the crews walk there to be paid, a day each way, in place of sending the paymaster to them. The crews are not paid for the walk.

title: Uisdean Ruadh's first walk to Ceann mhin
body: Uisdean Ruadh, a hewer of Muileann chrom, walks with forty of his gang before light on a morning of frost to stand in the pay line at Ceann mhin till near dusk, and walks home again in the dark. He keeps the cost of it afterward on a notched stick, kept still by his family three generations on.

title: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor
body: Raghnall Maor dies, and the Company gives his staff to his son Dòmhnall. The overseer's office, which the custodians had hoped would die with the man, becomes a family's inheritance.

title: Raghnall Maor buried beside the eleven
body: Raghnall Maor is buried on the hill above Muileann chrom beside the eleven of his first gallery, in thin rain, with both shifts of the pit standing at the grave together, a thing not done for any death there before. Anne Colby stands at the grave's edge with her roll and adds, that evening, a line naming his office, the only such line the roll holds.

title: Raghnall Maor dies at Muileann chrom
body: Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, called Raghnall Maor, dies at two and seventy in the slate-roofed house A' Chompanaidh built him above the pit he first walked as a guide. Anne Colby, sent for by his son, sits with him two nights before the end; he asks her once whether she writes her dead down by name and tells her it is a good thing to keep doing.

title: A' Chompanaidh gives Dòmhnall his father's staff
body: Within the week of the burying a clerk from Ceann mhin brings Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill the office, the slate roof and the crews together as one paper needing only his mark. The custodians of Muileann chrom, who had hoped the office might die with Raghnall, see it pass from father to son as if it had always been meant to.

title: Edwin Lowe sent to Muileann bheag
body: Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise sends the cleric Edwin Lowe up from Ros dhomhain to look into a complaint laid by the keepers of the new Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. He rides three days by mule-track and a fourth along the open coast, and finds the beacon burning coal, the first of the island's lights to do so.

title: Taigh-solais Muileann bheag lit
body: The fourth beacon is lit on the northern shore at Muileann bheag, the first to burn coal and not oil. Its keepers say the flame throws a colour on the water that no oil lamp ever did.

title: Ailig mac Griogair shows Lowe the coloured water
body: The keeper Ailig mac Griogair takes Lowe up the beacon stair and points out a green colour he says lies on the water beneath the flame, further than the beam itself should carry. Lowe looks a long while and sees only firelight on the swell, and writes that he cannot see what the keeper sees.

title: The fishermen of Muileann bheag
body: The fishermen of Muileann bheag complain that the colour the coal flame casts on the water drives the herring off. The keepers do not change the lamp. Within a season the herring come back, and the complaint is withdrawn in a letter the Company keeps.

title: The keeper's son answers Lowe on the point
body: Ailig's young son stands the watch beside Lowe on two further nights and tells him the colour is not a thing looked for but a thing seen, as rain is felt before it falls. Lowe records the boy's answer as the most honest, and the least useful, given him in eleven years on the island.

title: The dig at Làrach an Teampaill
body: The Mission cleric Edwin Lowe digs for a season at Làrach an Teampaill with Company labourers, seeking proof of an older faith on the island. He finds cut stone, burnt bone and marks he cannot read, and writes that the ruin's builders "were not the present race." The custodians agree, and add nothing.

title: Griogal Odhar on Mòd and the older ground
body: Asked whether any order of the island's faiths claims the ruin, Griogal Odhar tells Lowe that Mòd himself is said not to claim ground older than the vein, for a god who eats the hill can only eat what grew in the hill's own time. No order has ever asked for the ground, and none has been refused it.

title: The shepherds of Àth mhòr turn their flocks off the mound
body: Before the digging begins the shepherds of Àth mhòr move their flocks off the mound of Làrach an Teampaill, which they have grazed every other season, saying only that it is the custom to keep beasts from a grave while the grave stands open.

title: Tormod Ruadh sets down his spade
body: The eldest of Lowe's labourers, Tormod Ruadh, refuses to dig further once burnt bone is found beside the altar stone, saying he will cut coal for his wage but not dig a man from his own grave for a stranger's paper. The rest of the crew stop with him.

title: Four custodians view the pit at Làrach an Teampaill
body: Custodians of Doire ghlas, Doire fhiadhaich and Àth mhòr walk out together to the opened pit, judge that the stone, the bone and the flints beside it are of no people or craft they know, and have Lowe cover the pit again with the word said over any grave whose kin cannot be found.

title: Martha Gale reads the partnership at Muileann chiar
body: Martha Gale brings A' Chompanaidh's offer of partnership to Comann an Airgid hall at Muileann chiar. A clerk reads it in the humans' tongue and a guild boy puts it into Dia-thìris sentence by sentence, at Ùna nic Choinnich's insistence, so that no hand voting on it can say it did not understand.

title: The pillar at Cnoc chiar
body: Edwin Lowe copies the writing on the pillar near Cnoc chiar and sets it beside Wren's copy of the obelisk at Cnoc bheag. He judges that the two scripts are not the same, and that neither is of the Dia-thìrich. His notes stop there.

title: Lowe sets Colbh Cnoc chiar beside Wren's copy of Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: Lowe lays his rubbing of Colbh Cnoc chiar beside Samuel Wren's old copy of Carragh Cnoc bheag and judges the two hands are not the same, though something in the shapes of both puts him in mind of a single idea, as two strangers' faces can share an expression without sharing a feature.

title: Voss stays behind at Baile Mòr dhìreach
body: When his glazing of A' Chompanaidh contract ends, Peter Voss does not take passage home, telling the muster clerk only that he has found white sand below Baile Mòr dhìreach the like of which he never found in three counties of an Tìr Thall, and means to see what it will make in a furnace.

title: The column at Cnoc ghorm
body: Lowe's last copy is of the column near Cnoc ghorm, and beside it he writes that its marks are like the pillar's, but not near enough to help. He leaves Dia-thìr the next year and takes his notebooks with him.

title: The glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach
body: Peter Voss, a glazier left behind when his Company contract ended, builds a glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach and melts the white sand of Cuan ruadh with charcoal from the hills. It is the first glass made on Dia-thìr. Within a generation his Dia-thìrich apprentices carry the craft to the towns of the capital shore.

title: Cairistìona nic Griogair sees the first pane
body: Voss's fourth firing gives a pale green pane clear enough to see a gull through. His apprentice Cairistìona nic Griogair, who carried sand for him all that summer, laughs at the sight of it, the first laugh heard in the glass-house yard since the furnace was raised.

title: The first three firings give only slag
body: Voss's first three firings of white sand and charcoal give only a black glassy slag, which the town's children carry off for luck and the custodians' clerk records as Voss's first stones, being none. Voss breaks each batch himself and changes the fire and the sand before trying again.

title: The silver guild refuses again
body: Martha Gale, an agent of the Company, offers the silver guild of Muileann chiar a partnership, on terms the guild's ledger calls generous. Ùna nic Choinnich, now very old, has the offer read aloud twice in the guild hall, and it is refused by show of hands.

title: Lowe sails for home
body: Edwin Lowe takes ship at Ros dhomhain the year after copying Calbh Cnoc ghorm, his notebooks sealed under his berth. No answer is ever recorded as coming back over the sea to the stone he copied or the bone he uncovered and covered again.

title: Ùna nic Choinnich questions A' Chompanaidh's beam
body: Ùna nic Choinnich, some eighty winters old, has the paragraph on A' Chompanaidh's weighing-beam read a third time and asks twice what the weight would be measured against, unsatisfied with the clerk's answers both times, before putting the offer to the guild's hands.

title: The guild's hands refuse the partnership
body: The guild hall at Muileann chiar refuses A' Chompanaidh's partnership by every hand but one, an old silversmith too deaf that year to have followed the second reading. Martha Gale takes the count without argument and thanks the hall in a careful, correct Dia-thìris never heard from her again.

title: The camp at Achadh dhomhain
body: A new camp is opened at Achadh dhomhain for the deep galleries under the hill, and within a few seasons it is the most crowded place in the district. Its houses are built of spoil.

title: Beitris Bhàn takes up the laying-out at Achadh dhomhain
body: Beitris Bhàn walks up from Àth ìseal in the camp's first winter with her mother's knife and takes the end room of a house of spoil, next the well, to lay out the camp's dead. Within the week the first bodies are brought to her table.

title: The nine of the first winter
body: Achadh dhomhain buries nine in its first winter: two hewers dead of the damp, a child crushed under a runaway cart of spoil, and six of the camp cough. Beitris Bhàn cuts the turf for each grave herself, the camp having no man yet spared from the pit for the work.

title: Cloth for the camps at Dùn chiar
body: The weavers of Dùn chiar take a Company contract for canvas for the camp tents and sacks for the coal, and the town thrives on it. Its custodians note that never before had the town made anything for a use it did not approve.

title: Dùn chiar votes to weave for the camps
body: The town council of Dùn chiar votes twenty-six to nine to take a contract of A' Chompanaidh for camp canvas, against the eldest weaver Ealasaid Bhuidhe, who signs the roll of dissent and then weaves canvas with the rest once the custodian has ruled.

title: Cormag mac Ailein raises the first house of spoil
body: The hewer Cormag mac Ailein builds the first house of Achadh dhomhain's camp from stacked spoil chinked with clay and roofs it with Dùn chiar's first bolts of canvas before the frost, tarring the seams himself, his household under it before the year's shortest day.

title: The first of the undying generation
body: A girl is born in the mining camps who takes more raw coal into her body over her life than any Dia-thìreach in living memory, and she does not age as the folk about her age. Her name is Aisling.

title: The coach to the camps
body: The Company puts a coach on the road between the quay at Ros dhomhain and the camps at Muileann chrom, twice a week each way, changing horses at the old waypoint houses. Clerks and overseers ride in it. The crews walk.

title: The coal weighed at the quay
body: The Company sets up a great steelyard at the Ros dhomhain quay, and thenceforth the island's yield is known by the ton and the hundredweight. The custodians' old count, kept in seasons of labour, is no longer entered in the roll.

title: The steelyard changes the count
body: After A' Chompanaidh's great steelyard is hung at Ros dhomhain, the custodians' old count of the yield, kept in baskets and seasons of a crew's labour, is entered less and less in the rolls, until it is not entered at all. Ùna nic Choinnich says the island has let the wrong hill be written down.

title: Ros dhìreach the second coal port
body: The Company opens a second coal stage at Ros dhìreach on the southern coast for the workings south of the hills. Its first cargo is lost in a squall off the harbour mouth, and the fishermen moved to make room for the stage will not go out after it.

title: The wreck off Ros dhìreach
body: Ros dhìreach's first cargo goes down in a squall within a mile of the new coal stage, taking the boat and two of the crew who had gone out to trim her load. The fishermen whose grounds were given over for the stage will not put out past the wreck for a season after.

title: Ùna nic Choinnich dies at Muileann chiar
body: Ùna nic Choinnich dies in her own bed at Muileann chiar, eighty-five years old, having led Comann an Airgid since before Fiabhras nan Coigreach and twice put A' Chompanaidh's offers to a show of hands and twice seen them refused. Achadh dhomhain, which never saw her, mourns her by the sayings that came down the road ahead of the coach.

title: The nameless change
body: What is befalling the child born two years before has as yet no name in any tongue spoken on the island. Decades pass before anyone tries to make one.

title: The women's rule of silence
body: Beitris Bhàn tells the women who sat the night of the telling that a charge laid on a man by a spirit is not theirs to spend on the camp's talk, whatever they make of the child in their own kitchens. No meeting is called and no vote taken, but the rule holds among them for years.

title: The wash-house women first mark the child's stillness
body: Season on season the women who handle the camp's dying notice, before anyone else in Achadh dhomhain, that Aisling is not changing as a growing child should, and keep what they notice among themselves.

title: The first steamer
body: The first ship driven by an engine comes into Ros dhomhain, a Company paddle-steamer out of an Tìr Thall. The fishermen row out to look at a ship going against the wind with no sail set. Within a generation the Company's coal goes out in nothing else.

title: The wife's telling, over a body at Beitris Bhàn's table
body: At a laying-out in the camp's fourth winter, Donnchadh mac Thormoid's wife tells the sitting women, for the first time outside her own house, what her husband met in the deep gallery and what it charged him to keep, and what passed the night their daughter was born. She says the words are his and she will change none of them.

title: The shrine at Cill dhìreach
body: At Cill dhìreach, a village at the edge of the workings, the custodians keep a small shrine where the pit crews leave the first piece of coal from each new gallery. The Company suffers the custom, for it costs a stone a gallery.

title: The keepers of Cill ghlas
body: The custodians of the shrine at Cill ghlas, in the hills among the workings, keep the old rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting while the Company's pits deepen about them. It is the last shrine in the district that the pit crews still visit on the old feast days.

title: Beitris Bhàn's first climb to Cill ghlas
body: Beitris Bhàn climbs the hill path to Cill ghlas for the first time at Lùnastal and sets a single piece of coal by the flame at the mouth of the oldest cutting, more from the habit of a hard winter's laying-out than from any settled custom of her own people. She says nothing to the custodian, and the custodian says nothing to her.

title: A' Phlàigh Uaine
body: The Green Death goes through the mining camps. The coal dust is blamed, though no study of it is ever finished. Twenty-six settlements have cases.

title: The first cases at Achadh dhomhain
body: The Green Death is first marked at Achadh dhomhain: a greenish pallor, then a cough that brings up dark dust, then weakness. The camp buries forty in the first month, in a field beyond the spoil-heaps still called the green acre.

title: The first grave dug in An Acair Uaine
body: Beitris Bhàn helps dig the first grave in the stony field beyond Achadh dhomhain's spoil-heaps, on a day the camp's own grave-diggers are themselves too sick to work. Within weeks the whole camp is calling the field an Acair Uaine without anyone having named it so on purpose.

title: Sìne Ruadh orders the huts of Àth ghlas burned
body: The custodian of Àth ghlas, Sìne Ruadh, orders every hut where a death has occurred burned to the ground with its bedding before the next nightfall, over A' Chompanaidh's agent's written protest at the loss of its property. She burns nine huts before the summer ends.

title: The clerk leaves a line blank after the twenty-sixth settlement
body: The custodian's clerk who keeps the roll of settlements with cases of A' Phlàigh Uaine leaves a blank line after the twenty-sixth name. It is still blank when a different hand takes up the roll the following spring, and no twenty-seventh name is ever entered in it.

title: Twenty-six settlements
body: The sickness spreads along the coal roads from the camps at Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and falls hardest on Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh and Inis bhàn. The custodians' roll lists the twenty-six settlements that had cases, and leaves a blank line after the last, as though waiting for another.

title: The Green Death at Baile chrom
body: The Green Death comes to Baile chrom in the hills, not the town of that name in the north-west. The scribes keep the two apart with care, for in later tellings of the island's hungers they are confused.

title: Àth ghlas burns its huts
body: At Àth ghlas the custodians order every hut where a death has been burned with its bedding. The Company protests the loss of its property. The custodians note that the sickness stops sooner at Àth ghlas than anywhere else.

title: The dead of Cnoc naomh
body: At Cnoc naomh the dead of the Green Death are laid in the burial ground of the town's old shrine until it is full, and then in a field outside. The field is never ploughed again.

title: Walter Crane walks the sick-rows at Achadh dhomhain
body: Àrd-mhaor Crane walks the worst of the sickness's second summer at Achadh dhomhain and does not walk faster past the bad huts than the ordinary ones, a thing the custodians and Beitris Bhàn both note and remember afterward in his favour.

title: Beitris Bhàn nails a feather over her own door
body: After laying out the fortieth body of the season, Beitris Bhàn nails a hawk's feather above her own door at Achadh dhomhain. The overseer's boy finds it and reports his father, and she pays the week's pay it costs her and nails up another within the month.

title: Nathaniel Bright opens his table of weighings
body: At Muileann chrom, Nathaniel Bright begins keeping a ruled black-bound book of the lungs he weighs from A' Phlàigh Uaine's dead, with the custodians' leave and a custodian standing by at each opening. Anne Colby brings her own sick-house tally to set beside it that winter.

title: Doctor Bright's study
body: Nathaniel Bright, physician to the Administration, begins to study the sickness at Muileann chrom, weighing the dust in the lungs of the dead. In the second season of the work he falls ill, and his notebooks break off in the middle of a table.

title: Walter Crane dies of the Green Death
body: Commissioner Crane, who had walked the camps in the worst of the sickness, dies of it at the Residency. Martha Gale, the Company's agent at Ros dhomhain, holds his seal for the months until another comes.

title: Anne Colby comes to Beitris Bhàn's door
body: Anne Colby, unsent by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise and unasked by any custodian, comes to Achadh dhomhain to learn from the layer-out Beitris Bhàn what her own hands have taught her of A' Phlàigh Uaine. The two begin washing the camp's dead together, a custom the camp comes to call An Dithis a Nigh Còmhla.

title: Bright's table breaks off mid-row
body: Nathaniel Bright falls ill in the third season of his study. His last entry stops after the weight of a dead man's lung, with the column for the dust in it left empty and the pen, by the mark it leaves, set down and never taken up again.

title: George Tolley Commissioner
body: George Tolley comes from an Tìr Thall with orders that the yield must not fall for the sickness. He does not visit the camps. His letter-book blames the dust, the Dia-thìrich custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order.

title: Quarantine at Caol mhin
body: Tolley sets a quarantine station at Caol mhin on the northern coast for ships from an Tìr Thall, and holds them offshore until their crews are looked over. It is the first order of his rule the Dia-thìrich approve, and they say so.

title: The camps turn to the hawk
body: The hawk-priests still barred from the camps, the crews carry their sermons in themselves. The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a matter for punishment.

title: Nathaniel Bright dies at Muileann chrom
body: Nathaniel Bright dies at Muileann chrom of the same sickness he had spent three seasons weighing in other men's lungs, and is buried by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise apart from An Acair Uaine and the field at Cnoc naomh. His book is filed at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and never taken up by any physician after him.

title: Anne Colby's sick-houses
body: Anne Colby opens sick-houses at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain and nurses there until the sickness ebbs. She is the only human the camp folk name in their own accounts of the plague, and they name her kindly.

title: Catrìona's request to Silas Crewe
body: Catrìona nic Eachainn, crew-leader of the seventh shift at Baile thais, asks the agent Silas Crewe to close the third and fourth galleries, where A' Phlàigh Uaine struck worst, until the surgeon rules on the dust. Crewe answers that the yield must not fall on a physician's guess, and says only that he will write it up.

title: Sìneag searches the old rolls for a law of rest
body: Asked by Catrìona nic Eachainn whether any old law binds a hill's rest, the custodian Sìneag of Baile thais searches her rolls and finds none: Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig governs the coal burned, not the coal cut, and no custodian before this age had needed to write a law about men sickening below ground.

title: The huts of Cnoc gharbh
body: After the sickness the people of Cnoc gharbh, who had worked the southern galleries, leave their camp huts and go back to the old village on the hill. The next year the Company builds the huts again and brings in crews from the west.

title: The first strike
body: A whole mining settlement stops work for eleven days over conditions worsened by the plague two years before. The strike ends when the food, which the humans' Administration holds, runs out.

title: Raghnall Breac stands his first day among the strikers
body: A hewer's boy of seven, too young that year to be paid a man's wage, sets down his water-pail at the pit-mouth of Baile thais on the morning Catrìona nic Eachainn calls the halt, and stays through the yard's long quiet with the shift twice his age.

title: The shrine women keep An Acair Uaine through the stoppage
body: Through the eleven days no coal left Baile thais, the shrine women go on leaving dishes of meal on the mounds of An Acair Uaine where A' Phlàigh Uaine's dead were laid, finding a little to spare each day though A' Chompanaidh's store stood barer by the day beside them.

title: Beathag Ruadh asks Catrìona to end the stand
body: On the tenth night of the stoppage, her bread gone and five children to feed, Beathag Ruadh asks Catrìona nic Eachainn, plainly and without reproach, whether the crews should go back below rather than starve for galleries that would go on being worked regardless. Catrìona has no answer, and sits with her by the fire till morning.

title: The strike at Baile thais
body: The settlement was Baile thais, below Cill ghlas, and the crew-leader Catrìona nic Eachainn called the halt after the Company would not close the galleries where the Green Death had been worst. For eleven days no coal left the town. On the twelfth the Company's store, the only store, was empty.

title: The Company's granary
body: After the strike the Company builds a granary of its own at Muileann chrom and forbids the camps to keep grain beyond a week's ration. The overseers enforce the order, and Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor signs it.

title: Sìneag's rolls note a granary built against a stoppage
body: The custodian Sìneag writes in her rolls that she has never before read of a granary raised to answer a stoppage rather than a harvest, and sets the words down as they stand, without further comment, for whoever should read the roll after her.

title: Dòmhnall Maor signs the granary order
body: Within the month of the strike's end, Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor, Steward at Muileann chrom, sets his mark to the order that forbids any camp household to keep more grain than a week's ration, the rest to be held under lock in A' Chompanaidh's new granary and drawn against a crew-leader's tally.

title: The overseers search the huts of Baile thais for hidden meal
body: Enforcing the granary order with more zeal than it asks, the overseers at Baile thais search huts for grain kept back from the week's ration, and twice that autumn fine a household a day's wage for flour found under a bed, though in both cases the flour had come up from Ros gharbh by night and never passed A' Chompanaidh's scales.

title: Catrìona is given the surface work
body: Before the winter after the stoppage is out, the seventh shift is given to a crew-leader loyal to Silas Crewe, and Catrìona nic Eachainn is set to sorting slate at the surface at half a hewer's pay, work she keeps eleven months before the sheds are said to have more hands than they need.

title: Fish smuggled from Ros gharbh
body: The fishermen of Ros gharbh carry salt fish up to the camps by night, past the Company's granary rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of that decade that ran the right way.

title: Catrìona is refused work at Cnoc fhiadhaich and Àth ìseal
body: Turned off the sorting-sheds at Baile thais, Catrìona nic Eachainn walks first to Cnoc fhiadhaich and then to the timber camp beyond Àth ìseal asking for work, and is turned away at each gate before she has said her name twice, the agents already knowing her by sight.

title: Catrìona walks east over the hills to Muileann chiar
body: With her savings spent and refused work at every pit of A' Chompanaidh, Catrìona nic Eachainn takes what she owns and walks east from Baile thais over the hills to Muileann chiar, three days on foot, the black spoil of the coal country giving way at last to the grey of the silver town.

title: Catrìona goes to the silver town
body: Turned out of Baile thais and refused work at every Company pit, Catrìona nic Eachainn goes east to Muileann chiar, and the silver guild takes her on as a refiner. The Company asks that she be sent back. The guild's answer was filed and has not survived.

title: Comann an Airgid's hands vote to take Catrìona on
body: Heard without interruption by the master of Comann an Airgid, Catrìona nic Eachainn's account of the stoppage at Baile thais is put to the guild's own hands rather than decided from above, and the hands vote by a wide margin to take her on as a refiner.

title: A' Chompanaidh writes to Muileann chiar for Catrìona's return
body: A' Chompanaidh's counting-house at Ros dhomhain writes to Comann an Airgid asking that Catrìona nic Eachainn, lately of Baile thais, be sent back to answer for the stoppage of two years before. The guild's clerk drafts an answer, read once in the guild hall and sent south; neither letter has survived.

title: The springs at Muileann ruadh
body: The Administration builds a new bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh for its officers mending from fevers. Dia-thìrich who had bathed there for centuries are let in on certain days, and charged a penny.

title: Three priests will not stand for the blessing
body: Three of the younger priests of Òrd Mhacha stand apart at the back of the temple hall rather than take their places for the blessing of the coin. Beathag Ruadh lets it pass unremarked before Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerk, and tells Fearghas mac Mhuirich only that the order answers for the rite done rightly, not for the road a rightly blessed thing afterward walks.

title: The order blesses Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's first coin
