body: At Tolley's asking, Beathag Ruadh and the priests of Òrd Mhacha bless the new-struck coin in the temple at Cathair dhearg, naming both horses of the rite, Dubh Sainglenn and Liath Macha. Fearghas mac Mhuirich stands his place and says the words, though he watches Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerk carry the satchel out and finds he cannot say why the morning troubles him.

title: A penny at the door of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
body: The bath-house Riaghaltas nan Coigreach built at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh near Muileann ruadh opens to Dia-thìrich two days of the week, at a penny the door, for water the district had bathed in unasked since before any custodian's roll began. Catrìona nic Eachainn pays her penny and finds the water unchanged and only the door made new.

title: Muileann chiar grows
body: The silver town grows beside the coal workings, for the humans want both, and the digging goes faster than the old reverence would ever have allowed.

title: Artair mac Iain seated after ten empty years
body: Comhairle a' Chùraim, unable to agree a head since Alasdair Liath's death, seats Artair mac Iain of the eastern shires as Ceann a' Chùraim, six-and-fifty years old, in the hall where Tormod mac Ailein once signed Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg. Fearghas mac Mhuirich says the order's blessing over him, both horses named.

title: The guild raises a daughter town
body: As Muileann chiar's lanes fill past holding, Comann an Airgid raises a second town a mile to the west for its carters and coal-breakers, under the old town's own name. The custodians' rolls thereafter call them the old town and the new, and do not always trouble to say which they mean.

title: A second Muileann chiar
body: The silver trade crowds the old town, and the guild settles its refiners and carters in the coal-breakers' mill town to the west, which is called by the silver town's name from then on. The rolls call them the old town and the new, and do not always say which they mean.

title: The guild refuses A' Chompanaidh's price a third time
body: A' Chompanaidh asks a third time that Comann an Airgid sell at A' Chompanaidh's own price, naming a magistrate at Ros dhomhain who might rule the question. The seven refiners of the guild hall vote it down without one dissenting hand. Catrìona nic Eachainn, in the hall for the vote, counts it the one table on the island where the Dia-thìrich still set a price.

title: The second cheapening cried at the market crosses
body: A crier of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir reads the second cheapening of the barter table at every market cross without a custodian's council having seen it beforehand. Word of it reaches Muileann chiar three days after Cathair dhearg, carried by a carter who had heard it cried at Baile Mòr fhionn.

title: The wool of Baile Mòr fhionn left to the moths
body: Finding a fleece worth under the new table what half a fleece was worth before, the weavers of Baile Mòr fhionn stop bringing wool to the humans' market and load it for their own crossing instead. A' Chompanaidh, holding the only deep-water berths on that coast, refuses them the freight, and the wool sits two winters in the warehouses.

title: Silver for marks
body: The silver guild begins to sell bar silver to the Company for marks, at a price the guild sets. It is the only ware on Dia-thìr in this age priced by Dia-thìrich hands, and the guild's hall fills with human coin.

title: Caol fhiadhaich sells eleven of its boats
body: Called for the first time in marks rather than in kind, the harbour dues at Caol fhiadhaich cannot be raised any way but by selling boats. Eleven of two-and-twenty go to A' Chompanaidh at its own asking price, and the men who sailed them go into the pits the following season under A' Chompanaidh's contracts.

title: Silversmiths at Muileann bhàn
body: Silversmiths settle at Muileann bhàn on the road to the silver town and live by working the guild's bar into ornaments for the humans' market. Theirs is the one Dia-thìreach craft sold in an Tìr Thall under a Dia-thìreach name.

title: The washing-women name nighean an rìgh
body: At the stream below the camp of Àth ìseal, the eldest of the washing-women first says aloud what the wash-stones had for some seasons only thought: that a girl of the camp who does not age as other children age may be of the old line of kings, and names her nighean an rìgh. Most of the camp says they do not believe it and use the name anyway.

title: Macha's priests bless the coin
body: At Tolley's asking the priests of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg, the order of the capital and the crown, bless the Residency's new coin. The priesthood of Macha teaches that the two horses of her rite, Dubh Sainglenn the black and Liath Macha the grey, each have their due; the dissenting priests say the coin is only one of them.

title: Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir notes the order divided
body: Word of Fearghas mac Mhuirich's refusal reaches Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir within the month. Tolley, near his own retiring, does not send for him; Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-book records only that the order of Òrd Mhacha at the capital is divided on a religious nicety, and does not say what the nicety was.

title: Fearghas refuses to bless the second coin
body: Asked to bless Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's larger second coin as the first was blessed, Fearghas mac Mhuirich, now eldest of the order at Cathair dhearg since Beathag Ruadh's death, tells the order he will not say the words, holding that a rite for a wheel cannot answer a road that turns only one way. None of the order says the words in his place.

title: The second change of coin
body: The barter goods of the Dia-thìrich are marked down against the humans' coin a second time, on terms the humans' Administration alone sets.

title: Wool marked down at Baile Mòr fhionn
body: At Baile Mòr fhionn, where wool had been the measure of every bargain, a fleece is now worth by the Residency's table what a half-fleece was worth before. The town's weavers stop bringing wool to market and send it over the sea on their own account, until the Company refuses them freight.

title: The boats of Caol fhiadhaich sold
body: The fishing fleet of Caol fhiadhaich, unable to pay the new harbour dues in marks, sells half its boats to the Company. The men who sailed them go into the pits under the next year's contracts.

title: The dissenters go to Cnoc bheag
body: Priests of Macha who refused the blessing leave the capital's temple and settle in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag. There they keep the older reading of Macha's two horses, and take in custodians who have lost their seats.

title: Iain Maor
body: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor dies, and his son Iain takes the overseer's staff. Iain Maor is the first overseer schooled at the Mission; he keeps his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Dia-thìris.

title: Dòmhnall Maor dies at Muileann chrom
body: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor, overseer of the coal country five-and-twenty years and signer of the granary order that stood against Catrìona nic Eachainn's strike, dies at Muileann chrom in his sixty-seventh year. Word reaches Muileann chiar by carter, and the guild hall names him a hard man gone before a harder trade going on.

title: Fearghas leaves the capital's temple for Cnoc bheag
body: Fearghas mac Mhuirich walks north with eleven of the order who think as he does, to Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag. Griogair, eldest of those who stay at Cathair dhearg, walks with them as far as the north road and calls it two roads to the one rite rather than a falling-out.

title: The dissenters' first fire under the oaks
body: Custodians without seats and priests without a temple begin to gather at the forest of Cnoc bheag through the summer, until the grove holds near as many of one kind as the other. On the last evening of the spring Fearghas mac Mhuirich lights Teine a' Chlachair there and says the rite of the two horses whole.

title: The Levy
body: Tolley issues an ordinance, the Levy, by which every farming village in the west and north must send one in five of its able grown folk to the pits for two years. The villages are paid in marks, at the new rate.

title: Levy officers at Caol mhòr
body: The Levy's officers take their first tally at Caol mhòr in the north-west, reading the names of the chosen from a list in the humans' tongue. The custodians of the town write the names again in Dia-thìris, that they may know whom to look for.

title: The Levy in the north-west
body: The Levy falls hardest on the villages about Baile chrom and the northern concession, which had never sent crews to the pits. The Dia-thìrich of the concession are taken; its human farmers are spared.

title: An Togail read at Cnoc thais
body: An Togail's officers read their list at Cnoc thais, and the mason Dùghall Clachair hears his own name and his whole crew's called for the pits. Two days into the eastward march they are turned out instead to the headland at Baile chrom, where the fifth and last coast beacon is begun.

title: The wrong son taken at Caol mhòr
body: A guessed name is matched to the wrong face at Caol mhòr's reading, and a son is marched a day's walk east before the error is found. The right man is fetched in his place; the officers' own tally and the town's roll never afterward agree by one head.

title: The concession's human farmers spared An Togail
body: In the northern concession An Togail falls on every Dia-thìreach household while Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own leaseholders pay nothing, the officers' list giving the reason that the concession's tenants answer to Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's leave alone.

title: Baile ìseal sends its people
body: Baile ìseal sends forty-one of its people to the pits under the Levy, and nineteen come back when their term ends. The custodians' roll names the other twenty-two and the camps they were sent to.

title: Muileann naomh buys its way out
body: The custodians of Muileann naomh pay the Levy's officers in silver to halve the town's tally. The officers take the silver and the whole tally. The complaint is lodged at the Residency and filed.

title: The druid school's hall shut
body: George Tolley shuts the hall of the druid school at Dùn thais over a lecture on whether the humans' blindness to the coal's colour is a kind of sickness. The masters go on teaching in their own houses, to smaller rooms each year.

title: A gale strips the beacon's scaffold
body: A two-day gale out of the north-west tears the scaffolding from the third course of the rising tower at Baile chrom. Dùghall Clachair climbs the bare walls alone in the wind to judge whether the stone has shifted; it has not.

title: The last disputation at Doire chiar
body: At Doire chiar, a village of the druid schools north of the eastern workings, the masters hold the last open disputation of the school on the eve of Bealltainn, in the open air on the village threshing-floor. Its matter is whether a question may be forbidden. The Administration's clerk who attends writes that it may.

title: Teaching in the sacred forest
body: Druid masters who may no longer teach in a hall begin to teach under the trees in the sacred forest of Flidais near Muileann chiar, where the Administration has no building to shut.

title: Building the last beacon at Baile chrom
body: Work begins on the fifth and last beacon, on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, with masons taken by the Levy from the very villages whose fields they leave untilled.

title: Uisdean mac Lachlainn named keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom
body: Uisdean mac Lachlainn of the headland villages is named the beacon's first keeper, on the recommendation of the very masons who built it: Dùghall Clachair among them, who signed the letter along with two of his crew.

title: The masons of Cnoc thais
body: The Levy takes the masons of Cnoc thais to build the beacon at Baile chrom. Their foreman, Dùghall Clachair, cuts the names of his crew into the lintel of the lamp-room, the only writing on any of the five towers.

title: The five beacons complete
body: The ring of coast beacons is finished: Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg. They serve a trade that is by now plunder in all but name.

title: Cuan ruadh loses its trade
body: The ring of beacons finished, the Company's steamers round the island without putting in, and within a few years the old coasting trade of Cuan ruadh up and down the eastern shore dies.

title: Taigh-solais Baile chrom lit
body: The beacon at Baile chrom is lit with a coal flame, and the ring is whole. The Company's ships can now round the island by night, and the keepers' daybooks show the sailings doubled within a few years.

title: The draft read at Baile chrom
body: An Togail is read at the market cross of Baile chrom, first in the humans' tongue and then in Dia-thìris by a clerk who stumbles over the numbers. It falls hardest on the coast and hill villages; the concession farms to the north, worked by the strangers' own people, send no one.

title: The first harvest short
body: The harvest round Baile chrom comes in at less than half the carts of the year before, the fields sown thin for want of hands and beaten further by two summer storms. Uisdean counts the carts against his own earlier tally and finds the shortfall for himself.

title: Gorta Baile chrom
body: The Great Hunger follows a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements, made worse because the Levy has taken so many to the pits that too few are left to till the land.

title: Baile chrom goes hungry
body: The hunger is worst at Baile chrom itself, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields. The custodians write that more died there than anywhere else, and the Administration, which kept its own count, does not gainsay them.

title: The famine country
body: The custodians' roll draws the bounds of the famine country along the north-west shore and the hills behind it. Within them lie Baile chrom in its own shire; Ceann mhòr, Àth fhionn and Àth dhearg in the shire of Ceann mhòr; Muileann àrsaidh in the shire of Cnoc thais; and Achadh àrsaidh in the shire of Muileann àrsaidh. Thirty-four settlements are counted within the line, and the roll gives the dead of each.

title: Uisdean begins to write beyond the weather
body: In his second spring keeping the daybook of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Uisdean mac Lachlainn writes down more than the wind and the oil for the first time: that a farmer of his acquaintance ploughs alone, with none of the hands who worked beside him the year before.

title: The hunger at Doire ghlas
body: At Doire ghlas in the north the hunger takes the old and the very young first. The village sends its young folk to the camps for the Company's rations, and by the year's end it is half empty.

title: Inis mhin eats its seed
body: In the second winter of the hunger the townsfolk of Inis mhin on the north coast eat their seed corn. The Mission kitchen at the harbour feeds three hundred a day for a season.

title: Mòr nic Aonghais sends her son south
body: At Doire ghlas, a woman named Mòr nic Aonghais walks her fourteen-year-old son as far as the boundary stone and no further, by the coast's custom, and sends him to the camps for A' Chompanaidh's ration rather than keep him at a table with too little on it.

title: The kitchen at Inis mhin's harbour
body: With its seed corn eaten and no crop sown, Inis mhin is fed through the second winter of the hunger by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's kitchen at the harbour, which serves three hundred a day on fish broth and biscuit brought by sea from Cathair gheal.

title: Anne Colby's letter to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
body: With the relief ship idle at anchor, Anne Colby writes to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir at Ros dhomhain asking only who should be told to unload it. Eleven days pass before an answer that names no one and settles nothing, noting only that Àrd-mhaor Tolley has heard her concern.

title: The relief ship unloaded without an order
body: After a month idle in the roads at Ros dhomhain, the relief ship's holds are opened at last when a clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and a clerk of A' Chompanaidh set men to the work themselves, without waiting for either office to settle the dispute between them.

title: Anne Colby takes the kitchen at Baile chrom
body: Anne Colby goes north to Baile chrom to run Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's kitchen in a net-shed by the harbour, and keeps it through the worst of the hunger on the relief ship's grain and whatever the boats can add to it.

title: The hunger reaches Seann Bhrenn
body: The hunger reaches as far east as Seann Bhrenn, where the custodians open the old grain-pits of the Holy Age, unfilled in living memory. They hold only dust.

title: The relief ship
body: A relief ship with grain from an Tìr Thall lies a month at Ros dhomhain while the Residency and the Company dispute who shall pay for its unloading. Meanwhile the Mission opens kitchens at Cathair gheal and Baile chrom, and Anne Colby, come back to the island, keeps the one at Baile chrom.

title: Uisdean's hand on the valve
body: In the second winter of the hunger, Uisdean mac Lachlainn climbs to the lamp of Taigh-solais Baile chrom and stands a long while with his hand on the oil valve, weighing whether to let the light fail. He writes the thought into the daybook and lets the lamp burn on.

title: Anne Colby's private roll of names
body: At the Baile chrom kitchen Anne Colby keeps a book of her own, apart from Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's, writing every name she feeds and crossing it through, gently, in the corner of the page, whenever that person does not come again.

title: The Levy set aside
body: The Levy is set aside in the famine districts, too late for the harvest. It is not repealed. The custodians note that it was never used again, nor needed to be, for the villages had learned what it meant.

title: Cnoc mhòr walks south
body: Rather than starve, the families of Cnoc mhòr in the north walk south to the camps and take work under the Company. Their village stands empty for a generation.

title: An Togail read ended at Baile chrom
body: The clerk who first read An Togail at the market cross of Baile chrom returns to read that it is set aside in the famine districts, two harvests after the failure it caused. The custodians note it is not repealed, only set by, and expect no more of it.

title: The grass in Cnoc mhòr's street
body: A carter passing through empty Cnoc mhòr some weeks after its people leave finds every door shut but unbarred, and grass already coming up between the stones of the street, a sign that reaches the kitchen at Baile chrom before the village itself is spoken of again.

title: Robert Haskins Commissioner
body: George Tolley retires with honours. Robert Haskins, who follows him, orders that the custodians' council be consulted on the tithe, and then sets the tithe before the council has met.

title: Word of Tolley's retiral reaches Cill ghlas
body: A carter brings Peigi Ghlas, custodian of Cill ghlas, the worn word that George Tolley is going home with honours and that Robert Haskins, who follows him, means to ask the custodians' council its mind before he sets anything down. Peigi trims the shrine lamp and tells the flame, not the carter, what three such promises have been worth before.

title: Customs at Seann Dunn
body: Haskins opens a customs house at Seann Dunn on the eastern coast, and a Company store with it. The store sells the east its seed and its tools, and within a few years its ledgers hold the debts of half the district.

title: The custodians ride to Ceann àrsaidh
body: Custodians of nineteen settlements come in to Ceann àrsaidh through am Faoilleach, on foot and by cart, and camp along the inside of the town wall while they wait for the last of their number. Peigi Ghlas of Cill ghlas walks it in two days, carrying her cloak and her village's slate of An Togail's and the famine's dead rolled with it.

title: Aonghas Ruadh calls the custodians of the east
body: Once the tithe goes up on A' Chompanaidh's boards before any custodian's answer has reached Ros dhomhain, Aonghas Ruadh of Ceann àrsaidh sends riders to the settlements of the east and the hills, naming a day in am Faoilleach to draw up one grievance in one hand rather than let it be filed apart, settlement by settlement, as every single letter before it had been.

title: Coinneach Òg tells of the store's ledgers at Seann Dunn
body: At a fire inside the wall of Ceann àrsaidh, Coinneach Òg of the eastern coast tells the gathered custodians how A' Chompanaidh's store at Seann Dunn, opened as help against a bad year, now holds the debts of near half his district, entered against named households, and grows no smaller in any year, only more slowly.

title: The first petition
body: For the first time the custodians of the Dia-thìrich act together, and not settlement by settlement, and lay a written grievance before the humans' Administration. It is not answered.

title: The drafting argued over three days
body: In the hall behind the market square at Ceann àrsaidh the nineteen custodians argue three days over how to set their grievance down. An old custodian of the hills wants every death named; Aonghas Ruadh argues for one plain page that might be read where a long roll would only be filed. The shorter paper carries, and the old man signs it all the same.

title: The gathering at Ceann àrsaidh
body: The petition was drawn up at Ceann àrsaidh by custodians of nineteen settlements, meeting for the first time as one body. Peigi Ghlas, custodian of Cill ghlas, carried it to the Residency and handed it to a clerk.

title: Peigi Ghlas at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
body: Peigi Ghlas carries the fair copy of the nineteen settlements' petition to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir at Ros dhomhain, is turned back twice at the gate, and on the third day is shown into a stone passage smelling of lamp-soot to wait on a worn bench before a young clerk takes the paper, thanks her, and lays it on an unremarkable pile.

title: Aonghas Ruadh's letters go unanswered
body: Through the year after the petition is filed, Aonghas Ruadh writes twice more to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir asking only whether the paper of am Faoilleach was received and read. The first letter gets no reply at all; the second, in the autumn, is answered in a strange clerk's hand that the matter remains under consideration.

title: Two days on the bench in the lamp-soot passage
body: Before the clerk receives her, Peigi Ghlas is turned back at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's gate once and kept waiting a second day in a yard and a windowless passage, on a stone bench worn pale in the middle by everyone who has sat there before her, with the boy of Ceann àrsaidh who carries the second copy standing at her shoulder.

title: Three more names cut into the slate at Cill ghlas
body: In the year the petition waits unanswered, Peigi Ghlas adds three more names to the slate she keeps by the shrine door: two of a fall of stone at Baile thais, and an old hewer of Cill ghlas who does not come up from the gallery one evening in an t-Sultain, of nothing but the going down itself, done too many years too many times.

title: Peigi Ghlas trims Brìde's lamp at the year's end
body: On a frost-still evening near the close of an Dùbhlachd, with no answer yet come from Ros dhomhain, Peigi Ghlas climbs to the shrine at Cill ghlas and trims the flame called Brìde's square and clean, as she does every evening of her life, the one thing no clerk's pile can take out of her hands.

title: Àth fhionn signs
body: Ruairidh mac Thormoid, custodian of Àth fhionn in the south-east, is the eldest of those who signed the petition. He was born before the humans' coin was struck, and says so beside his name.

title: Ruairidh mac Thormoid writes 'born before the coin'
body: Ruairidh mac Thormoid of Àth fhionn, who walked to Ceann àrsaidh on his own feet and remembers, by his own count, a world before the mark was struck, signs the petition last and slowest, and adds beside his name the only line any of the nineteen thought to add: born before the coin.

title: Grievance first written
body: From these years come the oldest writings of grievance among the Dia-thìrich that survive. No hand is yet raised in them; yet in them it is first written that something has gone wrong.

title: Leabhar Baile thais
body: The oldest of them is a book of complaints kept at Baile thais, set down by many hands over some years: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. The custodians' copyists call it Leabhar Baile thais.

title: Griogair mac Aonghais tells Fearchar to sing it
body: Old Griogair mac Aonghais, who broke coal beside Fearchar's father before him, tells Fearchar that a column is for men who have given up hoping to be heard, and that he should sing the grievance instead of writing it. Fearchar carries the book back to Baile thais and begins working verses to the granary's short week.

title: Fearchar sits two nights over Leabhar Baile thais
body: A copy of the grievance book reaches Muileann dhearg folded in a meal-sack, and Fearchar Bàrd, a breaker of coal at the belt since boyhood, reads it by tallow light two nights running. He finds he can put nothing of his own into its columns, though he knows the granary's short week and the stream at Doire mhòr as well as any hand that wrote there.

title: The songs of Fearchar Bàrd
body: The poet Fearchar Bàrd, a breaker of coal at Muileann dhearg since boyhood, makes songs of the Levy and the famine, and they are sung in the camps. The overseers forbid them, and because they were forbidden several were written down.

title: Songs at An Taigh-òsta Grianach
body: The songs of Fearchar Bàrd are sung in the roadside houses of the east, and An Taigh-òsta Grianach becomes known for them. The Company's carters sing them too, the keeper writes, not always knowing what they sing.

title: Fearchar repays the docked wage
body: Fearchar Bàrd walks to Baile thais to repay out of his own wage the boy docked half a week's pay for singing his song, and the boy refuses the coin, saying he would rather have sung it than not. The song is sung again within the week, further than before.

title: Fearchar's first song sung at the pit-mouth
body: Fearchar Bàrd sings his first finished song, four verses on An Togail and the famine, at the pit-mouth of Muileann dhearg while the crews wait out a stopped winding-gear. It is carried to Baile thais within the month by crews he never asked to carry it.

title: The overseer's clerk copies the forbidden song
body: An overseer at Baile thais has Fearchar's song taken down word for word from a boy of the crews so that it can be shown forbidden, and a docker's pay is cut by half a week for the singing of it. The clerk's copy, made to condemn the song, becomes the only complete written record of it.

title: The Company's deep-water quay
body: The Company builds at Ros dhomhain a deep-water quay for the new iron steamships, which burn the island's own coal to carry it away. Fearchar Bàrd makes a song of that, the most quoted of all his songs.

title: The deep quay at Ceann chaol
body: A second deep-water quay is built at Ceann chaol in the south-east for the eastern coal. Its builders are brought from the coast, and the village of forty houses becomes a town of four hundred.

title: Fearchar hears his own song sung unknowing
body: Riding east on Comann an Airgid's business, Fearchar Bàrd sits unknown at An Taigh-òsta Grianach and hears six carters of A' Chompanaidh sing his granary song through, missing a line they cannot remember. He says nothing of whose it is, and finds the mis-singing harder to bear than the forbidding had been.

title: Baile thais walls its pithead
body: The Company rings the pithead at Baile thais with a stone wall and a gate, and pays a watchman to count who goes in. It is the first working on Dia-thìr walled against its own crews.

title: Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at the silver town
body: Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at Muileann chiar, a refiner of the silver guild to the end. The camp folk of Baile thais send men to her burying, and the Company docks each of them a day's pay.

title: The fire-ship loads at Ros dhomhain
body: Fearchar Bàrd, at Ros dhomhain on Comann an Airgid's errand, watches A' Chompanaidh's first iron steamship take on coal through the night at the new deep-water quay, burning the island's own fuel to carry the rest away. He stands at the rail until past midnight, watching the loading by lamplight.

title: Fearchar makes the ship song
body: That same night, sitting on the new quay's coiled rope, Fearchar Bàrd makes the song of the ship that eats the hill to carry the hill away, the most quoted of all his songs. He sings it first to the loading gang he stood beside, too tired themselves to do more than nod.

title: The wall rises at Baile thais
body: A' Chompanaidh rings the pithead at Baile thais with a stone wall and a single gate through the summer, and sets a lamed former hewer to keep the tally-book at the gate. Fearchar Bàrd, home from Ros dhomhain, walks the wall's length and makes no song of it that year.

title: Fearchar makes Catrìona's lament
body: On the walk home from Muileann chiar, Fearchar Bàrd makes the lament for Catrìona nic Eachainn, naming the coal-tub and the empty shelves she counted and the guild's bench where she stood to the end, and ending it, as her life had ended, without complaint. The dozen who had known her weep at it on the road.

title: The quay fire
body: A fire starts in the Company's coal sheds at Ros dhomhain and burns three days, taking two streets of the harbour quarter with it. The Company's inquiry finds no cause; the harbour quarter's own account has several.

title: The council without a high custodian
body: After the death of the last high custodian the Council of Custodians cannot agree on another, and sits for years with the seat empty. Robert Haskins writes to an Tìr Thall that this makes the council easier to deal with.

title: Artair mac Iain dies at Cathair dhearg
body: Artair mac Iain, Ceann a' Chùraim for twenty and four years, dies at Cathair dhearg at eighty years old. Word of his death reaches Fearchar Bàrd on the road home from An Taigh-òsta Grianach, carried faster than either fire or song by a rider changing horses at every post-house.

title: The carters sing the ship song for their own quay
body: At An Taigh-òsta Grianach, Fearchar Bàrd hears the fire-ship's carters sing his ship song louder and rougher than before, now that their own quay has burned, though none of them know the song or its maker. He sits again unknown, and does not tell them.

title: Tiormachd Achadh shean
body: The Long Drought lies on the island's dry season three years together, and bears hard on a people already worn thin by the tallies of the pits.

title: Iseabail begins her forty pages
body: Understanding that her petition will be answered with nothing but the words under consideration, Iseabail nic Leòid begins writing, over a winter, a full account of the drought's three years: the wells, the cattle, the fever's dead, the watchman recalled from Allt an Àigh, for whoever may someday want to know its cost.

title: The wells of Achadh shean
body: At Achadh shean, whose name the drought bears, the wells fail in the second summer, and the cattle are driven west in a column the roll calls a day long. Fewer than half reach water.

title: The dry country
body: The custodians' roll counts ten districts of the east as drought country, worst at Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh and Muileann chiar, and reaching down to Cuan ruadh and west toward Baile chaol. The Administration keeps no count of its own.

title: The cattle of Baile chaol
body: At Baile chaol the herds are slaughtered in the second summer of the drought, rather than watched as they die. The salt meat is sold to the Company for the camps, at a price the Company names.

title: Doire fhionn walks for water
body: At Doire fhionn in the east the women walk each day to the spring at Àth ruadh and back for water, half a day's journey. The custodians record it for the three dry years, and then cease.

title: Baile chaol slaughters its herd
body: With no grazing left within four days' driving, Baile chaol's custodian Ealasaid Ruadh orders the town's whole herd killed and the meat salted rather than risk the loss of it on the road. The town loses fewer of its people to hunger that winter than any other of the ten drought districts.

title: Iseabail drives Àth mhòr's beasts west and counts the dead
body: Iseabail nic Leòid leads the herds of Àth mhòr and Achadh shean on a day-long drive west to the tarn above Doire fhionn. Fewer than half the beasts reach water on their own legs; she keeps a private count of the fallen, ninety-eight marks by the drive's end, and of the eleven calves among them.

title: Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
body: The spring of Allt an Àigh, said never to have failed, runs on through all three dry years. Pilgrims who keep Na Seann Spioradan come to it from all the east, the first of them at Bealltainn, and the Administration sets a watchman to charge them for the water. He is called back after one season.

title: The pilgrims' road at Inis uaine
body: Pilgrims bound for Allt an Àigh gather at Inis uaine, and the townsfolk feed them freely, as the Old Spirits require. The town's own wells are low, and it gives away more water than it keeps.

title: Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's watchman recalled from Allt an Àigh
body: Riaghaltas nan Coigreach posts a watchman at Allt an Àigh to charge a set rate for the water. He is refused by an old woman of Achadh àrsaidh who will not pay a stranger for water that has run free since before his people came, and is called back before the season is out; the spring's keepers enter the word restored under his going.

title: Achadh chaol's households go down to the pits
body: With its grazing gone two years running, Achadh chaol sends its young to sign hewers' contracts at Cnoc fhiadhaich and elsewhere in numbers its custodian has never before had to record, families who had kept beasts and small fields for generations going down into the galleries for a wage that a dry year cannot touch.

title: Drought-fever at Baile Mòr ruadh
body: A fever of foul water follows the drought into the towns, worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been deepened into the old middens. Seventeen die. The Mission's report is the first to name the cause rightly.

title: The fever at Cnoc shean
body: The drought-fever spreads to Cnoc shean, whose one well is found tainted. The custodians close it, and for a year the town drinks from carts.

title: The Mission's wells
body: The Mission sinks deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom with a boring-rig brought from an Tìr Thall, and they hold. The custodians of the east set down the Mission's wells and the Company's tallies on facing pages, without comment.

title: Coll's report names the drought-fever's true cause
body: Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's physician at Baile Mòr ruadh, a young man named Coll, tests the town's water and finds it fouled by the old midden ground its deep wells were sunk through. His report to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's house at Cathair dhearg is the first that autumn to name the fever's cause rightly.

title: Every custodian of the drought country petitions Haskins
body: Each of the ten drought districts' custodians petitions Àrd-mhaor Haskins in her own hand, unknown to the others, asking that A' Chompanaidh's quota be set aside until two seasons of ordinary rain are counted. Iseabail nic Leòid rides her own petition to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and is told, as every other has been told, that the matter is under consideration.

title: Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise bores wells that hold at Achadh shean and Àth chrom
body: Following Coll's report, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise bores new wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom, dug deep and clean of old ground. The wells hold, and the drought-fever does not follow them; the custodians of the drought country begin entering Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's wells and A' Chompanaidh's unmoved quota on facing pages of their rolls.

title: Achadh chaol goes to the pits
body: Their fields burned out by the drought, the people of Achadh chaol in the north-east go to the pits for wages, the first villagers of the eastern farm country to do so. Their custodian writes it down as the end of the village, not a flitting.

title: The tally not lowered
body: The coal tally is not lowered in the drought. The custodians of the east, their joint petition unanswered, each write to Haskins alone; to each he answers that the matter is under consideration.

title: Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's rig strikes water at Achadh shean
body: A third well bored by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's rig on the moor above Achadh shean strikes clean, running water deeper than any well the drought country has dug, marking the drought's end there. Iseabail nic Leòid rides out to see it and adds the day to her forty pages.

title: The petition of Àth mhòr
body: Iseabail nic Leòid, custodian of Àth mhòr, writes the longest of the single petitions, forty pages listing her town's dead beasts. Haskins answers in two lines. Both survive, bound together by a later clerk.

title: A' Chompanaidh's survey marks the Hale cutting
body: A' Chompanaidh's surveyors, working out a new gallery above Baile dhìreach, mark the narrow customary cutting held by Eilidh nic Ruairidh's line for four generations. The agent Pryce offers Thomas Hale a small sum to sign it over rather than test A' Chompanaidh's claim.

title: Thomas Hale's suit filed at Ros dhomhain
body: Thomas Hale walks the three days from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain and files a claim at A' Chompanaidh's court, a copy of his grandmother's marriage roll in his coat and no other paper. The clerk gives a hearing date a full season off, at the back of the court's list.

title: Mairead nic Aoidh copies the marriage roll
body: The custodian of Baile dhìreach copies, under her own seal, the roll's page of the second year recording the marriage of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale in two tongues, so that Thomas Hale may carry proof of the line to A' Chompanaidh's court.

title: The first inheritance of mixed blood
body: A suit over whether the grandchild of a marriage between a Dia-thìreach and a human may inherit the customary rights of mining is decided, and the Administration makes the ruling wholly to its own gain.

title: The case of Thomas Hale
body: The child was Thomas Hale, grandson of the marriage at Baile dhìreach of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, who claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Dia-thìrich grandmother. Oliver Dunstan, magistrate at Ros dhomhain, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration owns, and that it owns only its own.

title: Dunstan's ruling read at A' Chompanaidh's counter
body: Oliver Dunstan's ruling against Thomas Hale is posted at the Ros dhomhain counter among a dozen others of the same list. It holds that no marriage entered in a custodian's roll, however old, creates a line Riaghaltas nan Coigreach recognises, and confirms the cutting to A' Chompanaidh.

title: Dunstan's rule applied
body: Within a few years Dunstan's ruling is used to pass eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each because some holder in the line had married a human or been born of one. The custodians stop entering such marriages in the roll.

title: Mairead nic Aoidh stops entering marriages in the roll
body: The custodian of Baile dhìreach ceases to enter marriages between Dia-thìrich and humans in her roll, judging that under Riaghailt Dunstan such an entry has become a paper a family's enemies may use against it rather than one that protects anything.

title: The cutting at Seann Bhral taken
body: A second magistrate at Ros dhomhain, citing Thomas Hale's case by name, decides a claim on a customary working at Seann Bhral against a cooper's daughter's line, married three generations back to a human pilot. The ruling runs to a single page.

title: The coast's custodians follow Baile dhìreach's example
body: Within the year other custodians of the western coast quietly stop entering two-tongue marriages in their own rolls, without any word agreed between the districts. The marriages go on; only the writing of them fails.

title: A cutting at Cnoc dhubh taken
body: Among the cuttings taken under Dunstan's rule is the old customary working at Cnoc dhubh, held by one family since the Holy Age. A great-grandmother of the line had married a human sailor; that is enough.

title: Griogair mac Ailein taken up at Cnoc chaol
body: Griogair mac Ailein, a breaker of the Cnoc chaol sorting-floor, is taken up by A' Chompanaidh's constables over a dispute at the pay office and refuses to sign for a short-weighted cartload he did not cut. He is held in A' Chompanaidh's lock-up pending a hearing never set.

title: The Lamp-Watch
body: A fellowship of pit crews calling itself the Lamp-Watch begins to meet at Baile thais and Cnoc chaol under cover of a burial club. Its first known deed is to pay for the burying of an old breaker who had died in the Company's lock-up.

title: Griogair mac Ailein dies in the lock-up
body: Griogair mac Ailein dies in A' Chompanaidh's lock-up at Cnoc chaol of a fever A' Chompanaidh's own surgeon records as already advanced when he was taken. He has no family living to claim him.

title: Thomas Hale sent for to read the surgeon's note
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh, a crew-leader of Baile thais, carries a letter to Baile dhìreach asking Thomas Hale, known along the coast for his hard-won knowledge of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's law, to stand at Griogair mac Ailein's graveside and read A' Chompanaidh's surgeon's note releasing the body.

title: The fellowship at Baile thais buys the ground and the box
body: Comann an Adhlacaidh newly begun among the pit crews of Baile thais and Cnoc chaol, calling itself Faire nan Lòchran among its own members, gathers its members' wages to buy Griogair mac Ailein's grave-ground and coffin, meaning his burying to be seen done properly in A' Chompanaidh's own eye.

title: Thomas Hale reads the surgeon's note at the grave
body: At a grave dug on the bare hill above the Cnoc chaol pit-head, Thomas Hale reads Griogair mac Ailein's release aloud in A' Chompanaidh's own tongue before some thirty of the fellowship, so that no clerk may afterward say the burying was done without A' Chompanaidh's leave.

title: Edward Vane Commissioner
body: Robert Haskins is called home after a quarrel with the Company over the price of steamship berths, and Edward Vane follows him. Vane is the first Commissioner born on Dia-thìr, at the Residency, and he speaks Dia-thìris, badly, but he speaks it.

title: Robert Haskins leaves Ros dhomhain
body: Robert Haskins, sixty-nine years old and Àrd-mhaor nine years, sails from Ros dhomhain after a quarrel with A' Chompanaidh over the price of a steamship berth. He never once, in nine years, spoke a full sentence of Dia-thìris without a clerk at his elbow to mend it.

title: Edward Vane answers the port custodian
body: Edward Vane, come up the same quay eleven days after Haskins sails, answers the custodian's customary greeting in Dia-thìris, badly and unprompted, the first Àrd-mhaor in living memory to do so without a clerk beside him.

title: The tram-road to Ros dhìreach
body: Vane lays an iron tram-road, drawn by mules, from the southern workings down to the coal port at Ros dhìreach. It halves the cost of shipping coal, and ends the carting trade of the villages on the old road.

title: Vane speaks Dia-thìris before the council at Cathair dhearg
body: Edward Vane goes up to Cathair dhearg unsummoned and speaks three sentences of Dia-thìris to Comhairle a' Chùraim before finishing through Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's interpreter, telling the council he has come home. The clerk enters the word exactly, wrong tense and all.

title: The night-shift order
body: For the first time the digging is made to run without ceasing, day and night, and the mountain is given no season of rest at all.

title: The night crews at Cnoc chaol
body: The order falls first on Cnoc chaol, where the Company's newest galleries are opened to crews working by coal-lamp in two shifts. The custodians' roll writes that the hill was given no silence at all, and leaves the rest of the page blank.

title: The custodian of Cnoc chaol writes the bare page
body: Vane's Àithne na h-Oidhche is read at every pit-mouth from Cnoc chaol to Muileann chiar. The young custodian of Cnoc chaol enters it in her roll and writes beneath it a single line, that the hill is given no silence at all, and leaves the rest of the page blank.

title: The day shift stands in the yard at Cnoc chaol
body: Three hundred hewers of the day shift refuse to go down for the night change and stand in the yard through the last light, saying nothing to the overseer who twice asks their meaning. No chant is raised and no threat made; they simply do not move.

title: New crews replace the standing shift within the week
body: A' Chompanaidh brings crews up the tram-road from the coast towns within a week, humans and Dia-thìrich both, and sets them to the night shift before the stand at Cnoc chaol is a fortnight old. The camp's own crews go back to the day shift they still have.

title: Muileann dhomhain shuts every door
body: The milling town of Muileann dhomhain refuses to house or feed the strikebreaking crews sent up from the coast. Every inn and counter turns them away, and the well at the crossroads is found blocked with stones on the second morning, by no hand the custodian troubled to guess at.

title: Baile ghorm's potteries take the lamp-body contract
body: The potteries of Baile ghorm take A' Chompanaidh's contract for clay coal-lamp bodies, thousands fired in a season on the same wheels that once turned bowls for the coast trade. Their own book notes them the first lamps made on the island for work commanded in the dark.

title: The night-shift strike
body: The crews at Cnoc chaol refuse the night shift, and within a week are replaced by crews brought from the coast under the Company's new contracts. The Lamp-Watch keeps the strikers' families for a season, and then its money is gone.

title: The strikebreakers of Muileann dhomhain
body: The crews that replace the strikers at Cnoc chaol are brought through Muileann dhomhain, where the townsfolk turn them from every door. They sleep in the Company's barns, and several go home the next season.

title: Faire nan Lòchran's purse runs dry
body: Faire nan Lòchran, keeping the households of the crews who stood at Cnoc chaol, empties its purse by the second winter. Its own reckoning, kept in an unnamed hand, closes the year's account at nothing, and beneath it notes only that the hill was not given back its silence.

title: Matthew Dunne's sermon
body: Matthew Dunne, the Mission's minister at Ros dhomhain, preaches against the night-shift order from the chapel pulpit, saying the Dia-thìrich are right that even the ground must rest. The Company complains to the Mission, and Dunne is called back to an Tìr Thall. The Lamp-Watch copies the sermon and reads it in the camps.

title: Matthew Dunne preaches the fallow year
body: Matthew Dunne preaches at Ros dhomhain that the Dia-thìrich are right, and that ground owed no season of rest was owed the same fallow year the humans' own scripture asks of a field. He does not name A' Chompanaidh; the chapel knows his meaning without it.

title: Matthew Dunne sails for an Tìr Thall
body: Recalled within the season on A' Chompanaidh's complaint, Matthew Dunne, three-and-thirty, preaches a last, ordinary sermon to a full chapel and goes down to the Ros dhomhain quay in the rain. Faire nan Lòchran has a copy of his fallow-year sermon within the week.

title: The camps begin saying Casad Dhonnchaidh
body: Among the Dia-thìrich hewers of Cnoc chaol Grodadh nan Scamhan spares more than it takes, unlike among the humans of the night crews. The old women of the camps, who know the telling of the hewer of Achadh dhomhain whose cough stopped on the night his daughter was born, call any such cough among their own Casad Dhonnchaidh, and say no more.

title: The lung-rot at Cnoc chaol
body: A wasting sickness of the lungs spreads among the night crews at Cnoc chaol and Baile thais. Unlike the Green Death it kills slowly. The Company pays the widows a pension for a year, then stops.

title: Iain Maor and the night shift
body: Iain Maor, overseer at Muileann chrom, writes to the Company that the night shift is killing his crews faster than it is paying for them. The letter survives because the Company filed it with his dismissal, which was undone a month later for want of anyone else.

title: Iain Maor dismissed and restored
body: Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir answers Iain Maor's letter with a notice relieving him of the overseer's staff for conduct unbecoming his office. His daughter Mòrag reads it to him by lamplight. Within a month, the crews having slowed the galleries to nothing, an unsigned notice restores him with no mention of the first.

title: The coal line
body: The Company opens its railway from the pits at Muileann chrom down by Cathair dhearg to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain. Its engines burn the island's own coal, as the steamships do, and the tram-road to Ros dhìreach is left to the mules. Within a year the carters' guild of Doire chaol, which had hauled the coal on Rathad na Mèinne for eighty years, loses the long haul. From the first day the Dia-thìrich call the engine carbad-iarainn, the iron chariot, and the railway the coal line.

title: Coal-lamps from Baile ghorm
body: The potteries of Baile ghorm take a contract for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year. The potters' own book notes that they are the first lamps made on the island for work in the dark by command.

title: The first coal train runs to Ros dhomhain
body: A' Chompanaidh's iron road opens from the pits at Muileann chrom, past the hill below Cathair dhearg, to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain. Iain Maor and his daughter Mòrag watch the first loaded train take the grade at a pace no mule ever kept; the crews name it carbad-iarainn before the day is out.

title: Fionnan born
body: A second child is born bound to the coal as Aisling was, half a century after her. So it is known that the thing is no chance of one birth: it comes of the digging, and it will go on.

title: Fionnan's birth reaches the cellar
body: The birth of Fionnan, entered by an eastern custodian among the ordinary births of the year, reaches Seilear Muileann chaol folded into a roll like any other. No hand marks the line for what it is; the copyists learn to find it again only once the word for the thing exists to look for.

title: The Administration's count of the people
body: The Administration counts the people of Dia-thìr by district for the first time. Its figures for the humans are true to the household; for the Dia-thìrich they are rounded to the hundred, and in the hill districts to the thousand.

title: Cailean mac Eachainn taken on at the cellar
body: Cailean mac Eachainn, a turf-cutter's son of Muileann chaol with a plain hand at his letters, is taken on by Na Trì Teaghlaichean of the cellar when Seònag Bhàn's eyes fail her past close work. He is asked first not whether he can write fair, but whether he can hold his tongue.

title: The count of the people copied in the cellar
body: Cunntas an Riaghaltais passes through the cellar among Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's business the custodians think worth keeping. Fearchar mac Ailpein remarks that it counts the Dia-thìrich the way a man counts trees, near enough for the timber and not near enough for the names.

title: The district of the outer coasts
body: The Administration makes the outer coasts one district and rules it from the harbour office at Seann Vell on Eilean ruadh, where its revenue cutters lie: the islands of the west and south, Eilean bhàn with Cuan dhearg and Cnoc chaol, and the southern edge of the windy coast in the far north-west. Its surveyors walk to the edge of the great moss there, which no chain can cross, and go no farther. Beyond it the district map is left blank.

title: The blank map of the outer coasts
body: A letter reaching the cellar notes that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's surveyors, walking the edge of the great moss beyond Seann Vell, found no way across it and left the rest of the outer district's map blank, and that the custodians of those coasts were no readier to be counted than the moss itself.

title: Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, last of the druid masters
body: Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, the last master of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean to teach openly in this age, dies at Dùn thais. No one is named after her, and the school's register ends with her death. It is taken up again only long after the humans are gone.

title: Seònaid nic Dhùghaill's death entered at the cellar
body: Word reaches the cellar that Seònaid nic Dhùghaill has died at Dùn thais in her seventy-eighth year, and that the register of her school ends with her, there being none of her house or pupils willing to keep it in the open. Cailean copies the line as it stands.

title: The custodians' rolls at Muileann chaol
body: The custodians of the east begin to send copies of their rolls for safe keeping to the town of Muileann chaol, which still kept Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of papers, beyond the Residency's reach. The copying is done in the houses of three families, and the copies kept in a cellar.

title: The cellar comes to know the eastern hills by heart
body: Winter on winter Na Trì Teaghlaichean of the cellar copy the whole record of the eastern hills, every birth and burial and fine and fever, until between them they come to know the district better than any single custodian who keeps only his own corner of it.

title: The second Muileann chaol
body: Some of the copies bound for Muileann chaol go by mistake to the smaller town of that name further north, and are kept there for years before the mistake is found. The custodians note that they were kept just as well.

title: Nothing of weight was lost
body: By lamplight Fearchar mac Ailpein and Cailean mac Eachainn match the recovered northern rolls against the cellar's own patched record of the missing years, and find that little of any weight had truly gone missing, only kept for a time in the wrong cellar.

title: The receipt for a delivery never made
body: Fearchar mac Ailpein finds among the cellar's bundles a northern custodian's receipt for a delivery the cellar never received. Na Trì Teaghlaichean learn only then that a second town of the same name, some hours to the north, has for years been taking in copies meant for their own cellar.

title: Cailean fetches the mis-sent copies
body: Cailean walks north on foot to the smaller Muileann chaol and finds three years of missing rolls kept whole and dry by an old custodian who says only that a roll is a roll, and that he kept it well until someone came to say it was theirs. Cailean carries the chest home unopened.

title: The word found at last
body: With two children now known, the custodians agree on a word for what is befalling them: fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as coal-touched. It is meant as a physician's word. It outlives that meaning.

title: The vote at the shrine of Cill ghlas
body: By the light of Brìde's lamp at the mouth of the oldest cutting, the custodians gathered at Cill ghlas argue two hours over a name for the coal-blood before a show of hands settles it. Cailean mac Eachainn, come up from the cellar to write it fair, counts more hands raised than not.

title: The custodians who named it
body: The word was agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, where the oldest cutting still stood open. They chose a plain word, fit for the physician's book. The roll gives the vote; who first put the word forward it does not say.

title: Peigi Ghlas calls the custodians to Cill ghlas
body: Peigi Ghlas writes to every custodian within two days' walk, calling them to the shrine of Cill ghlas on the night of the coming full moon to settle a name for the change that has now come twice upon a child of the pits, and asks the cellar to send a hand who can write it fair on the spot.

title: Cailean writes the word into the physician's column
body: At Peigi Ghlas's dictation, Cailean mac Eachainn writes the agreed word into a physician's register at the mouth of the cutting, then carries the leaf home to Muileann chaol for a second fair copy. His own hand is the first to set fuil-ghuail down among the ordinary births and burials of the roll.

title: The Line of Aisling found
body: Cailean mac Eachainn, a copyist in the cellar at Muileann chaol, finds in the roll of the camp at Àth ìseal the marriage of Aisling's father, Donnchadh mac Thormoid, with his line written seven names back, as the custodians write a marriage. He carries the seven names up to Tobar dhìreach, to Ealasaid of Clann na Ceiste, the last who says the lines, and she knows them for the line of Somhairle son of Ailean Mòr. She says Aisling's line to him backward, from her father to the mason who found the fire. So what the camps whispered at Aisling's birth is found to be true. Cailean writes the line in the margin beside her birth.

title: The third mark beside a birth
body: On the same page Cailean finds the birth of Aisling entered with a mark he has seen only three or four times in a year of copying, never explained in any book given him, and recognises it for the mark the camps' whisper had already fixed to one child in the settlement.

title: Cailean walks to Tobar dhìreach
body: Rather than report to the cellar, Cailean walks the hill road to Tobar dhìreach with the seven names copied onto a scrap of paper inside his coat, to ask whether a line so old could truly be Donnchadh's own.

title: Cailean reads the Àth ìseal marriage line
body: Copying the roll of the camp at Àth ìseal in Seilear Muileann chaol, Cailean mac Eachainn reads past the first name of a marriage line for the first time in a year of copying, and finds Donnchadh mac Thormoid's line carried seven fathers back to a name far older than a hewer's line should hold.

title: Ealasaid of Clann na Ceiste says Sloinneadh Aisling
body: Ealasaid, last of Clann na Ceiste who still says the old lines at Tobar dhìreach, hears the seven names Cailean brings and gives him Aisling's whole line back to Somhairle son of Ailean Mòr, the first king, telling him plainly that she has told him whose son the child's forebear was and no more than that.

title: Cailean writes the line in the margin
body: Cailean carries Ealasaid's recital back to Muileann chaol and writes it small in the margin of the Àth ìseal roll beside Aisling's birth, telling no one at the cellar what he has done.

title: The Administration's register
body: The Residency, hearing of the word, orders that any Dia-thìreach child showing the change be reported to the Commissioner's office. The custodians obey by reporting none.

title: The custodians' first return to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir: none
body: When Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir orders every child with fuil-ghuail reported to An t-Àrd-mhaor's office, the custodians from Cathair dhearg to the coast make their first return and report none, though every roll among them keeps its own quiet note of such births in a physician's plain word.

title: A custodian of Cill ghlas answers A' Chompanaidh's agent
body: Asked by an agent of A' Chompanaidh whether she knows of any child with fuil-ghuail in her district, a custodian of Cill ghlas answers that she keeps no roll of miracles, only of births and deaths, and that the office is welcome to search her books for either.

title: Peigi Ghlas dies at Cill ghlas
body: Peigi Ghlas dies at Cill ghlas, her petition still unanswered, having trimmed Brìde's lamp herself the week before her death and said that she had asked Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir once and meant to leave the asking there.

title: The third change of coin
body: The old barter of the Dia-thìrich is struck down as lawful payment altogether. Every bargain on the island now goes by the humans' coin.

title: The barter houses closed
body: The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish had changed hands without coin since before the Crossing, are shut by order. A clerk of the Residency writes that the ledgers are now "complete for the first time."

title: The fishwives of Inis mhòr
body: The fishwives of Inis mhòr, who had sold by barter at the river steps since before the Crossing, will take no coin for a week, in protest at the shutting of the barter houses, and give their fish away. The Company's clerks record it as a glut.

title: Marks borrowed at interest
body: Barter being struck down, the hill villages borrow marks at interest from the Company's stores to buy seed. Within a few years most of the villages of Muileann chrom owe the Company more than a year's crops.

title: The old market at Muileann òg
body: The old barter market at Muileann òg, where hill and coast had met to trade since the Holy Age, closes after its last season, and the ground stands empty.

title: Mòrag nic Iain Maor
body: Iain Maor dies, and his daughter Mòrag takes the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, the first woman to hold it. The Company approves her in a letter that calls her "a safe pair of hands."

title: Iain Maor buried at Muileann chrom
body: Iain Maor, third of that name to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, dies in the same house he held it from and is buried within the week, the camp's custom allowing no longer delay for an office that cannot sit empty.

title: Mòrag hangs the staff over her hearth
body: Mòrag nic Iain Maor, first woman to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, hangs it over her own hearth on iron hooks her father never had fitted, rather than keep it across her knees as he had.

title: Charles Merriman Commissioner
body: Edward Vane dies at the Residency. Charles Merriman comes after him with a small company of armed constables, the first standing force the Administration has kept on Dia-thìr.

title: The constable post at Muileann shean
body: Merriman's first constable post is built at Muileann shean on the northern coal road, a stone house with a yard for horses. The townsfolk call it the humans' second Residency, and do not mean it kindly.

title: Ruth Pallant teaches Hannah Webb the night watch
body: At Ceann mhòr, an old net-mender named Ruth Pallant tells the field-worker Hannah Webb of a night watch her own people's fisher-forebears learned from the island folk, kept in silence under a grey goose said to hold the sea shut. Hannah carries the telling of it home to the concession.

title: Hannah Webb's first vigil
body: In a field behind her landlord's byre near Baile chrom, Hannah Webb keeps the silent watch for the first time, and sees, or believes she sees, a pale shape cross the night sky before she sleeps through a whole night for the first time in ten years on the island.

title: The watch spreads along the concession's edge
body: Word of Hannah Webb's night vigil passes among the human labourers of the concession after a field hand sees her keeping it. Within a season a handful of others try it, and by autumn six or seven keep the field together on clear nights, spaced apart and silent.

title: Edward Vane dies at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
body: Àrd-mhaor Edward Vane, born at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir above Ros dhomhain, dies there in the bed he was born in. The custodians who come to acknowledge the change of stewards find, as they had all his rule, that they had liked him rather more than they meant to.

title: The post at Tobar ghorm and the custodian's rent
body: A second constable post rises at Tobar ghorm. The village's custodian, Uilleam Glas, takes the rent paid for the ground and clears the village of every debt it owes A' Chompanaidh's own store, to the written complaint of A' Chompanaidh's agent.

title: A barracks at Tobar ghorm
body: A second post is raised at Tobar ghorm, near the northern workings. The village's custodian is paid rent for the ground, and with it buys the village out of its debts to the Company store.

title: A grey-night vigil at Baile chrom
body: The Mission at Cathair gheal reports that human labourers near Baile chrom keep vigil by night in the fields, praying in silence under the sign of a grey goose, which they call the wild goose of the Spirit. The Mission cannot find whence the practice came, and calls it irregular, a superstition learned of the Dia-thìrich. The Dia-thìrich of Baile chrom disown it.

title: Manannan's priests on the grey night
body: The priests of Òrd Mhanannain at Ceann mhòr answer the Mission's report of the grey-night vigils. The practice owes something to the Dia-thìrich, they say, but to their own harbours and not to Baile chrom: the human fishing families of Ceann mhòr learned from them the night prayer to keep the sea shut, and the labourers inland keep it as a vigil of their Church, a night of silence under the wild goose of the Spirit in place of a prayer to Manannan. The priests call it Manannan's prayer gone astray, and do not admit its keepers to their house.

title: Minister Renn writes the vigil irregular
body: Obadiah Renn, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's minister at Cathair gheal's chapel, questions Hannah Webb about the watch and, finding no scripture that knows a goose, writes to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's house that the practice is irregular and its origin uncertain, though he does not call it wrongdoing.

title: Baile chrom disowns the humans' watch
body: The custodian of Baile chrom's lower row refuses any part of the human labourers' vigil, saying the town's own name should be left out of the keeping of it. The field folk, who had hoped to call the watch a thing shared between the two peoples, learn to call it their own alone.

title: The dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain
body: The dockers of Ros dhomhain, Dia-thìrich and human alike, refuse to load coal for nine days over the new berth charges. It is the only strike of the age in which human workers stand with Dia-thìrich. Merriman's constables break it, and the human dockers are shipped over the sea.

title: Seann Vell's dockers stay out
body: The dockers of Seann Vell, the harbour next to Ros dhomhain, refuse to load the coal sent to them during the strike. When it ends they are not shipped over the sea, for there are no humans among them; but they are not hired again either.

title: Lorccan born
body: A third such child is born, in a mining town and not a camp; the thing is no longer bound to any one place.

title: Manannan's priest names the goose gone astray
body: A priest of the harbour temple at Ceann mhòr walks to Baile chrom, watches Hannah Webb's vigil through a night, and tells her the goose she keeps is an Gèadh Fiadhaich, wandered from Manannan's own harbours into a shape no longer entirely his people's to reclaim or to stop.

title: The berth toll and the docker Tòmas Ruadh
body: A' Chompanaidh posts a new toll on every ton loaded at the Ros dhomhain coal berths. The docker Tòmas Ruadh, whom Daniel Webb once pulled clear of a falling beam, tells him of it, and the two speak for the first time of standing off the hooks together.

title: Merriman's constables break the stoppage
body: On the stoppage's tenth morning, Merriman's constables stand a rifle-line the length of the Ros dhomhain quay. The dockers, who had held nine days without a blow struck, go back to the hooks within the hour rather than test a tenth day against thirty grey coats.

title: The human dockers shipped over the sea
body: A' Chompanaidh takes the names of every human docker who struck and offers them passage over the sea within the week, once, with the plain understanding that it will not be offered twice. Hannah Webb watches her brother Daniel go up the gangway from the Ros dhomhain quay.

title: Raghnall Breac walks to Cill ghlas
body: With his knees gone stiff for the low work at Baile thais and two grandchildren to feed, the ageing hewer Raghnall Breac walks two days to the new galleries at Cill ghlas, where the pay is better and the headings still stand tall enough for a man to work upright. He writes to his daughter Eilidh twice a year.

title: Cian born
body: A fourth is born within a year of the third. Never again do the children of the undying generation come so close together.

title: Blasting-powder at Cill ghlas
body: The Company begins to drive galleries under the hills about Cill ghlas with blasting-powder shipped from an Tìr Thall. The custodians of the shrine ask that no charge be set within sight of the old cutting. The Company's engineer marks their asking on his plan, and sets the charges below it.

title: Powder landed at Caol ìseal
body: The blasting-powder for the new galleries is landed at Caol ìseal on the northern coast, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard. The town's custodians ask what is in the barrels and are told it is lamp-oil.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill given a seat at Faire nan Lòchran's table
body: The crew-leader Eilidh nic Raghnaill of Baile thais is asked, for the first time, to sit at the table where Faire nan Lòchran keeps its business, and copies its minutes into a second book kept in her own linen chest, where no clerk of A' Chompanaidh would think to look.

title: Fairley marks the custodians' asking on his plan
body: A' Chompanaidh's engineer Robert Fairley writes the custodians' request, that no charge be set within sight of the shrine at Cill ghlas, into the margin of his working plan. The plan shows the shrine as a bare shape with no depth drawn beneath it, and the numbered headings below are never measured against it.

title: Beathag Ruadh's roll at Caol ìseal
body: The custodian of Caol ìseal counts forty casks of blasting-powder off a ship of A' Chompanaidh, told to her carters as lamp-oil, and writes in her roll that the staves smelled of nothing when she put her hand to them. Her line goes unanswered into Seilear Muileann chaol with the rest of the year's roll.

title: Scàineadh Cill ghlas
body: The Rending: in the hills east of the capital, about Cill ghlas, the earth tears open along a fault beneath a common working. Dozens are killed, and a whole mining district is shut for a generation.

title: The first open fight
body: A mining death, which the Dia-thìrich workers lay at the door of the humans' carelessness, leads to the first bloodshed between the two peoples.

title: The shrine at Cill ghlas lost
body: The Rending swallows the old cutting at Cill ghlas, where the custodians had kept the rites through all the age, and its shrine with it. The custodians' roll sets down the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead; a later copyist has put them in the other order.

title: The district closed
body: The Company shuts the whole district of the Rending and fences it, leaving Cill ghlas, Àth chaol and their hamlets in the shires of Muileann dhearg and Muileann chiar without work. The villages empty toward Baile thais and Muileann dhearg, and the closed district is left to the thorn.

title: The meeting on the moor road
body: The folk turned out of the closed district send their eldest to the custodians of Muileann dhomhain, who meet them at a standing stone on the moor road below the town, lest the Company's clerks see them in the town hall. At the stone the custodians lend them the land at the edge of the fenced ground. The place is called Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, the meeting of the land.

title: Achadh chaol raised by the dispossessed
body: Folk of the closed district build a new village at Achadh chaol, at the edge of the fenced ground, on land lent by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. It is the only settlement of the age founded by Dia-thìrich for Dia-thìrich with no Company surveyor's hand in it.

title: The fight at Muileann chrom
body: The death that began it was a flooded gallery at Muileann chrom, where seven died after the pumps were stopped to save fuel. When the Company's agent came to the pithead the crews stoned him and his constables, and the constables fired. Four Dia-thìrich and one constable were killed.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill at the fenced ground
body: Eilidh nic Raghnaill walks to Cill ghlas to find her father's grave and finds instead the fence and the fallen headgear of the eighth heading. A constable turns her away from the closed ground. She writes nothing of the hour in Faire nan Lòchran's book.

title: Scàineadh Cill ghlas kills the thirty-one
body: On the ninth of an t-Ògmhios the fault beneath Cill ghlas tears open and the ground above the eighth heading and the old shrine cutting comes down together. The custodians' roll names thirty-one dead, among them the hewer Raghnall Breac, and says four bodies more were never brought up.

title: A' Chompanaidh fences the closed district
body: A' Chompanaidh's surveyors return within the week to fence the district from Cill ghlas to Àth chaol, and Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's order forbids any wage or working on any ground inside the fence. Households leave through the autumn and winter, first in twos and threes, then whole villages together.

title: Fionnlagh's warning at Muileann chrom
body: The overseer Fionnlagh tells the new agent Edgar Holt that the flooded ground under one heading at Muileann chrom has never gone a night without its pumps, drawing as it does from an unmapped old working above it. Holt orders the pumps stopped regardless, to spare coal for the winding-gear until a delayed barge arrives.

title: The flooded gallery takes seven
body: With the pumps idle overnight, the gallery at Muileann chrom fills to the roof, and seven men of the change of shift, Fionnlagh among them, do not come up. Mòrag nic Iain Maor stands at the pit-mouth as they are brought up and laid in a row on the wet boards.

title: Mòrag's testimony struck from the inquiry
body: At Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's inquiry at Ros dhomhain, the fourth Steward Mòrag nic Iain Maor carries A' Chompanaidh's own staff into the room and testifies that Edgar Holt ordered the pumps stopped against his overseer's warning. The commissioners rule her account improper and have the clerk strike it from the record.

title: Mòrag Maor at the inquiry
body: At the Administration's inquiry into the fight the overseer Mòrag nic Iain Maor bears witness that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order. Her words are struck out. The Lamp-Watch gets a copy of them all the same.

title: The grey fever
body: A fever of the chest comes in on the ships and runs over the whole island, from the capital to the eastern farms. It kills the young and strong more than the old, the Mission notes in alarm. The camps, already hungry, bury more than the towns.

title: The grey fever at Cathair mhòr
body: At Cathair mhòr the grey fever shuts the market for the first time in the town's memory. The custodians' roll gives the dead by street, and the longest list is of the street where the carters lived.

title: The grey fever at Dùn thais
body: At Dùn thais the fever takes the physician the Administration sent to treat it, and two of the Mission's nurses. The old houses of the druid masters are opened as sick-rooms.

title: Achadh chaol's first roll opened
body: Aonghas Mòr, once keeper of the lost shrine, opens the first custodians' roll of Achadh chaol on the day the new village's well is finished, its first line giving the well's depth and naming no shrine and no dead. It is the only settlement of the age raised without any surveyor of A' Chompanaidh's hand in it.

title: Faire nan Lòchran keeps the struck copy
body: A Dia-thìreach clerk who keeps A' Chompanaidh's own file copy of the inquiry's minutes has the struck-through page carried north to Baile thais folded inside sailcloth. Eilidh nic Raghnaill copies it a second time into Faire nan Lòchran's linen-chest book, the stricken line copied as stricken, and is given a full seat at the table that winter.

title: Tormod Buidhe's sister's boy dies of Am Fiabhras Glas
body: A boy not yet old enough for his first wage dies of Am Fiabhras Glas at Baile thais under Eilidh nic Raghnaill's sitting, having asked her, near the end, what month it was. His mother keeps his name from Comann an Adhlacaidh's book, and Eilidh does not ask for it twice.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill begins Comann an Adhlacaidh's book
body: Eilidh nic Raghnaill begins keeping a plain hand-written record for Comann an Adhlacaidh at Baile thais, answering to no custodian's roll, after watching her father Raghnall Breac carry twenty years of names in his memory and give none of them to paper. She means not to do the same.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill drafts An Dàrna Athchuinge
body: In Comann an Adhlacaidh's room at Baile thais, Eilidh nic Raghnaill drafts An Dàrna Athchuinge over three nights by a single coal lamp, with Griogal and two others reading each page back to her aloud. She writes its last sentence twice before settling the wording Griogal judges means it rather than asks permission to mean it.

title: The second petition
body: This one carries a threat beneath its words, not a plea. It is the first writing of the Dia-thìrich the Administration troubles to answer, and it answers with more guards, not with concessions.

title: The signatories of Cnoc dhìreach
body: Coinneach Ruadh, custodian of Cnoc dhìreach, signs the second petition, and in the same week is turned out of his post as clerk to the Company store. He is one of eleven who sign and lose Company work for it.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill
body: The second petition was drawn up by Eilidh nic Raghnaill, a crew-leader of Baile thais and one of the Lamp-Watch, and signed by custodians and crew-leaders of thirty-one settlements. It ends with a sentence the Residency underlined: that the hill would not be worked by people who were not asked.

title: A' Chompanaidh dismisses Coinneach Ruadh at his own store
body: A' Chompanaidh's agent at Cnoc dhìreach delivers Coinneach Ruadh's letter of dismissal at the store's door in front of the week's flour queue, the day his signature to An Dàrna Athchuinge dries. He is offered twice the chance to withdraw his name and twice declines it, saying a name once given is not the giver's to take back.

title: Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerk underlines the petition's last sentence
body: A clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir underlines in red ink An Dàrna Athchuinge's last sentence, that the hill will not go on being worked by people who are not asked, before passing the fair copy Eilidh nic Raghnaill made up the office. The custodians afterward agree it is the first sign Riaghaltas nan Coigreach has read a Dia-thìrich word and understood it.

title: The constables tripled
body: Merriman answers by tripling the constables and posting companies at Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, each with a walled store. The constables are paid from the tithe.

title: Barracks at Dùn chrom
body: A barracks for the constables is built at Dùn chrom, on the capital side of the hills, with room for two hundred men. For most of its first year it stands empty, for want of constables to fill it.

title: Ìomhar Seabhag
body: At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Ìomhar Seabhag preaches that Mòd's hunger has turned on those who have eaten the hill. The hawk-shrines of the west begin to serve as meeting-houses for the Lamp-Watch, and the constables do not yet know it.

title: The hawk-faithful of Ros gheal
