body: At Ros gheal the hawk-faithful fishing families, who had chased out the Company's customs officers a century before, raise a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall. The constables order it down. It is built again three times in a single season.

title: The hawk and the druids at Inis bhàn
body: At Inis bhàn the priests of the hawk and a few who still keep the questions of the druid school in private meet for a disputation, the first between them in living memory. It is written that it settled nothing, and that both sides afterwards signed the petition.

title: The grey fever in the north-west
body: The grey fever returns and settles in the north-west, about Baile chrom and the towns of the concession, where it kills humans as readily as Dia-thìrich. The Mission's hospital at Cathair gheal overflows, and for the first time Dia-thìrich and human sick lie in the same wards.

title: The first constables' company reaches Baile thais
body: Forty constables under an officer named Prosser march into Baile thais on the twenty-fifth of Gearran and wall the settlement's old open store within the fortnight, taking the camp's well inside the new wall. Eilidh nic Raghnaill and Comann an Adhlacaidh watch the company make camp on ground that had been common land that same morning.

title: The fourth shrine stands at Ros gheal
body: After the constables tear down the hawk-faithful's shrine on the Ros gheal harbour wall three mornings running, unnamed hands raise it a fourth time and the constables stop trying. The shrine stands afterward as the ordinary furniture of a wall that had always carried something.

title: An overman gives up his cot at Cathair gheal
body: In the crowded shared ward at Cathair gheal a Dia-thìreach overman of the north-west galleries gives up his own bed to a human boy of the concession no more than nine years old, and sits the night on the floor beside him. Hannah Webb writes of it to Eilidh nic Raghnaill at Baile thais.

title: Muileann fhionn shut in
body: Muileann fhionn, a Dia-thìreach mill town in the north-west, shuts its roads against the fever and keeps them shut for a season. Human carters of the concession are turned back with their loads at the town's edge.

title: The fever at Tobar fhiadhaich
body: At Tobar fhiadhaich in the north the fever takes one household in three. The custodians of the village burn no huts; they had heard of Àth ghlas in their grandparents' time, but judge it too late.

title: The road-houses make ready
body: The road-houses along the old mining roads begin to serve as waystations for bands of armed men. The roads make ready for a war not yet declared.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Òir
body: An Taigh-seinnse Òir, the great house on the eastern road beyond Dùn dhearg, digs a well in its yard and builds a wall round the well. The keeper tells the Company's carters it is against thieves.

title: An Leòmhann Buidhe
body: An Leòmhann Buidhe, the road-house on the northern road through the druid country, takes on six new ostlers in a single season, none of whom know anything of horses.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill reads Ìomhar Seabhag's sermon to Faire nan Lòchran
body: A fowler leaves a written copy of Ìomhar Seabhag's Seann Skell sermon with Comann an Adhlacaidh's door-keeper at Baile thais, and Eilidh nic Raghnaill reads it aloud to the room by the same lamp she drafted An Dàrna Athchuinge by. For once she does not write anything in the club's book afterward.

title: Aonghas takes the loft at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: A crew-leader from Baile thais asks Aonghas, keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr since Seònaid Bhàn's line came to him, whether the loft above his stable might hold men now and again with no questions asked. He agrees, and stops in time asking what they carry.

title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach walled
body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach, called the singing house since the songs of Fearchar Bàrd, raises a wall round its yard and sets a watch on its gate.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach barred
body: Am Buabhall Fortanach, the great road-house on the south-western road, bars its gates at dusk and keeps a watch on the roof. Its keeper, Tormod Buabhall, keeps a list of travellers and sends it up the road each week, to whom is not told.

title: The harbour of Doire shean
body: The little harbour of Doire shean, below Am Buabhall Fortanach, becomes the landing for the goods the house cannot take by road. The fishermen of Doire shean are paid in silver from the east.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
body: At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the northern road the stables are rebuilt with a loft for sleeping men. The Company's carters mark that the loft is never empty, and never holds the same men twice.

title: An Sligeanach Fad' às
body: An Sligeanach Fad' às, on the eastern road near the silver country, becomes the post-house through which the Lamp-Watch sends word from the camps to Muileann chiar. The silver guild pays its keeper's rent.

title: The runners of Àth fhiadhaich
body: Runners from Àth fhiadhaich carry the Lamp-Watch's letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town. They are boys of twelve and thirteen, too young for the constables to stop.

title: A boy of Àth fhiadhaich at Aonghas's door
body: A boy runner out of Àth fhiadhaich comes soaked from the ford into Aonghas's yard, asks for bread as any boy might, and leaves a folded scrap under the loose board by the stable door naming a date and nothing else. Aonghas burns it in the kitchen fire that night.

title: The fishermen of Doire shean paid in eastern silver
body: Old Coinneach nan Ràmh and the other fishermen below Am Buabhall Fortanach take to being paid, for certain nights never spoken of as work, in silver struck in an Tìr Thall rather than Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's coin. None of it is ever spent where a clerk of A' Chompanaidh might see it change hands.

title: Coinneach nan Ràmh's word on the loft at the Reòta
body: The old fisherman Coinneach nan Ràmh tells Aonghas that the loft at An Taigh-seinnse Reòta is never once found empty by A' Chompanaidh's carters passing through, and never once holds the same men two nights running: it comes and goes, he says, like the tide, and no man has ever caught the tide at its turning.

title: The Sligeanach's psalter
body: Marks for the loft at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr travel up Rathad na Mèinne folded inside a psalter, as innocent on the road as any priest's book, sent on from the ledger kept in the roof-space above the shrine at Achadh mhòr.

title: Achadh mhòr keeps the ledgers
body: The Lamp-Watch's ledgers of the money it has from the silver guild are kept at Achadh mhòr, a village near the house on the eastern road, in the roof of the village shrine.

title: Seònaid's house
body: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the carters' house on the coal road that Seònaid Bhàn opened again in the early years of the digging, is kept now by her great-grandson Aonghas. It is the busiest of the walled houses, the one the constables search most often and find least in.

title: The first stoppage together
body: For the first time the mining country stops work on one day in many places at once. Scattered as it is, the resistance of the Dia-thìrich can act as one when it chooses.

title: Muileann bheag in the north-east
body: The workings at Muileann bheag in the north-east, among the druid villages, stop with the rest. The town's custodian writes that it is the first thing the town has done with the hills in a hundred years.

title: The northern pits at Àth dhomhain
body: The pits north of the hills at Àth dhomhain stop with the rest on the day of the stoppage, the word brought by a runner and not by the beacon. Their crew-leaders are among those shipped over the sea.

title: Ceann bheag stops
body: The coal stage at Ceann bheag on the northern coast stops loading the same day. Its dockers had not been told; they stop because the coal stops coming.

title: The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal
body: The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal in the north-east, who cut stone for the Company's buildings, lay down their tools on the day of the stoppage unasked. Why, no one says.

title: The day the pits stopped
body: On the day of the stoppage every working in the Muileann chrom district halted at once, and with them Baile thais, Cnoc chaol, the silver town and the eastern pits at Ros fhionn. The sign was a beacon fire lit on the hills above Doire mhòr, which the Company took for a heath fire.

title: The coal ships wait
body: The Company's steamships lie six days at Ros dhomhain with empty holds. The agents at the quay write that they have never seen the harbour so quiet, and that it frightened them more than the crowds.

title: The stoppage broken
body: The stoppage ends when the constables shut the Company stores in every district at once. Forty crew-leaders are taken; thirty-two are let go without charge, and eight are shipped over the sea to an Tìr Thall for trial and never heard of again.

title: The fire on Cnoc an Rabhaidh
body: On 27 am Màrt, Aonghas watches smoke rise thin from Cnoc an Rabhaidh in a hard north-west wind, and every wheel within sight of his yard stops within the hour. A carter in his own yard names it a heath fire before anyone learns otherwise.

title: The heather burned thin
body: The constables burn the heather of Cnoc an Rabhaidh to deny the hill a second beacon. It grows back thin and late the following spring, and three years pass before anyone on Rathad na Mèinne speaks openly of what the fire had truly been.

title: Beacon hill at Doire mhòr
body: Doire mhòr, which refused the first contract and then lost its water, has by now but a few households. The beacon of the stoppage was lit on its hill by the children's children of Beathag Dhubh's people, and the constables burn the heather of the hill to deny it to them.

title: Fewer ships from over the sea
body: The keepers' daybooks at the five beacons show fewer ships from an Tìr Thall each year, and the ships that come are older. The Company's letters speak of troubles at home and do not say what they are.

title: Caol leathan's idle harbour
body: At Caol leathan the wool for the humans' market waits for room in ships that do not come. The merchants of the town begin to sell their wool inland again by barter, against the law.

title: Caol bheag's empty quay
body: The Company's quay at Caol bheag on the northern coast, built for the eastern trade, sees one ship in a season. The Company's agent there writes that he has been forgotten.

title: Tormod Buabhall's word on a house with nothing left to guard
body: Meeting Aonghas at the horse-fair after the ships have thinned to nothing, Tormod Buabhall tells him a house with no custom left keeps its gates shut for a different reason than before: a house that guards everything still has, behind its locked door, something it means to keep.

title: The forgotten agent of Caol bheag
body: A' Chompanaidh's agent at the idle quay of Caol bheag sees one ship in a whole season and writes to Ros dhomhain that he has been forgotten. So far as Rathad na Mèinne ever hears, no answer comes back to him.

title: Leave no longer asked
body: The humans' Administration begins to give commands without seeking the counsel of the Dia-thìrich at all. The pretence of leave asked and given is dropped.

title: Lionel Strake Commissioner
body: Charles Merriman leaves Dia-thìr in ill health, and Lionel Strake, a soldier, comes after him. His commission, read aloud at the Residency, makes no mention of the Council of Custodians, and he does not call on it.

title: Strake's commission read without the council's name
body: At Ros dhomhain, Aonghas stands in the market square while Lionel Strake's commission is read from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's steps: it names A' Chompanaidh and Riaghaltas nan Coigreach in an Tìr Thall, and, for the first time in any Àrd-mhaor's commission, does not name Comhairle a' Chùraim at all.

title: The council locked out
body: Strake has the council hall at Cathair dhearg locked and its keys lodged at the Residency. The custodians meet instead in Macha's temple, whose priests, who had blessed the humans' coin, now shelter those who petitioned against it.

title: The iron bird
body: Strake brings a flying machine from an Tìr Thall in the hold of a Company steamship and has it flown from a field above the Residency over the coal country, to count the workings from the air. The Dia-thìrich call it eun-iarainn, the iron bird. The custodians enter it in the roll as the first thing seen over Dia-thìr that flew and was not alive.

title: The edict of seizure
body: The humans' Administration claims the right to take any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich it deems needful for the widening of the workings. Of all the grievances it is the one most often named in every surviving account of what followed.

title: The seizure of Doire mhòr
body: The first dwellings taken under the edict are those of Doire mhòr, for a new shaft beneath the hill, and constables carry out the last households. The village that refused the first contract is the first emptied by the last.

title: Evictions at Baile dhomhain
body: At Baile dhomhain, the first camp laid out on paper, two streets are pulled down for a spoil-tip. The families are offered huts at Àth ìseal and marks for their timber; most go to kin in the hill villages instead.

title: The old man of Doire mhòr
body: An old man carried gently from his own doorstone by constables clearing houses under Àithne a' Ghlacaidh asks only that it be written down that they were gentle about it. Mòrag nic Iain Maor, come from Muileann chrom, carries the sentence home with no book to hand.

title: The iron bird seen over Muileann chrom
body: A flying machine passes twice over the Muileann chrom valley without beating its wings, and the crews at the pit-mouth stop their barrows to watch it go. By evening the district has a name for it, eun-iarainn, borrowed from nowhere and understood at once.

title: Mòrag's private book
body: Mòrag nic Iain Maor sets down word of the iron bird in the private hand her father taught her, kept apart from A' Chompanaidh's own tally, the same hand in which her struck-out testimony at the pithead inquiry had first been copied for Faire nan Lòchran.

title: Mòrag Maor lays down the staff
body: Mòrag nic Iain Maor, fourth of her line to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, will not carry out evictions in her district, and breaks the staff at the Company's door. Three other overseers give up their places in the same month, and the Company puts humans in them.

title: The silver guild arms
body: The silver guild of Muileann chiar, still holding its seam under the compact of a century before, begins to buy rifles through the eastern pirates. Its ledger enters them as refining tools.

title: Rifles by way of the pirates
body: The silver guild's rifles come ashore from the raiders' boats in the eastern waters, where no Company gunboat has sailed for years. The raiders take their pay in bar silver, by weight.

title: The council in the forest of Cnoc bheag
body: Custodians, crew-leaders of the Lamp-Watch and the dissenting priests of Macha meet in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag and make one council for the mining country, and choose Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for it. No human writing records the meeting.

title: Sìneag's ride to Muileann chrom
body: Sìneag, custodian of the camp at Baile dhomhain, rides to the steward's house at Muileann chrom to ask whether the overseer's staff can answer for the two streets pulled down for the new spoil-tip. Mòrag nic Iain Maor can offer her nothing that year.

title: The order for the third and fourth rows
body: A printed order reaches Muileann chrom's overseer naming eleven households of the camp's third and fourth rows for clearance before the new gallery mouth. A' Chompanaidh's agent Osgood carries it to Mòrag nic Iain Maor's door, and carries her answer back unwritten.

title: Griogar Camshron breaks his staff
body: Griogar Camshron, six years overseer of the north pit's eastern gallery, throws down his staff in his own yard within the week of Mòrag nic Iain Maor's refusal at Muileann chrom, rather than be the one overseer left holding wood A' Chompanaidh has marked for treachery.

title: The staff left standing
body: The overseer at the silver country's edge walks away from his office without a word and leaves his staff propped against the counting-house wall, the third resignation of the season after Mòrag nic Iain Maor's and Griogar Camshron's, and word of it does not reach Muileann chrom until winter.

title: Coinneach Ruadh brings word of the guild's rifles
body: Coinneach Ruadh, riding the district roads with unpaid news since his clerkship was taken, brings Mòrag nic Iain Maor word of Comann an Airgid's rifles and of a single council the custodians and priests mean to hold in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag before autumn.

title: Mòrag rides to the forest by night
body: Mòrag nic Iain Maor rides twenty-eight miles by night off the ridge road to Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, and is among those who raise a hand for Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for the whole mining country's council.

title: The order to seize
body: Strake orders the taking of Eilidh nic Raghnaill and the members of the forest council. The constables go to Baile thais and find the house empty and the town silent.

title: War
body: The Dia-thìrich, acting together across the whole mining country for the first time, pass from grievance to open war.

title: Coinneach Ruadh's ride of the twenty-eighth
body: Coinneach Ruadh rides into Muileann chrom on the twenty-eighth of an Gearran with word that the grievance is called across every mining district at once, and that Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir has already had its answer that morning from Muileann chrom and Baile thais both.

title: The beacons of the coal country answer
body: On the night war is called, signal fires long kept secret are carried openly to every beacon height the mining districts hold, ridge answering ridge from Doire mhòr to the silver hills, the first time the whole coal country has shown itself lit at once.

title: The stores taken at Muileann chrom
body: The war opens in the hills. At Muileann chrom crews under Mòrag nic Iain rush the walled store at first light, and its eleven constables yield without a shot. The rifles and the grain of the store are carried off before noon.

title: Tòmas Odhar's hand on the gatepost
body: At the fallen gate of the Muileann chrom store the old hewer Tòmas Odhar rests his hand flat on the gatepost and says he has carried coal out through it for six-and-thirty years and never thought to see rifles carried out through it instead. His words are repeated round the camp for a week after.

title: Mòrag takes the sergeant's rifle herself
body: Mòrag nic Iain Maor lifts the surrendered sergeant's rifle from the cobbles of the Muileann chrom store with her own hand rather than leave it to be gathered by another, the first weapon she has carried since she broke the overseer's staff the summer before.

title: The quay at Ceann fhada seized
body: Crews from the camps take the Company's coal quay at Ceann fhada and sink two barges across its mouth. No coal leaves the hills by water again in this age.

title: Pàdraig Reamhar scuttles his own barge
body: The boatman Pàdraig Reamhar, who built the larger of the two barges sunk at Ceann fhada with his own father twenty years before, knocks the plugs from her hull with his own hands and says afterward only that she had been a good boat.

title: Oswin Frayne rowed out from Ceann fhada
body: A' Chompanaidh's harbour-master at Ceann fhada, Oswin Frayne, is rowed out past his own sunk barges and set aboard a boat for any harbour still flying Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's flag, unharmed, on the crews' own order.

title: The siege of the store at Baile thais
body: At Baile thais the constables hold their walled pithead against the town for eleven days, as long as the first strike a lifetime before, and yield on the twelfth when their water fails. Eilidh nic Raghnaill sends them under guard to the coast unharmed. The Residency did not look for such mercy, and did not return it.

title: Bread goes to the half-loaf at Baile thais
body: By the seventh day of the siege of the walled store, the camp at Baile thais cuts its bread to a half-loaf a household, and the children who had at first jeered at the wall grow quiet and keep to their mothers' fires.

title: The constables of Baile thais sent to the coast
body: On Eilidh nic Raghnaill's written order, carried down from Comhairle na Coille by a girl of fourteen, Seumas Ciar sends the thirty-one constables who yield the Baile thais store to the coast whole and fed, over the objection of hewers who have buried kin to the same walls.

title: The crews meet on the moor
body: Crew-leaders of Baile gharbh and the other northern pits meet by night on the moor above Cnoc naomh and fix the week of their rising. Each brings a stone of spoil from his own pit, and the stones are left in a cairn. The place is called Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh, the meeting of the moor.

title: The northern pits rise
body: The crews at Baile gharbh and the northern pits rise in the same week, take the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and send the constables south on foot.

title: The coal road cut
body: Aonghas, keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, shuts the gates of the house across the coal road, and the men in its loft come down armed. The road between the capital and the hills is cut at its half-way stage, and stays cut.

title: Uilleam Gobha's first grenades tried
body: On a moonless night behind his forge at Muileann dhearg, Uilleam Gobha tries the first of his tin-cased grenades, with only his eldest son holding a lamp a safe way off, and says it will do.

title: A finger lost before Uilleam Gobha's care
body: Before Uilleam Gobha takes up the crimping of the powder tins himself, another smith of Muileann dhearg loses three fingers to the work, a loss Uilleam afterward says he was determined it would not cost him.

title: Uilleam Gobha's forge
body: At Muileann dhearg the smith Uilleam Gobha makes the Company's own blasting-powder into grenades cased in tin from the coal sheds, and forges pike-heads from rails torn up in the galleries. The rebels' council writes that without him it could not have fought its first season.

title: The capital rises
body: At Cathair dhearg the custodians break the Residency's locks on their council hall and sit in it again. The townsfolk hold Drochaid Cathair dhearg against the constables sent up from the harbour, and barricade the bridge built for the coal-carts with the carts themselves.

title: The council-hall lock broken with a coal-hammer
body: The custodians of Cathair dhearg break Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's locks on their own council-hall doors with a coal-hammer borrowed from the smithy across the square, and sit down again in the chairs shut from them for two years.

title: The coal-carts turned on their sides
body: The townsfolk of Cathair dhearg barricade the coal-cart bridge with A' Chompanaidh's own carts, turned on their sides and lashed together with ironmonger's chain, and hold it three days until the constables sent against it are called back to the harbour.

title: Cathair dhomhain joins
body: At Cathair dhomhain the townsfolk break open the Company's warehouse, the first building on Dia-thìr the Company ever owned, and carry off its tools for the council's companies.

title: Muileann mhin takes sides
body: At Muileann mhin, a river port just east of the capital, the townsfolk argue for three days, and then send boats to the council. Through the winter the boats carry food down the Abhainn fhionn to the capital.

title: The Residency fortified
body: Lionel Strake draws the Administration back into the Residency above Ros dhomhain and fortifies the Company's quarter of the harbour. The city below, Dia-thìrich almost to a man, neither joins the rising nor withstands it, and the constables do not trust it enough to leave the walls.

title: Strake's letter asking for a ship before winter
body: Lionel Strake writes to A' Chompanaidh's directors over the sea that the harbour town below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir holds itself apart from the fighting only until it judges which side will leave it better off, and asks for more men, powder and a ship before the northern passage closes.

title: The fight at the ford of Àth chiar
body: A column of constables and Company guards under Major Peter Ashdown marches up the coal road to relieve the hills, and is met at the ford of Àth chiar, where the rebels hold the far bank. Ashdown loses forty men and his baggage and turns back. The rebels lose nineteen, and the council's roll names them all.

title: The house swept at Baile thais
body: Constables sent under Strake's order find Eilidh nic Raghnaill's house at Baile thais standing open, its hearth three days cold, and the whole town silent around it, its people gone from door and window before the constables' captain can ask why.

title: The turnip cart to the ford
body: A cart with a false floor of turnips carries Uilleam Gobha's grenades up Rathad na Mèinne, past the cut, to the crews waiting at the ford of Àth chiar, the first of his work to leave Muileann dhearg for open fighting.

title: The nineteen of Àth chiar buried
body: The council's clerk Fionnuala writes down by lamp-light the names of the nineteen dead of Àth chiar and reads the list aloud the next morning; within the week they are buried on the moor above Cnoc naomh, within sight of the cairn raised there before the fighting began.

title: Ashdown's retreat through Dùn chrom
body: Ashdown's column falls back through Dùn chrom and lies a night at the barracks there. In the morning the town has shut its gates behind them, and the column goes on to the coast without its wounded, whom the townsfolk keep and nurse.

title: The silver town rises
body: The silver guild of Muileann chiar declares for the council and opens its armoury, and the Company's agents in the town are escorted to the coast with their papers. The guild's ledger notes that here alone the rising took nothing, for the humans had never held anything there to take.

title: The surrender at Dùn ìseal
body: The small constable post at Dùn ìseal, cut off by the rising at the silver town, yields to the silver guild's riflemen after a single exchange of fire. The east of the island is clear of human arms.

title: Dùn dhearg declares
body: The custodians of Dùn dhearg declare for the council and send it grain. Theirs is the town whose custodian wrote the only surviving defence of the Small-Burning Law, and their declaration quotes it.

title: Cnoc leathan's riflemen
body: Riflemen raised at Cnoc leathan in the east join the silver guild's companies and hold the eastern road. The Company's carters on the road are let go home with their carts.

title: The eastern pits at Ros fhionn
body: The crews of the eastern workings about Ros fhionn stop the pumps and walk out, and the lower galleries flood. The Company's engineers there go down the Abhainn chaol and take ship at Seann Mhorn for Ros dhomhain. The bridge on the eastern coal road falls silent.

title: Seann Toll shelled
body: A Company steamship comes up the Abhainn uaine and shells the coal stage at Seann Toll to deny it to the rebels, and sets the fishing town behind it burning. Twenty-three townsfolk die. For the first time the humans turn the island's own coal, burning in their boilers, against a town of the Dia-thìrich.

title: The Leaden Hawk company
body: At An Cupa Dàna, the inn at Cuan dhearg, seven hawk-faithful crewmen of the river towns wait nine hours for the council's letters to the Hawk coast, and leave with them at dark. Each wears a hawk cast in lead from the cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, and they are called Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company.

title: The Leaden Hawk walks to the Hawk coast
body: The company goes on foot and lightly laden: past the burned stage at Seann Toll, through Baile thais, over the hills by Achadh dhomhain and Cuan bheag, down the Abhainn ìseal by Ceann òg and Inis ìseal to Cnoc bheag, and along the Hawk coast by Inis bhàn, Ros gheal and Seann Skell to Inis mhin, some fifty-five miles in a little over two days. At every hawk-house on the way they read the council's letter aloud, and at Seann Skell they leave it with Ìomhar Seabhag.

title: Rumours at Inis mhin
body: At Inis mhin, the northern landing the humans had walled, the company lies twelve hours in a boat-shed and hears that Strake's constables ride the western roads out of Ros bheag every day. They hire a carriage of a carter of the town and leave the roads altogether.

title: The watch in the grasslands
body: A day and a half by carriage across country, off every road, brings the company to the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain in the western hills. They lie eleven hours in the long grass above the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession and count the constables' riders who pass. Their own list gives forty-one riders, none of them going north.

title: The Leaden Hawk at Inis thais
body: A day and a half more by carriage, still off the roads, brings the company down to Inis thais, six days after it left Cuan dhearg. The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the council's letter in the temple of the Stone. They will send no men, but they shut the harbour of Inis thais to the Company's ships and give the hawk-faithful the use of the Fianna's roads. There the Leaden Hawk's road ends, and its seven join the hawk company when it is mustered at the western Seann Skell.

title: Coaling from Inis mhòr
body: The Company's steamships take their fuel from the coal stacked on the quays of Inis mhòr, the river port just east of the capital, whose barges carry it down the Abhainn fhionn to the ships at Cathair dhomhain. The townsfolk set the stacks alight. The ships put in at Ros dhomhain instead, and burn their own stores.

title: The fishermen of Seann Chwen
body: Fishing boats of Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast, board a Company coaster at anchor and burn her. The Company draws its coastal shipping back to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.

title: The other Seann Chwen
body: The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, further west on the south coast, join the raids along the shore. The rolls tell the two towns apart by the names of their boats.

title: Cathair gheal behind its walls
body: The human town of Cathair gheal in the northern concession shuts its gates and raises a militia, but sends none of it south to the Residency. Its magistrate writes to both sides asking to be left alone. The council grants it; Strake does not answer.

title: Muileann àrsaidh closes its road
body: Muileann àrsaidh, a town of the concession, blocks its road with carts and keeps a watch on it against both sides. No one attacks it. The watch is kept to the end of the war.

title: The hawk-shrines open
body: From the shrine at Seann Skell Ìomhar Seabhag declares that the war is Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it. The hawk-shrines of the west become mustering houses, and a company of the hawk-faithful marches south to join the council.

title: The hawk company at Seann Skell
body: The company of the hawk-faithful is mustered at Seann Skell, the western city, a short march north-east of the human port of Ros bheag. It holds the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war.

title: The southern beacon dark
body: The keepers at Tobar dhearg put out the beacon, and the keepers at Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal do the same. Company ships feeling their way along the coast by night run on the reefs the beacons were built to light, and two are lost.

title: No relief from over the sea
body: The Administration's letter-books ask again and again for troops and ships from an Tìr Thall. In the whole first year of the war one ship comes, with dispatches and a few crates of cartridges, and sails again within the week.

title: The lines at midsummer
body: The lines stand at midsummer where the first winter of the war left them: the council holds the hills, the east and the capital; Strake holds the Residency, the harbour quarter below it, and the western ports. Neither side has the strength to attack the other.

title: Grain from Seann Warr
body: Seann Warr, the farming town in the south-east and not the salt port of that name in the west, has sent grain to the hills by the eastern roads since the winter. The council's roll lists the carts.

title: Dùghall counts the grain carts from Seann Warr
body: At the harbour quarter's upper gate Dùghall Dubh, once a weigher of coal for A' Chompanaidh, keeps the council's tally of the grain train down from Seann Warr, twelve carts against a capital's hunger, and sends the last load on to the sharing-yard behind the custodians' hall.

title: Hunger in the capital
body: Its harbour held by the Residency, Cathair dhearg has gone short since the winter. The custodians share out the grain by household, and the roll records that they took the same share as everyone else.

title: The sharing-yard of Cathair dhearg keeps an equal share
body: Through the siege the custodians of Cathair dhearg measure the city's grain out by household at a scale behind their hall, and take no more from it than any household waiting in the line before them, a fairness the city's own hunger remembers afterward better than any speech.

title: The burning of the tithe-books
body: In three raids the rebels destroy the tithe ledgers of the humans' Administration. Later chroniclers make much of it; it did little.

title: Dùghall puts the question to six men of the quarter
body: Asked by the council's captains whether the harbour quarter can reach A' Chompanaidh's counting-house without a shot fired, Dùghall Dubh puts the question first to six men born within sight of its roof, and all six answer that a fire lit quietly will hold Strake's men longer than a shot ever could.

title: The counting-house at Ros dhomhain
body: The first raid was on the Company's counting-house at the Ros dhomhain quay, within the lines. Men of the harbour quarter under Dùghall Dubh came in over the roofs, carried the tithe books into the yard and burned them.

title: The night clerk of the counting-house is taken without a blow
body: The counting-house's night clerk is found sitting on its steps in his shirt with his hands laced over his head before the raiders reach the ground floor, and Dùghall Dubh judges, from the look of him, that some part of the man had waited a year for the night to come.

title: Seven men cross the roofs in stocking feet
body: On a night of low cloud Dùghall Dubh and six men of the harbour quarter cross the net-loft roof-ridge to A' Chompanaidh's counting-house on hands and knees, in their stocking feet, and go down by rope through garret windows marked beforehand in daylight.

title: The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh
body: The second raid burned the Administration's tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, where the share owed by every settlement in the hills had been entered since the first schedule. The clerks were let go. The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared for the record, and their own people refused them.

title: Word of the spared ledger refused reaches the harbour quarter
body: A rider from Ceann àrsaidh brings the harbour quarter word that the custodian there asked one tithe ledger be kept whole for the record, and that his own townsfolk, naming the danger of any debt kept on paper, carried it to the burning pile with the rest.

title: The weigh-house at Muileann chrom
body: The third raid burned the Company's weigh-house at Muileann chrom with its steelyard ledgers, where the coal of the hills had been entered by the ton since the first contract. The rebels' own chronicler writes that the fire burned green.

title: The camps set the burning of the ledgers to a verse
body: Before the ash of the Muileann chrom weigh-house has cooled, the camp folk are already singing eight words of it at market, and the verse travels the coast faster than any rider: they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill.

title: The fight at Cnoc ghorm
body: Company guards and constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road are driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital. It is the Administration's last attempt in the war to reach the mining district.

title: Fearchar Beag sights Blàr Cnoc ghorm
body: Sent up to the net-loft roof with a borrowed glass, Fearchar Beag reads Strake's last sally on the eastern road by its riderless horses coming back down alone, and brings the harbour quarter word by noon that the guns have gone quiet.

title: The harbour quarter changes sides
body: After the raid on the counting-house the Dia-thìrich of the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter open the lower gates to the council's companies, and Strake is left holding only the Residency and the Company's quays. The same night men of the quarter burn the Company's flying machine in its shed above the town. It had not flown since the war began, for want of the spirit its engine burned, and nothing has flown over Dia-thìr since that was not a bird.

title: The captain of Muileann dhearg asks first for the wounded
body: When the harbour quarter's lower gates open, the council company's captain, a woman of Muileann dhearg unknown to Dùghall Dubh by name, thanks the gate-wardens and asks before anything else where the wounded of the counting-house alarm had been carried.

title: Cuan uaine opens its quays
body: The river quays of Cuan uaine, east of the capital, open to the council's boats. With them and the harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain both lost, the Residency can be fed only by water, up the Abhainn gheal from the sea.

title: Strake forsakes the Residency
body: Lionel Strake leaves the Residency by water, down the Abhainn gheal, with his officers, the Mission's clergy and the Company's agents, and takes the Administration to Ros bheag. The council's companies enter the Residency the next morning and find it stripped of all but its furniture.

title: The letter-books found whole at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
body: Where Strake has taken plate and account-papers down the river by night, Dùghall Dubh finds a room of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books left standing untouched on an unlocked shelf, thirty years of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own correspondence with an Tìr Thall, and sends word of it to the council's clerks that evening.

title: Prentice the counting-house clerk goes down the river
body: Dùghall Dubh learns from a clerk taken at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that Prentice, who weighed coal beside him nine years at the counting-house scales, went down the river with Strake's household the night Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir fell, leaving the ledgers he had kept behind as ash.

title: Clerks of the council begin to read Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books
body: By the morning after Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir falls, a table stands in its stripped hall with the first of the letter-books open under a lamp, and men who have never before read a stranger's hand bend over the close foreign script with the patience of a scale that will not balance.

title: Ros bheag the last seat
body: At Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the early years, Strake sets up what is left of the Administration. The human families of the west and south, a few thousand in all, gather behind its walls.

title: Outposts at Ros àrsaidh
body: Strake posts constables at Ros àrsaidh, north of Ros bheag, to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh. The townsfolk bring them food and news, and the news is always a day old.

title: Hunger in Ros bheag
body: The roads cut and no ships coming from over the sea, Ros bheag runs short of food within months. By Strake's order the Company's stores are opened to the human families and the Dia-thìrich townsfolk alike, the one deed of his the Dia-thìrich rolls give him credit for.

title: Cuan shean refuses the humans
body: The custodians of Cuan shean, where the first humans came ashore, shut its harbour to Company ships. The council's roll sets it down and says no more.

title: The families of Baile dhìreach
body: At Baile dhìreach each side asks the children of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, which they are. Most of them, it is written, would not answer, and neither side made them.

title: The last ship from the east
body: The last ship known to come from an Tìr Thall anchors at Ros bheag at Samhain. She brings no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and sails again on the next tide with as many passengers as she can hold.

title: The truce of Àth àrsaidh
body: Envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession, and agree a truce: the humans left on Dia-thìr shall withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council shall leave the towns of the concession standing.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns
body: The truce names Baile Mòr ruadh, the greatest town of the north-west, as the place where the columns will be received. Its Dia-thìrich folk are given the choice of staying or going south. The roll gives the numbers of each, and they are close.

title: The columns go north
body: The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west march north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies. Few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and none was helped.

title: The columns at Àth chrom
body: The columns cross the ford at Àth chrom on their way north. The custodians of the town stand at the ford and count them over, and it is the last count the Dia-thìrich make of the humans on Dia-thìr in this age.

title: Àth leathan
body: At Àth leathan, the last stage before the northern country, the columns camp for a night. The custodians of the town write that the humans asked the name of the place, and that several of them wrote it down.

title: The ship that sailed east
body: Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, sails from Cuan shean for an Tìr Thall with his officers in the last ship on the island able to make the crossing. The keeper at Taigh-solais Baile chrom sets down her passing in his daybook. Nothing on Dia-thìr tells of her coming anywhere.

title: The beacons relit
body: The council orders the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, are still kept, with nothing in them.

title: The rolls sent to Muileann chaol
body: The custodians send what survives of the rolls of the age, their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais and the letter-books left in the Residency, to the cellars at Muileann chaol. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake is not known.

title: Coinneach Beag puts his name forward
body: When the crew-leaders of the river towns ask for seven men who can keep their feet on a hill road and hold their tongues, Coinneach Beag, a boatman of Cuan dhearg raised on the river since boyhood and no stranger to A' Chompanaidh's rule over his own family, puts his name forward before he has properly decided to.

title: The letter read at a nameless hawk-house
body: On the road past Seann Toll, Coinneach Beag reads the council's letter aloud in a bare hawk-house of six benches, his voice unsteady at first; an old woman by the fire answers only that it has come to that, and no one else speaks.

title: The boy of Baile thais shows the wall
body: Passing through Baile thais, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe is shown by a boy of nine or ten the marks on the store's outer wall from the siege's eleven days, told with more pride than fear, the town's memory of its own fight already settling into telling.

title: Word of Ashdown's retreat reaches Cuan dhearg
body: Through the fire's talk at Cuan dhearg the news of Ashdown's beaten column travels garbled and half-doubted: that Dùn chrom shut its gates on the soldiers who had slept a night in its barracks, and let the column go on to the coast without its own wounded, whom the town kept to nurse.

title: The seven wait nine hours at An Cupa Dàna
body: Seven men of the river towns gather at the inn of An Cupa Dàna and wait nine hours for the council's last letter, and in the waiting learn one another's names and fears: Coinneach Beag, Gillebrìde the hawk-priest's server, the coal-barge brothers, Ailig, and Pàdraig Buidhe, who says nothing at all.

title: The lead hawks given out
body: Each of the seven is given a small hawk cast in lead from cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, worn at the throat on a cord of tarred twine as a token of the council's trust to whoever along the road might read it rightly.

title: The carter of Inis mhin
body: At Inis mhin, warned that Strake's constables now ride the western roads out of Ros bheag daily, the seven hire a carter with a covered cart and a mule, and leave the road for cart-tracks and field-edges known to no map, asking nothing of what he carries.

title: Eleven hours in the grass above Tobar dhomhain
body: Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lies eleven hours in the long grass above the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession, counting every rider that passes; Gillebrìde keeps the tally on a strip of bark, a line for each rider and a cross for each leader.

title: Forty-one riders, all going south
body: The company's count ends at forty-one constables' riders in a single day, and not one riding north; Gillebrìde reads the sign as Strake's attention turned elsewhere, and Coinneach Beag cannot say whether the empty road is the safest on the island or the most dangerous.

title: The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the letter
body: In the low temple above the harbour at Inis thais, the priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the council's letter through in silence and will send no men, but shut the harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships and open an Fhianna's own roads to the hawk-faithful.

title: The seven become one company
body: At the muster of the hawk-faithful under Ìomhar Seabhag at the western Seann Skell, the seven of Cuan dhearg stand in the company's first rank and are told they are one thing now, with one name: Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe.

title: Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill puts out her own light
body: At Tobar dhearg, Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill, keeper of the light since her mother's death, climbs the tower alone on a night of her own choosing and puts out the beacon on her own authority, before any order from the council reaches her; the order finds the tower already dark.

title: Word of the burned coal at Inis mhòr
body: At the Seann Skell muster Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe hears that the townsfolk of Inis mhòr fired their own coal stacks rather than let a ship of A' Chompanaidh carry them off to burn against another Seann Toll, and that the ships put in at Ros dhomhain and burned their own stores instead.

title: Coinneach Beag stands his first watch
body: By midsummer Coinneach Beag stands watch on the road north of Ros bheag with a rifle he has not yet fired, still turning over the forty-one riders and what road Strake judged worth watching instead, while the war's lines hold unmoved from where the first winter left them.

title: Eilidh Hale will not choose
body: Asked on the steps of the council hall at Baile dhìreach which people she is, Eilidh Hale, who has kept the joint council's books three winters running, answers only that she keeps the books, and no more. She is neither pressed further nor turned away, and stays in the town through the rest of the war.

title: Hannah Webb walks north
body: Hannah Webb, who keeps her vigil behind Baile chrom and nursed at Cathair gheal through the fever, walks out to meet the columns at the concession's southern edge and walks back north with them, an old woman of the last families out of Cuan shean on her arm who will not be carried.

title: The keys given up at Cuan shean
body: The harbour officers of Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh ride two days south with their towns' chests of harbour keys and set them at Strake's feet on the quay at Cuan shean before his ship sails, saying only that the accounts are even and that who wants the keys after is not theirs to decide. Strake takes the chests aboard with him.

title: The sealed letter kept close
body: The last ship from over the sea puts a single sealed letter ashore for An t-Àrd-mhaor at Ros bheag before filling her berths with passengers and standing out again. Strake reads it alone by a window over the harbour, burns its wrapping in the grate, and is seen to carry the letter itself inside his coat for the rest of the winter. No clerk of his ever claims to have read a word of it.

title: Two scribes, one truce
body: At the meeting-house of Àth àrsaidh, envoys of Comhairle na Coille and of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach set down the truce of the withdrawal in two hands at once, neither side trusting the other's clerk alone with the writing of it. Three days of argument over the line on the map are settled in less than an hour once the terms are agreed.

title: A name given at Àth leathan
body: Camped a last night before the north country, several of the marching humans ask the custodians of Àth leathan the name of the place and write it down for themselves. A child born that same night under a hedge by lantern-light is given the name as though it were a christening name, none other yet being settled on her.

title: The keeper watches her out of sight
body: From the gallery of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Lachlann mac Uisdein watches Lionel Strake's ship stand out north-about past the headland at evening, showing one light at her stern until the dark of sea and sky close over it. He writes the passing into his father's daybook in his father's own words for a night with no ship left to come.

title: Cha tàinig long
body: Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh burn again from Baile chrom to Tobar dhearg, relit by the council's order, but for nothing that comes. The keepers go on filling their daybooks through the winter, oil and wind and a line where a ship would once have stood, until most of them stop troubling to leave the line at all and simply write the three words that were once Uisdean mac Lachlainn's alone.

title: The Severance
body: The war ends, and the crossing itself is shut: whatever way let the humans reach Dia-thìr closes. The humans still on the island are led into the northern country that their children's children hold to this day. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in the wake of it.
